New Delhi, Sep 14: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Droupadi Murmu on Monday congratulated the Indian women's cricket team for winning the T20 Asia Cup Championship, with both terming the triumph a proud moment for Indian.
Harmanpreet Kaur-led Team India defeated Sri Lanka by 72 runs in Dubai on Sunday to lift their record-extending eighth Asia Cup title.
"A proud moment for Indian cricket! Congratulations to the Women's team on winning the Asia Cup," Modi said in a post on 'X'.
The prime minister said the confidence of the players, their consistency and remarkable spirit were on full display throughout the tournament.
"May this triumph inspire millions of youngsters across the country to play more and shine," he said
The President of India, Droupadi Murmu, also expressed pleasure over the victory, saying that the girls in blue are a source of inspiration for our youth, especially our daughters. "They are a source of great inspiration for our youth, especially our daughters. I am sure, they will script many more inspiring chapters of success and excellence," she said in a post on X.
"My heartiest congratulations to all the members of Team India on winning Women's T20 Asia Cup Championship 2026. They played superbly as a team throughout the tournament, winning all the matches. They have done the country proud," the President said.

BioNTech said its experimental drug gotistobart nearly doubled the median survival of patients with an aggressive form of lung cancer compared to chemotherapy.
Patients treated with gotistobart lived for a median 18.5 months, compared with 10 months for those given the standard-of-care chemotherapy, BioNTech said in a release Monday. The updated results are from a late-stage study evaluating patients with metastatic squamous nonsmall cell lung cancer whose disease progressed on prior immunotherapy and chemotherapy.
Earlier data showed that gotistobart reduced the risk of death by 54% compared to chemotherapy, though median overall survival wasn’t reached at the time.
“Current survival expectations with established therapies remain less than a year, and despite numerous development efforts, chemotherapy has remained the standard of care in this setting for more than a decade,” said Rama Balaraman, a principal investigator in the trial and medical oncologist.
If the survival benefit is confirmed in the next leg of the late-stage study, the drug could provide a chemotherapy-free option and “transform the standard of care” for this patient population, Balaraman added.
The results bolster BioNTech’s efforts to bring multiple cancer medicines to market by 2030 as sales of its COVID-19 vaccine decline. The German company is also undergoing a leadership transition, with co-founders Ugur Sahin and Ozlem Tureci preparing to leave the company by the end of the year for a new venture. Guido Oelkers is set to succeed Sahin as the company’s chief executive officer by February at the latest.
The company suffered a setback last month when it abandoned a study for a personalized vaccine for colorectal cancer patients. Hopes for the mRNA treatment had been raised by the success of rival drugmakers Moderna and Merck for a treatment of the same class for melanoma.
For gotistobart, BioNTech is collaborating with U.S. company OncoC4. The drug is designed to help the immune system attack cancer by removing cells that help tumors evade the body’s defenses. BioNTech said the safety profile of the drug was “consistent with previously reported data and remained manageable.”

A Bengaluru commercial court has temporarily restrained hyperlocal news startup Way2News from using confidential information and intellectual property belonging to AppsForBharat, the operator of spiritual tech platform Sri Mandir. The court passed the ad-interim ex parte injunction on Thursday (September 10) in a commercial suit filed by AppsForBharat against Way2News and its former employee Shivam Kumar Singh. The order restrains Way2News, its directors, employees, agents, and others acting on its behalf from using AppsForBharat’s confidential information, intellectual property, and other data allegedly received from Singh until the next hearing. Since the order was passed ex parte, Way2News and Singh were not heard before the interim relief was granted. Inc42 has reached out to AppsForBharat and Way2News for comments on the development. The story will be updated on receiving a response. What AppsForBharat Has Alleged According to court filings accessed by Inc42, Singh worked as a senior operations associate at AppsForBharat and was involved in coordinating with priests and temples and managing on-ground pooja operations. He resigned on August 3, 2026, citing “personal exigencies”, and his last working day was August 7. AppsForBharat alleged that one of its employees received a request from Singh on August 25 seeking access to the startup’s Google Drive. The request was allegedly sent using a Way2News email address, prompting AppsForBharat to launch an internal investigation. The startup claimed the drive contained videos, marketing material, operational information, financial data, and details of suppliers and customers. AppsForBharat further alleged that Singh joined Way2News in violation of the non-compete provision in his employment agreement and shared its confidential information with the platform. It also accused Way2News’ spiritual tech platform Veda Mandir of publishing promotional videos identical to marketing material created by Sri Mandir. AppsForBharat also accused Way2News of approaching its employees and customers and sought separate ex parte injunctions against such solicitation. However, the court declined to grant these two injunctions without hearing the defendants and issued notices to them instead. The current injunction is limited to Way2News’ alleged use of AppsForBharat’s confidential information. The interim order does not constitute a final finding of data theft or copyright infringement. AppsForBharat Seeks ₹1 Cr AppsForBharat has sought ₹1 Cr in compensation for alleged losses and contractual breaches. It has also sought the return of its confidential material, permanent injunctions against its misuse and the solicitation of employees and customers, and an account of revenue generated through its alleged unauthorised use. Founded in 2020 by Prashant Sachan, AppsForBharat’s Sri Mandir app enables users to book online pujas and offerings, receive prasad, and access devotional content. In July 2025, AppsForBharat raised ₹175 Cr in a Series C round led by Susquehanna Asia VC. It has raised about $65 Mn to date. Meanwhile, Way2News was founded in 2015 by Raju Vanapala. It primarily offers short-format hyperlocal news in vernacular languages. It later entered spiritual tech with Veda Mandir, which facilitates pooja, chadhava, and daan offerings at temples. The startup raised $14 Mn in a WestBridge Capital-led Series B round in 2024 and has raised nearly $30 Mn to date.

Apple is now rolling out its iOS 27 update to compatible devices today, alongside the watchOS 27, iPadOS 27, and visionOS 27 updates. Siri AI is the headline feature across all four updates, the delayed AI-powered overhaul of the Siri assistant. Siri AI is available as a beta today for English-only devices, and Apple says support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish is coming in October.
Apple releases iOS 27 with Siri AI overhaul
watchOS 27, iPadOS 27, and visionOS 27 also debut today.
Siri AI isn’t the only big feature in iOS 27, though. Apple is adding a new Liquid Glass opacity slider that lets you pick between a clearer UI or a more frosty one. A lot of built-in apps are also getting new icon designs, with subtle tweaks to colors, as well as extra large widgets and different volume settings for ringtones, alarms, timers, and alerts and system sounds.
watchOS 27 gets new Workout Buddy features, a new tap gesture, some Liquid Glass refinements, new Smart Stack suggestions, and an improved Find My app. Apple has also improved file transfer speeds to external drives on an iPad, sped up browsing on iPad, and added smoother connectivity moving between Wi-Fi and mobile data on iPads.
Apple Vision Pro users are also getting the Siri AI overhaul today as part of visionOS 27, as well as the ability to preview notifications by using your eyes, UI updates to the Control Center, improvements to Wi-Fi connectivity, and support for using the panoramas you’ve photographed as immersive scenes and environments.
The iOS 27 update will be available for iPhone 11 and iPhone SE (2nd gen) and later devices, with watchOS 27 available for Apple Watch SE 3, Apple Watch Series 9 and above, and Apple Watch Ultra 2 and above. iPadOS 27 is available for iPad Pro (4th generation and later, M1 and later), iPad Air (4th generation and later, M2 and later), iPad mini (6th generation, A17 Pro), and the base iPad (9th generation and later, A16).

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Trump’s Secret Points System for Cabinet Members
The White House held a summer contest to see who could appear in the most congressional districts and states with competitive midterm elections.
Nearly every day, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles meets with Meghan Bauer, a presidential assistant who coordinates with Cabinet members, to review who’s recently traveled where, who’s heading out into the country, and—perhaps most important—who’s in a swing district at that very moment. The debrief is part of the administration’s unofficial Cabinet Travel Competition, overseen by Bauer, in which the White House encourages Cabinet secretaries to traverse the country to promote President Trump’s agenda and tracks their visits to politically competitive congressional districts or states ahead of the midterm elections.
We first found out about the competition when chatting with a Cabinet secretary about an event that person had declined to attend in Manhattan, in part for fear of being docked points in the White House contest for going to a solidly blue area. (Several White House officials said that no one ever loses points, and two added that a trip to New York for a cable-news hit praising the administration’s policies, for instance, would still count toward the contest.)
When we talked with Karoline Leavitt late last month, in her final days as White House press secretary, she marveled: “I think we have seven or eight of them out on the road in targeted districts just today.” The formal competition ran from Memorial Day to Labor Day, although secretaries will likely be encouraged to keep going through November. There were rumors of a prize—possibly a dinner with the president for the winning Cabinet secretary, plus their family—but several White House officials insisted that the competition is simply for bragging rights. They all spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were discussing internal matters.
These officials said that contestants are encouraged to travel to key congressional districts or competitive states, appear with members of Congress, and participate in local media interviews. The thinking, in part, is that local press coverage is more valuable than talking with national outlets in Washington, and that Cabinet officials can help drive Trump’s message by highlighting how his actions and policies have improved the lives of voters. Any midterm-related travel must be flagged for White House approval—and everyone is instructed to comply with federal rules that forbid certain forms of partisan politicking. As in previous administrations, taxpayers foot the bill for travel related to the secretaries’ official duties, and the top officials are expected to pay for any personal political travel themselves. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. got approval to use a more costly military jet for some of his trips, The Washington Post reported.
In February, Wiles told agency heads they should limit their international travel so that they could focus on helping Republicans win the midterm elections. The president would do the same, she said at the time, and he would spend every other week stumping through the country, ramping up to at least once a week as the November elections neared. Punishment for those who disobeyed was swift; among the various reasons Kristi Noem was pushed out as Homeland Security secretary were images of her atop a camel in Bahrain and well-documented horseback-riding jaunts in Argentina’s Campo de Mayo and near South Dakota’s Mount Rushmore, where there are no competitive federal midterm races. “They know not to take 10-day-long vacations in Wyoming,” Leavitt said of the Cabinet members. “The president is working all the time, and he expects them to as well.”
The White House declined to provide us with its tally of each Cabinet member’s political travel, but it did send us a list of the numbers of visits made to at least 13 states over the summer. In the lead with 46 visits was Texas, where Republicans are spending millions to try to hold on to a Senate seat. Following close behind was Pennsylvania with 42, and New York with 40. (Manhattan may not be MAGA country, but New York has several competitive House districts.) On the lower end of the most-visited states were New Jersey and North Carolina (both 10), Alaska (five), and Nevada (four). In a little more than three months, the White House said, Cabinet members made a total of 265 visits to those 13 states.
We made our own list, searching through publicly documented domestic travel by members of Trump’s Cabinet starting on Memorial Day and ending on August 31. To try to emulate the White House’s tracking system, we gave each person a point for traveling to a competitive congressional district or a state with a close Senate race. We used the Cook Political Report ratings to determine competitiveness, focusing on the 37 districts with races that Cook rated as a toss-up or leaning toward one political party, as well as any states with a similarly competitive Senate contest. (Though the White House might reward someone who went to Manhattan for a media interview, we did not. We also awarded only one point for multiple stops in one state during a single trip.)
According to our tally, the winner is likely Small Business Administration head Kelly Loeffler, who took at least 18 trips to competitive states, including more than one stop each in Georgia, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia. She is followed closely by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins (at least 17), Acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling (at least 15), and Kennedy and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (at least 10 each). In certain ways, the competition is really just among the handful of members whose job lends itself to regular national travel; folks such as the U.S. trade representative, the CIA director, and the director of the Office of Management and Budget seem to have each taken only one trip to a competitive area since Memorial Day. We could not find any midterm-related trips for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who since his confirmation has clocked thousands of miles overseas. And though Duffy tied for fourth place during this period, we were nonetheless surprised his travel wasn’t a bit more robust, given that he previously spent several months traversing the country with his family for his six-episode reality series, The Great American Road Trip. Perhaps he was just recovering from his long joyride across the United States.
The White House spokesperson Olivia Wales praised both Trump’s Cabinet and his policy achievements in an emailed statement. “Cabinet officials will continue to meet with everyday Americans across our country to inform future policymaking and tout these victories, drawing a strong contrast to the record of failure by radical Democrats on the border, inflation, and crime,” she wrote. Since Trump’s first term, Democrats and watchdog groups have accused Trump officials of violating the Hatch Act—a 1939 federal law that, to minimize partisanship in government, limits federal employees from engaging in certain political activities. And in the run-up to these midterms, at least one Cabinet member—Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—has come under intense criticism for seemingly blurring the line between personal and government travel.
Two decades ago, President George W. Bush’s staff similarly tracked Cabinet travel before the 2006 midterms, and offered incentives to federal employees who volunteered in battleground races. The Office of Special Counsel condemned the operation years later, objecting to the use of federal funds for political purposes. Back then, the Republican National Committee kept an “Administration Tracker” spreadsheet to log the travel of political appointees to targeted races, and the White House kept its own list of Cabinet “assets” and where they had deployed. The investigation found that the Bush tracking system spurred a “friendly competition” between White House liaisons that, ultimately, was part of the “type of electioneering proscribed by the Hatch Act.”
The partisan travel of federal officials has long been legally and politically fraught. During the Biden administration, in 2024, House and Senate Republicans investigated trips that top officials from the Small Business Administration, including the administrator, took to crucial battleground states. Federal watchdogs found in 2021 that members of the Trump administration had shown “willful disregard” for the law by pushing for Trump’s reelection in their official capacities.
Whether the White House is violating the law now would depend on what internal safeguards have been created to prevent federal funds from being spent on political purposes, Donald Sherman, the president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, told us. “The details do matter,” he said. “But it is also hard to imagine that that compliance is being prioritized in a competition-like scenario, particularly in an administration that has been hostile to the Hatch Act in pretty much every other instance.”
Trump fired the head of the Office of Special Counsel when he returned to office, and the Hatch Act has not been enforced against senior Trump-administration officials since then, despite complaints from watchdog groups about apparent violations. A White House official told us that the administration has implemented a process in which the White House and agency ethics officials review political appearances by Trump’s appointees. “All Administration officials who chose to participate in political activity and travel have been encouraged to work with their respective agency counsels and the White House to ensure that they are in full compliance,” the official wrote in an emailed statement.
In the run-up to the 2010 midterms, then-President Obama and his team invented the “Recovery Summer,” a six-week push—featuring, yes, Cabinet secretaries and other senior officials—to spotlight infrastructure investments from their stimulus bill. In 2022, the Biden administration deployed its top messengers across the country to highlight his policies as well. Then–Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg proved the most in-demand Cabinet surrogate, and his position allowed him to tout the administration’s roughly $1 trillion infrastructure bill.
But those administrations were more diligent than Trump’s in distinguishing between personal and government travel, and took pains not to mix the two. And despite the Trump administration’s alleged disregard for the Hatch Act, many of the Cabinet members we’ve tracked have similarly avoided blurring political and government trips, albeit with (at least) one notable exception. In May, before the official competition began, Hegseth appeared in Kentucky alongside the former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, who successfully challenged Representative Thomas Massie, a Trump irritant, in the Republican primary. Hegseth’s star turn on the stump raised questions about whether he’d violated the Hatch Act; though a Pentagon spokesperson said Hegseth had attended in his “personal capacity,” he appeared the same day at Fort Campbell in Kentucky in his official capacity to award Purple Hearts. Past Pentagon chiefs and other top Defense Department officials have avoided even a whiff of partisanship. Then, in August, Hegseth appeared at the Iowa State Fair alongside Representative Zach Nunn, where he endorsed Nunn’s reelection bid and praised him as an ally of both the Pentagon and the president.
Perhaps emboldened by his previous campaign-trail appearance—which prompted much griping but no meaningful consequences—Hegseth declared, “According to the lawyers, I’m only here in a personal capacity.”
Agriculture Secretary Rollins—a frequent traveler, by our count—journeyed in early June to a farm in North Carolina, where she walked between rows of tobacco and stood in front of John Deere tractors, touting the Trump administration’s labor reforms, which she said had reduced costs for the state’s farmers. In July, she joined a radio interview in Georgia with Representative Brian Jack—a Republican expected to win his reelection campaign—and described a new program for shipping meat as “so exciting” and “so important” for the state. And in late August, she appeared at the Iowa State Fair, where she defended Trump’s controversial decision to ease restrictions on imported beef, which she said was necessary to lower prices for struggling families. All three states have competitive Senate races that are essential to Republicans maintaining control of the chamber.
Her fellow Cabinet members traveled to other key states to spread similar enthusiasm. Energy Secretary Chris Wright—with nine trips to competitive areas, by our count—traveled to Alaska to deliver “a giant thank-you” for the state’s copious oil exports. And Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins tied with him, including travel to a military event in Virginia Beach with Vice President Vance and a day of stops in central Michigan to meet with local veterans, alongside the district’s Republican representative.
The agency chiefs tailor their messages to their specific audiences. But if the competition is any indication—and mere mention of it elicited knowing nods and smiles from agency staff and White House officials—the Cabinet officials understand their singular mission: to spread the Trump doctrine far and wide, but especially to purple battlegrounds. They are eager to comply.
Madison Hahamy, Jack Rodriquez-Vars, and Marie-Rose Sheinerman contributed to this report.

Mental health conditions that may develop following a traumatic incident could contribute to a higher risk of future cardiovascular issues such as non-fatal heart attack and stroke or a fatal cardiac event, according to new research.
"Traumatic events are common experiences and can include serious fires or explosions, physical assault, transportation accidents, the suicide or death of a loved one, and severe medical illnesses or injuries," lead author Jennifer A Sumner, an associate professor in the department of psychology at the University of California Los Angeles, said.
"Experiencing traumatic events can significantly affect mental health as well as cardiovascular health. Although most work to date has focused on PTSD and cardiovascular health, our research suggests that we should think about a wide range of mental health consequences when looking at cardiovascular disease risk after trauma," Sumner said.
The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, examined national health registries in Denmark, looking at 2,19,866 adults who did and did not develop major heart or brain conditions following a traumatic event.
About 44,000 of the 2,19,866 participants experienced a non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death between 1995 and 2019.
Researchers compared 1,75,872 people who experienced a trauma but not a cardiovascular event to peers who experienced a heart attack, stroke, procedures to restore blood flow to the heart or cardiovascular death during the 24-year period.
A wide range of mental health conditions were considered as possible cardiovascular predictors, and machine learning was used to identify the 15 most important mental health disorder predictors of heart and brain outcomes.
Alcohol abuse was found to be the most important mental health risk linked to serious heart or brain conditions for men and women.
"For men and women, the most important psychiatric predictor of MACCE (major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events) was alcohol use disorders," the authors wrote.
"After a traumatic life experience, individuals may turn to alcohol to cope and help manage their emotions. Over time, this new behaviour might develop into alcohol abuse, thus increasing their risk of a serious heart or brain condition," Sumner said.
Mood disorders, including depression, were found to be strong indicators of post-traumatic psychiatric issues associated with cardiovascular outcomes for both men and women. However, mood disorders were a more prominent predictor for women, compared to men.
Psychological conditions that can arise after a traumatic event connected to a higher risk of heart and brain conditions in the future included PTSD, mental disorders caused by brain or physical issues, non-substance-induced confusion, different substance use disorders, personality disorders, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and anxiety disorders.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

For some people, particularly youngsters, an AI chatbot is becoming the first place they turn to when they are distressed. It has its advantages: it is available at any hour, does not appear to judge them and can respond instantly. But when conversations involve thoughts of suicide, the limits of this interaction become consequential. Every conversation with an AI chatbot may not be harmful, but an apparently empathetic response could reinforce hopelessness, prolong rumination, or delay professional help in some people already at risk, say experts.
What the evidence shows
AI use for mental health support is now common. A U.S. survey of 1,009 people aged 12 to 21, published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025. Nearly 43% of these users did so at least monthly, while 5.8% used them daily or almost daily. Nearly two-thirds had not told anyone about this.
Another analysis of more than 620,000 publicly available ChatGPT conversations found that 4.9% could be classified broadly as involving mental health, although only 0.21% met a stricter definition involving an identifiable person explicitly seeking mental health help.
Studies have also found that chatbots are generally better at recognising very low- and very high-risk scenarios, but struggle to distinguish between intermediate levels of suicide risk. This is particularly concerning for psychiatrists, as suicidal distress is rarely expressed in a single, explicit statement and often emerges through a combination of subtle or changing cues.
When reassurance becomes a loop
“Suicidal distress is not always direct; people may hint, use humour or gradually disclose their thoughts,” said Mithun Prasad, consultant, psychiatry, SIMS Hospital, Chennai. Keyword recognition alone, he said, is therefore inadequate; the context and consistency of a conversation matter.
Sabaresh Pandiyan, consultant, psychiatry, Rela Hospital, Chennai, pointed to another issue: the ‘internal loop’, particularly among younger users, who may derive comfort from the empathetic part of an AI response, while ignoring advice to seek professional help. Repeated reassurance can also make suicidal thinking seem less urgent. “Talking about suicide or venting about suicide is not the problem, reinforcing hopelessness is,” he said.
Nithya M., consultant psychiatrist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, emphasised that AI could amplify existing distress, prolong rumination or substitute validation for intervention.
In clinical practice, psychiatrists see patients use AI to discuss relationships, workplace problems and other personal concerns before speaking to family or friends. Dr. Pandiyan said around 60-70% of patients in his setting discuss such matters with AI first. For some, this may help them recognise a problem and seek care earlier. Others may spend months trying to manage difficulties themselves before consulting a professional.
Dr. Nithya said warning signs can include patients quoting AI responses verbatim, withdrawing from human confidants, resisting professional help or developing a rigid view of themselves or their relationships based on chatbot responses.
Not a substitute for care
There may be limited situations in which patients use AI alongside clinical care. Dr. Prasad said some patients use chatbots between appointments to record medication effects or organise their thoughts, and later bring a summary to their psychiatrist. This can provide the clinician with information about what happened between consultations.
But such use does not make AI a substitute for psychiatric assessment. A chatbot does not have access to a person’s psychiatric history, personality, psychological defences, adverse life experiences, protective factors or current mental state. It may validate an emotion without recognising when urgent assessment is needed. This is particularly concerning when a person has psychosis, mania or distorted beliefs.
Need for safety checks
Psychiatrists call for mandatory safety audits, independent clinical assessments and clearer liability frameworks. Companies should be required to investigate and report serious safety incidents. . Public education should also explain where AI is and is not appropriate.
Experts add that any response must also address the stigma that prevents people from seeking mental healthcare. Families and communities need to create safer spaces for people to talk about distress and seek help.
When a person is in a mental health crisis, experts said, the priority should remain timely human assessment and support. AI cannot take the place of that care.

The Bengaluru City Police have launched ‘Project Khushi’, a structured health and wellness programme aimed at supporting the long-term physical and mental well-being of police personnel, Home Minister Priyank Kharge said on Tuesday.
The programme will initially be implemented in the Electronics City police division, covering around 600 police personnel. Each batch will undergo a three-month programme comprising health check-ups, expert-led guidance sessions, and digital engagement activities.
The initiative will focus on preventive healthcare, nutrition, physical activity, quality sleep, and stress management, besides other lifestyle factors crucial for the long-term well-being of police personnel.
Pilot programme shows encouraging results
According to the Home Minister, an earlier pilot programme conducted as part of Project Khushi produced encouraging results. Around 61% of participants recorded a reduction in blood sugar levels, while 70% corrected Vitamin B12 deficiencies. In addition, 59% of participants reduced their body weight.
Mr. Kharge said that the results demonstrate that sustained and scientifically designed health interventions can have a positive impact on the well-being of police personnel.
Partnership with health and corporate organisations
“Our police personnel work every day in challenging and stressful conditions to ensure the safety of our communities. It is essential to pay continuous attention to their health. Healthy police personnel are the backbone of an effective and resilient policing system,” Mr Kharge said.
He added that equal importance must be given to mental well-being, a healthy lifestyle, and stress management, along with physical health.

Apple has officially started rolling out iOS 27 for eligible devices, and it brings a lot of useful additions. If you are using any Apple audio product, iOS 27 gets a new native custom equalizer to fine-tune the music from your AirPods and other Apple audio products (requires Apple’s H2 chip; you can see full compatibility here).
In this guide, you will learn how to use the new custom EQ for your AirPods and other Apple devices.
Table of Contents
How to Use the New AirPods Custom EQ in iOS 27
The new native equalizer is only available in the latest iOS 27. If your iPhone is eligible for the latest iOS 27, you can go to General > Software Update and update to the latest iOS 27.
Custom EQ Supported Device List:
Custom EQ for Apple iOS 27 is only available for audio devices with an H2 chip or later. Here is the official compatibility list.
- AirPods Pro 2
- AirPods Pro 3
- AirPods 4
- AirPods Max 2
Now, if your device supports it, follow the steps below.
First, Update Your iPhone to the Latest iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down.
Step 3: Tap on General.
Step 4: Tap on Software Update.
Step 5: Tap on Update Now (if the update is available).
Please ensure that your iPhone is on the iOS 27 eligible device list.
Next, Update Your AirPods Firmware
Step 1: Connect your AirPods to your iPhone.
Step 2: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 3: Tap on your AirPods (you will see this option if your AirPods are connected to your device) and next go to Step 5.
Step 4: If you don’t see it, open Bluetooth.
Tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 5: Now, scroll down and tap on AirPods Beta Updates.
Step 6: Enable the option that says AirPods Beta Updates.
Ensure your iPhone is connected to the internet and your AirPods are connected to your iPhone. Your AirPods will automatically update to the latest software.
How to Use the Custom Equalizer on iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on your AirPods.
Or else, you can go to Bluetooth and tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 3: Scroll down and tap on Audio and Routing.
Step 4: From here, scroll down and tap on Equalizer.
Step 5: Select the Custom option.
Step 6: Now you can adjust lows, mids, and highs based on your preference. You can move the slider to the top and bottom. The line above refers to high, and the line below refers to low.
1. Lows: Increase or decrease bass.
2. Mids: Meant for vocals, where you can increase or decrease the vocal presence, especially if the music has singer vocals.
3. Highs: Treble, which AirPods are mainly known for. You can adjust treble sound using high settings.
Step 7: If you want to reset, tap on the Reset option.
Step 8: If you don’t want custom controls, you can tap on “Recommended,” and it will use Apple’s default recommended sound signature.
Currently, the iOS 27 custom equalizer is very basic. Even though Apple has the best ecosystem, Apple only decided to give you basic controls to customize the sound output from your audio devices.
I know most people are fine with the default settings on the AirPods, but sometimes even I prefer more control over the music.
Adding custom equalizer settings natively on your iPhone eliminates the need to download third-party apps, which sometimes have compatibility issues. However, Apple’s basic equalizer still leaves room for third-party options. Apple also offers you the option to reset the changes you have made.
This is a good start. Hopefully, in iOS 28, Apple will bring more features to this custom equalizer to fine-tune the sound signature of the AirPods. Using EQ does bring a noticeable sound difference. If you don’t see this option or are facing any issues, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.
FAQs about iOS 27 AirPods Custom EQ
1. Does AirPods Custom EQ Work on iPad and Mac?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ is also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27
2. Can You Save Multiple Custom EQ Presets for AirPods?
As I said before, current EQ settings are basic. As of now, you can only have one custom EQ profile
3. Does Custom EQ Work With Spatial Audio and Adaptive Audio?
Yes, it works with spatial audio and adaptive audio, but those settings are different from custom EQ. Currently, custom EQ only allows you to adjust lows, highs, and mids.
4. Does Custom EQ Affect Calls and Videos or Only Music?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ applies to all media playing on your iPhone, including videos, music, TV shows, and much more.
5. Why Is the Custom EQ Option Missing on Supported AirPods?
If you don’t see the custom EQ option on your iPhone, make sure that you update to iOS 27. Custom EQ options are available for AirPods that have an H2 processor. At the time of writing this article, current supported models include AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

Immigrants held in small outdoor cages at 'Alligator Alcatraz' in Florida, investigators find
- Published
Immigrants held at "Alligator Alcatraz", a now-shuttered detention centre in Florida, were kept in small metal cages for hours, according to a report from the US Department of Homeland Security's watchdog.
The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) found the use of the outdoor cages - about 18sq ft (1.67sq m) - was "unprecedented among detention facilities" and dangerous.
Investigators concluded the centre also did not comply with a number of standards for hygiene, medical care, food, health and safety.
The BBC has contacted DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis for comment. DHS told the watchdog that state officials ran the facility.
In its response included in the investigation report, DHS officials said Florida - not the federal government - had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility.
The facility was established by the state of Florida through an executive order signed by DeSantis, but the federal government paid for operational costs.
In January, the OIG conducted a surprise inspection at the detention facility, which had become one of the most notorious immigration detention centres in the US. The OIG is an independent internal watchdog at DHS. The current inspector general was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term.
In 2025, the detention facility was built over the course of eight days in the Everglades, a protected wetland known for its alligators. Trump once joked that immigrants held there would need to learn "how to run away" from the reptiles at the facility, which civil rights groups have decried as inhumane.
In June 2026, DeSantis said the facility would close as it was only meant to be temporary.
According to the OIG report, between July 2025 and January 2026, the facility kept 79 immigrants in the small metal enclosures, describing them as "calming areas" for people to "deescalate and have time alone". They were held there from periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, at least once as a disciplinary measure, OIG said.
"The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report stated.
Detainees at the facility have previously told the BBC they were denied necessary medication and regular showers and other hygiene measures.
In their report, OIG inspectors said they found immigrants held at the facility had to use showers infested with small bugs and were only allowed to do so three times a week.
The facility did not provide them with sufficient living space, "creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units", according to the report.
Immigrants at the centre also told OIG that they did not have access to clean drinking water and could not clean the plastic cups from which they drank.

What Is the Good Life?
The philosophy professor Meghan Sullivan doesn’t just want to teach her students about virtue; she wants to make them better human beings.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
David Brooks: Hi, I’m David Brooks. If you are listening to or watching this, you’ve stumbled across the first episode of a new podcast called The Permanent Questions.
The idea of the podcast is that there are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life. How do you find your purpose? How do you confront death? How do you save a relationship that’s going through a rough patch? How do you build a just society?
Now, you may be asking yourself, “How the hell did a political pundit get into these deep waters?”
When I was 18, an incredibly lucky thing happened to me: The admissions officers at Columbia University, Wesleyan, and Brown decided I should go to the University of Chicago. I didn’t know anything about Chicago. I’d never visited. I never knew anybody who went there, but it was the only school I got into.
It turned out to be the perfect school for me. My favorite joke about Chicago: It’s a Baptist school where atheist professors teach Jewish students Saint Thomas Aquinas. And I fit right in.
There’s a saying, “If you catch fire with enthusiasm, people will come for miles to watch you burn.” My professors had caught fire with enthusiasm.
Those teachers were filled with a certain conviction. The conviction was, if you read important books, had important conversations, and addressed big questions, you would have the keys to the kingdom.
They gave us new things to love: new ideas, new heroes, new activities, new subjects. They tried to teach us how to see, not only to see with your preconceptions and the things you think you see, but to see with the clarity of a Tolstoy, the moral depth of George Eliot, the empathetic outrage of James Baldwin.
Mostly, they introduced us to the Great Conversation. The Great Conversation is a tradition of debate that goes back for thousands of years. It’s a collective attempt to find a workable balance between the inevitable tensions of life—the tension between autonomy and belonging, between freedom and order, between diversity and cohesion, safety and exploration, tenderness and strength, intellect and passion. The Great Conversation never ends, because there is no permanent solution to these tensions, just a temporary resting spot that works in this or that circumstance.
I never wanted to leave the Great Conversation, and I never have. I went off and became a journalist and a political pundit, and that was a worthwhile thing to do, and I still do it. A lot of the big questions in life are political questions. Who should lead us? What does a just society even look like? But none of my six books are about politics. They’re about the kind of questions my teachers asked me back in Chicago: How do you educate your emotions? How do you survive a setback?
As my career has gone on, I came to the conclusion that we as a society are over-politicized and under-moralized. That is to say, we pay attention to every little political scandal, but many people have been given no instruction on the basic questions of how to live, of how they should find their calling, what they should really want.
And over the last 15 years or so, this sensation has taken a deeper urgency. Like a lot of countries, America seems to be going through some sort of spiritual, relational, and social, and maybe moral crisis. You know all the stats: rising loneliness, rising despair, rising distrust, rising polarization.
We’re living through a period of great technological advance, but we’re losing our humanistic core. Because of technological improvements and social deterioration, our lives are objectively better, but subjectively worse. The elements of civilization that lift the spirit and nurture the affections are playing a smaller and smaller role in our national life. Religion, literature, art, theology, history, philosophy, friendship, even conversation.
In previous periods of technological advance, there was a humanistic counterreaction. Humanists said, “Okay, bring us your science. Bring us your machines. Bring us your efficiency. Bring us your technology. That’s fine. But don’t turn us into machines ourselves.” And the humanists made an aggressive counter-push to say, “We will preserve our humanistic core. We will preserve what is essentially human. ”
This podcast is an attempt to be a small part of that kind of humanistic reaction.
We asked Meghan Sullivan to be the first guest on the show because she’s the kind of great teacher I’m talking about. Meghan teaches one of the most beloved courses at Notre Dame University, which is called “God and the Good Life.” She’s won Notre Dame’s Joyce Award for Excellence in Teaching, and as you’ll see, she’s got a dynamic personality. She co-authored a book based on the course, called The Good Life Method: Reasoning Through the Big Questions of Happiness, Faith, and Meaning.
Meghan doesn’t just do education, providing students with facts they can regurgitate on a test. Meghan does formation. She helps students become better versions of themselves. And so it’s a great pleasure to welcome Meghan Sullivan to this table.
Brooks: Welcome, Meghan Sullivan. You are the first guest on The Permanent Questions. You are the founding figure of our podcast. So thank you for being here.
Meghan Sullivan: Heavy is the crown. This is a tremendous responsibility, David.
Brooks: I know. All future guests will be measured by your exemplary example.
Sullivan: Exactly. I’m hopefully gonna create a large ceiling for this podcast.
Brooks: So, you grew up in North Carolina, and I assume you had a moderately normal childhood. And then you became a philosopher. So how the hell did that happen?
Sullivan: I did not grow up in an academic family. My mom was a receptionist in a dental office, and my dad worked a bunch of different jobs, but for most of high school he worked at this company called Replacements. They basically replaced, like, broken plates. My dad was in the plate-replacement business. My mom was in the dental-billing business. So that was not particularly academic background, but very, very loving. And if you would’ve told me when I was a high-school student that I would end up a philosophy professor, I would have asked you to throw me off a bridge.
Most of my students have never met a professional philosopher before they take my class. But in high school, actually, one of my best friends, her dad was a philosophy professor at our local university, and we were very, very judgy, snotty teenage girls, and we devoted probably two years of high school to thinking, “We cannot understand this guy’s job.”
So in high school, I had a well-considered, extremely negative opinion of the profession of philosophy that was based on nothing but vibes about my friend’s dad’s books.
I got a scholarship and went to the University of Virginia, so this big public school where, as a freshman, you’re just sort of fed into the meat grinder. You just get whatever classes are left over after all of the big kids register for their classes. And my academic adviser was talking to me, and I was so stressed because I couldn’t get any of the pre-law classes that I desperately wanted, or econ classes. And he’s like, “I think that you would really love this ethics class called ‘Issues of Life and Death’ in the philosophy department. It’s really debate-y, and I just think given your background, you’re gonna have a blast in there. ”
So I was like, “Okay, fine. Philosophy. ” And I enrolled in that class, and I was hooked by the second week. The exact moment—I remember this really vividly—I was sitting in Alderman Library, in the library at UVA, and we’d just gotten our first assignment for all of our classes, our first writing assignment, and I was writing all these boring book reports for my other classes.
In “Issues of Life and Death,” the question we were assigned is: “Should you end your life?” And I remember talking to the TA being like, “Do you want me to write about what, you know, David Hume says about suicide?” And he’s like, “Absolutely not. I want the strongest possible argument about whether you should continue living.”
And I was like, “Are you allowed to ask me that? Like, is that allowed?” And he’s like, “Not only is it allowed, but there are better and worse answers, and if you don’t have a really tight, really well-argued position, you’re gonna get a bad grade in this class.” And I just remember sitting in the library, the kind of blinking cursor on Microsoft Word staring at me, thinking, Ah, we’re firing live ammunition here. Like, this is real. And that just totally got me hooked.
Brooks: Now, a lot of philosophers write abstruse academic articles with a lot of notations and numbers and diagrams. You actually teach this class, and you’ve written this book, on how to live. Why’d you become that kind of philosopher?
Sullivan: I had an epiphany my third year at Notre Dame. I was getting ready to go up for tenure, and I’d been teaching our big intro philosophy class. And when you go through the tenure process, at first, you’re only focused on keeping your job, and then you start to hit a point where you imagine a future where you’re just a professor and you’re not worried about getting fired all the time. And I was in that kind of mindset of thinking, What do I wanna do with the rest of my career after I hopefully survive this tenure vote?
And I felt very, very strongly that I wanted to focus the next chapter on my teaching. That’s what really I loved about my job. And I’d been teaching Aristotle. And we inflict Aristotle on every single freshman at the University of Notre Dame. And Aristotle has this line in the second chapter of his book about the good life that I’ve always loved, and I always assign students to write essays about.
He says, “We conduct this examination not so that we can know what virtue is, but so that we might be good.” We do all this not so we can know what dead people said about virtue and philosophy, but so that we can become happier people. Otherwise, there’s no benefit of it, he says. This whole enterprise is pointless if it doesn’t find some way to make us better.
Brooks: Now, you’re in the business of helping people become, as you said, happy and good. And this podcast is in the same business. I’m joining your team.
Sullivan: Yeah, all right.
Brooks: And so, as we enter this conversation, I thought I’d raise some objections to the life we have chosen.
Sullivan: Bring it. Objections are the love language of philosophy.
Brooks: So the first one is what’s—why is this necessary? I get up in the morning; I have my Frappuccino; I surf my media feed; I go to work, which is good, I like my work; I go home; I watch Netflix. Why should I read a bunch of complicated books and have hard conversations?
Sullivan: So one assumption I think we should challenge is that there are some people who do philosophy, a small number of people, like my friend’s dad, and then everybody else doesn’t do philosophy.
That’s like saying there are some people who exercise, and everybody else doesn’t exercise. I get why you’d make that assumption if you think that exercise or philosophy is this really, really narrow prescribed activity. But that’s just not true.
My doctor would be the first person to tell you, you use your body every single day. It’s just some people exercise well and train, and other people are potatoes (laughs) like me. Which is why my doctor brings this up all the time.
It’s the same with philosophy. If we think about philosophy in the ancient tradition, like Socrates’s tradition, philosophy is caring for your soul. And everybody has to do this. It’s just a question about whether or not you’re gonna do it well or you’re gonna do it in a really immature way. You could do better or worse at reasoning through these soul questions that are—they’re gonna slap you in the face.
