Sullivan: Just, just owning the book and having it on your shelf. The more books you buy, actually, my publisher told me, the more character you acquire.
Brooks: Yeah, it’s absolutely true. So the theory of that book was self-confrontation. You say, What’s my key sin? And so one of the characters in that book is Dwight Eisenhower. And his key sin was anger. He had a temper problem.
Sullivan: I didn’t know that.
Brooks: He produced this persona of being this cheerful, country-club kinda guy, but that was manufactured. And so, in the middle of World War II, when he was general, he would take all the people he hated that day, and he would write their names on a piece of paper, and he’d shred it.
And that was his way of trying to purge his hatred for these people, these incompetents. And so that’s one form, and I still think that’s—it’s a useful exercise to say, What’s my key sin? And, What can I do about that?
Sullivan: What’s your key sin?
Brooks: I would say shallowness. I’m very prone to being shallow. And I’ve tried to spend my entire life being a little less shallow. So that’s definitely my key sin. I won’t ask you yours.
Sullivan: Actually, I would say pride, which actually in the Catholic world is a really, really bad one. You’re playing with nitroglycerin if you’ve got that in your life and you’re not really trying to address it. But,yeah, that’s a pretty bad one for me, with a little bit of anger.
Brooks: I’ll try not to cross you.
Sullivan: Exactly. I need to try the Eisenhower trick, though. Did it work? I wonder if it worked for him. If it gave him release.
Brooks: It doesn’t work. There’s been research. The idea of purging your anger, that doesn’t work, that doesn’t work.
Sullivan: You know, a really strongly worded email at 5 a.m. on a Saturday morning.
Brooks: That totally works.
Sullivan: That makes it worse.
Brooks: But now I think it’s loving the right things. I’m less impressed by willpower than I used to be. But if you can love the right things in the right way, in the right order, and mold your heart in that way, then—for example, giving up cigarettes and alcohol is really hard. But millions of women do it every year, because they get pregnant, and they love their kid more than they love cabernet.
Sullivan: It’s amazing.
Brooks: And so, but, how you mold your heart is a tricky thing, but being aware of, of loving things in the right order. I’m talking Augustine to a Catholic philosopher.
Sullivan: Exactly. The ordo amoris.
Brooks: The question is how you change somebody’s heart. Like how do you change their inner life? That seems really hard. I mean, let alone your—even changing your own is hard.
Sullivan: Yeah one of the biggest insights from social psychology and 2,500 years of philosophy is if you think that caring for your soul is a solo endeavor, like you write down your New Year’s resolutions and you commit yourself quietly in your own mind to following it, that’s a fool’s errand. No human changes their habits in that way. Change is inherently social and, you know, for a woman who becomes pregnant, the realization that I’m two people right now in this body, that’s a kind of social pressure. Not a bad social pressure, not like, your unborn child is not going to shame you about your decisions. But just this feeling of love creates a second self. It creates another self that’s permanently intertwined with your own, and that absolutely shapes your perspective about what your endeavor or journey is.
Brooks: The one I think that we don’t do enough of is basic skills, moral skills. Like, how do you sit with someone who’s depressed? How do you sit with someone who’s just lost a child? A lot of students, and a lot of people, nobody’s ever taught, and I would include myself in this. My friend suffered from severe depression, and I had no idea how to react, and I think I’m kinda literate. I don’t know. But I think we should do more basic skill building.
Sullivan: Oh, absolutely. We spend the first two weeks of the “God and the Good Life” course just on this question of how to ask questions at a dinner party. Most of my students don’t go to very many dinner parties, because they’re teenagers. They will later on in life, probably. But they think that all questions are created equal. And so they think you ask a question in class to just demonstrate how smart you are, if you talk at all.
Or to try to nail another student if you wanna have a moral debate. Like get them on record, like a prosecutor, of saying something that you’re then gonna attack. I think they must learn some of this in high school, too, but we spend the first two weeks just trying to deprogram them and help them realize you can ask a question of another person because you just wanna hear part of their story.
And the very best questions you might ask are ones where you genuinely have no clue what the person is gonna say next. And this is a revelation. We’ll have our students write down sample questions about whatever topic we’re doing in class. Should you be religious? How much money is enough to decide you would quit your job?
And they initially want to just lock into simple yes or no answers, and then start immediately offering their reasons. And we’re like, “Hold the phone. We don’t want your reasons yet. You’ve barely thought about this.” Instead, I want you to try to understand all of the other people that are in this conversation with you and where they might be coming from and what their possible reasons are.
Brooks: I find a lot of people don’t ask those questions. Well, either they’re not curious about people, or else they’re afraid they’re gonna invade someone’s privacy. And I would say, I’ve been a journalist since I was 22, and my job is asking people questions, often in difficult circumstances, and how often has anybody ever said to me, “That’s none of your damn business”? And the answer is zero. Zero. I’ve asked this of other journalists or people in the question-asking business. If you respectfully ask somebody to tell you the story of their life, no one has ever asked them, and they’re delighted to do this.
Sullivan: We started teaching this Good Life class 10 years ago, so it’s the 10-year anniversary. And one of the things we have all the students do is write this long confessional essay, basically, their confessions like Augustine, their apology like Socrates, where they share key moments from their life and then debate with themselves about what its significance is in light of the philosophy that we’ve been reading in class.
And this is 40 percent of their grade, this one big confessional essay. And I remember when we were unleashing the course, I got a lot of criticism from well-meaning but mistaken faculty who basically said, “You cannot ask a student to disclose aspects of their life like this. That’s professionally inappropriate. And you can’t grade them on it, you fool. This is not possible. ”
And we don’t grade them based on are they good people or not. We grade them based on their philosophical reasoning. But I have taught thousands of students in the last decade in this class. I have never once had a student complain about going through this exercise.
Sometimes they’ll complain about their final grade, but they never complain about the self-disclosure part. It’s the opposite. I get notes and emails from students, oftentimes from their parents, often like a year after they’ve taken the class, saying, “Hey, I just want you to realize that meant a tremendous amount to me at the time. Nobody had ever listened to me or paid that much attention to me in my life.”
Brooks: I’ve gotta ask, I was curious about this, about the apology. Like, they’re 18, 19, whatever. What do they say?
Sullivan: There are some common themes. They have to pick three of 10 possible topics.
Politics, money, work, moral responsibility, suffering, love, death, God, contemplation, et cetera. I think I got nine out of the 10. They tend to always pick three. They never pick politics. You’d be shocked to learn, they never think that political debate is a very important part of their lives, which is hilarious because we’re constantly pressured now as faculty to teach our students how to have political debates, this is all the rage right now, and I wanna tell them, none of my students actually care that much about this topic. Maybe they should, but they just don’t.
They usually choose work and love. My students are obsessed with work. That part of their essays tends to be very funny, because I will more often than not read these extremely sincere sections of their essays about their experiences with what Karl Marx calls alienation from your “species-being,” which is when you feel like the capitalist conditions you’re forced to operate under separate you from your deep sources of meaning and your essence. And they will say that their experience being the treasurer of the Ultimate Frisbee team has been a constant grind and has caused them to believe that they’re only valuable insofar as what they produce for the Frisbee club, and they’re experiencing burnout because of that.
But they do put a high value on work, and we let them. We indulge that. I give the students about four weeks on work and money in the class to just talk through all their questions, ’cause you can’t try to suppress it.
And then the second big theme is love. And one surprise, or I don’t know if this would be a surprise or not. You would think lovesick college students would write about romantic love and what it means to them. And we do a little bit of readings on that. They never write about romantic love.
The vast majority of my freshmen have actually never had a serious boyfriend or girlfriend by the time I get them. That’s still in the future for them. They write about their parents, and occasionally their siblings. And so I get to read a lot of really beautiful essays about their reflections on what these relationships have meant to them. I think a lot of them are experiencing some homesickness by the time I see them. But that’s very moving. And again, figures like Aristotle that we obsess about in the class, Aristotle gives a whole chapter over to parent-child relationships. These are extremely philosophically rich parts of our lives.
The most profound moment for this actually was in 2020. I was teaching my Good Life class, and I had two young women in the class. This was peak pandemic. Notre Dame went back in person in the fall, so we were all sitting there. We taught that class in the football stadium, and we were all wearing face masks in one of the sky boxes that the donors have in this massive room, and wearing face masks and struggling through the pandemic. And I had two young women in the class, and they’d just worked on the first draft of their apology essay, and they were crossing the street coming back from an event, and were hit by a drunk driver and killed.
And they were international students, and their family had to travel to the United States a few days later for the memorial masses for these two young women, and it was a huge ordeal. And Notre Dame, to their credit, put on this big in-person memorial service for these two women, even though it was really challenging.
And we got to give the parents the first drafts of these essays that these women had written, and they’d both chosen to write about love, unsurprisingly. When people are asked what really matters in their life, that’s one of the key sections. And one in particular had written about how much she loves her brother and what that feels like for her now that they’re separated.
And for us to be able to give—they’d never vocalized these things, or they had maybe in a quick text, like, “LOL, hugging face.” But it had never—their parents had never experienced five single-spaced pages of, “This is what love of you has meant in my life.” And to be able to take that artifact and give that to these grieving family members reminded me: This is the most important thing we could do.
I don’t care, you know, your “Compare and contrast Kant and Marx.” Yeah blah, blah, blah. That’s great. This is a little fragment of these women’s souls that we finally managed to wrap our hands around that we could give back to you when the rest of it is just grievously ripped from your hands.
Brooks: Wow. That’s an incredible story. Very moving.
So we’ve talked about love a lot in this conversation, and so my question to you is: Are you in the wrong business? I think of philosophy as about cognition. And so that would imply that being a good person is about having the right beliefs. You guys work on beliefs. But it doesn’t seem to me that being a good person is really mostly about beliefs. If it was, moral philosophers would be better than the rest of us. And sorry, you guys aren’t. I mean, you’re obviously better than the economists.
Sullivan: Yeah, for sure.
Brooks: But, but they’re not better than—
Sullivan: No, definitely not.
Brooks: But then when you think about, say, the church scandals. The guys who abused those children and then covered up for it, they had sat through a million sermons. They probably had the right beliefs. But we would say there was something poisoned in their soul that they are willing to damage another human being or cover up that damage.
So how do you think about the relationship between what I would call the desires and emotions, and reason? Are you too much in the reason business?
Sullivan: I think you could definitely accuse a lot of philosophers of that. My friend Eric Schwitzgebel did this really interesting study about, a social-psychology study, where he basically looked at whether your typical professional philosopher is more or less moral in everyday decision making than the kinda standard human. And you’ll be shocked, stunned to learn that your typical philosopher is a little bit less honest in ordinary situations, a little bit less moral than maybe their baseline American.
But this should not come as a surprise to those of us who study the tradition of philosophy. Aristotle, our guy, our main man again, addresses this in his second lecture in Book 2 of the Nicomachean Ethics. He says, Here’s the deal with philosophy and the good life. A lot of folks spend time collecting data, collecting beliefs, collecting ideas. But they don’t actually practice what these beliefs preach. They are like people who collect a lot of advice from physicians and then never follow it.
Your doctor says, “You need to get healthy. You need to stop eating so many fatty and sugary foods, and you need to exercise every day.” And I collect this, and I write about it on Twitter, but then I never actually do the thing, and then I’m shocked that I’m not healthy.
So many philosophers are like doctors who don’t exercise. They have studied the theory of the case pretty well, and it’s good that human beings have this kind of theoretical knowledge, but if you’re not willing to actually make this a way of life, you are not gonna receive the benefits of it.
And unfortunately, way too many professional philosophers and professional scholars generally are like the doctors who aren’t willing to give up the sugary treats. They just collect all the data, but they don’t actually make it any part of how they care for their souls. So that’s not surprising.
That’s not to say we don’t want the data, we don’t wanna think about the ideas. It’s just to say the ideas get you, like, 20 percent of the way there. The rest of the 80 percent is actually trying to have a way of life.
Brooks: I’ve really enjoyed our conversation, and I am so grateful and honored, and now proud, if I can say that—
Sullivan: Ooh, dangerous.
Brooks: —to have had Meghan Sullivan as our first guest on The Permanent Questions. Thanks so much for being here.
Sullivan: Oh, it’s great to be with you, and I’m so glad that this exists.

Bangladesh wants to ‘reset’ ties with India, calls Hasina-era relationship ‘uncomfortable’
Relations between India and Bangladesh came under strain over New Delhi's decision to provide refuge to ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina.
Bangladesh wants to "reset" its ties with India and establish a new bilateral relationship centred on mutual interests, the country’s state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said, adding that the relationship during the tenure of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina was "uncomfortable".
The remarks came days after Bangladesh said that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would not attend the BRICS Summit in India as he was not “properly invited” to the event.
Notably, India had invited Rahman for a bilateral visit and also to attend the BRICS Summit as the chair of BIMSTEC. However, Dhaka reportedly did not formally accept either invitation, HT reported earlier.
Bangladesh says it wants to ‘reset’ ties with India
Relations between India and Bangladesh came under strain over New Delhi's decision to provide refuge to Hasina, who fled to India after being ousted from office amid a youth-led movement in August 2024.
Kobir told reporters in Dhaka on Sunday that Bangladesh wants to "reset" its bilateral relationship with India.
"We want to move towards a new relationship, which should be done through bilateral discussions, not through a multilateral forum," he said.
Kobir said Bangladesh should move away from what he called an "excessive preoccupation" with India and deal with New Delhi in a more balanced way. He said the focus should remain on shared interests and be viewed as part of its broader ties with other countries.
Replying to a question, the minister said, "Breakfast in India, lunch in India, dinner in India -- then when will you eat your own food?"
"We have to get out of the India fascination. India is just another country, and Bangladesh wants good bilateral relations with it," he said.
He clarified that his earlier comments were specifically about India and the need to rebuild ties through direct talks.
“What I said was mainly applicable to India. We want to build a good working bilateral relationship with India,” he said.
Bangladesh says reviewing 101 pacts signed with India
Nurul Islam Moni, the chief whip of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) in parliament, said on Friday that Dhaka was reviewing 101 agreements signed with India.
Asked whether agreements allowing ships from friendly countries to use the Chattogram and Mongla ports would be cancelled, Moni said, “We are reviewing the agreements, all 101 MoUs. You will get the outcome very soon, very soon.”
Kobir was asked about the review of the 101 MoUs. He told reporters that the agreements were being examined as part of the parliamentary process, Bangladesh's The Daily Star reported.

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.
The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.
Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.
The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.
Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”
UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.
Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.
“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.
Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.
The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.
Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.
“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”
She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”
Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.
“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.
“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”
FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.
A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

Kosovo gets new government but political impasse persists
Kosovo lawmakers have voted in a new government led by Prime Minister Albin Kurti
PRISTINA, Kosovo -- PRISTINA, Kosovo (AP) — Kosovo lawmakers on Sunday voted into office a new government of Prime Minister Albin Kurti following an early election in June in the small Balkan nation that remains locked in a prolonged political crisis.
Kurti's government received support from a slim majority of 62 lawmakers in the 120-member assembly. Opposition lawmakers boycotted the session, accusing Kurti of violating postelection procedures.
Disagreements between key political players in Kosovo have led to an impasse over more than 18 months, which has not been resolved despite two early ballots.
Lawmakers failed to elect deputy speakers of the assembly. Opposition parties insisted on their election before the vote on the new government is held.
The crisis first started after an election in February 2025, when no party won enough votes to form a government. An early election in December 2025 ended with Kurti forming the government but parties could not agree on the president.
To choose a president, Kosovo’s 120-member assembly needs a quorum of at least 80 lawmakers, which Kurti did not have.
Kurti's ruling center-left Vetevendosje party again won most votes after the election in June, but less than the previous time as voter disappointment and frustration appeared to grow.
Opposition parties said they will take the alleged postelection procedural mistakes to the Constitutional Court. If the crisis drags on, it could push Kosovo into yet another early election.
Kosovo is among the youngest and poorest countries in Europe. The predominantly ethnic Albanian nation declared independence from Serbia in 2008 following a 1998-99 war that ended in a NATO bombing that forced Serbia to withdraw.
Kosovo has been recognized by the United States and most EU countries but not by Serbia and its allies Russia and China. Pristina and Belgrade have been told they must mend relations to move forward with their EU membership bids.

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) South-East Asia Region head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday (September 10, 2026) following fraud investigations by the U.N. agency and Bangladeshi authorities, according to sources.
The WHO placed Ms. Wazed, who took office in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025, in a move that followed Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filing cases for fraud, forgery, and misuse of power against.
The WHO accused Ms. Wazed of “committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China” and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026. She has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
What Saima Wazed said in her reisgnation letter
Ms. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country’s independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, osuted PM Hasina’s father. “I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done,” Ms. Wazed said in her resignation letter to Mr. Tedros sent late on Wednesday (September 10, 2026).
“Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO,” she wrote. “Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside.” She declined to comment further.
Saima Wazed | Rise of the daughter
The role of WHO regional head
In the role of South-East Asia regional director, Ms. Wazed was mandated to direct international health work in 11 countries, an area with a population of over two billion people. She is a licensed school psychologist, nationally certified in the U.S.
Ms. Wazed’s appointment as Regional Director had also been under the scanner, with charges of having used her mother’s influence during the campaign, and of providing false information on her academic record during in her candidature for the post, allegedly violating Section 468 of the Bangladesh Penal Code (forgery for the purpose of cheating), and Section 471 (forging a document).
Regional directors are among the world’s most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the South-East Asia region.
Two sources told Reuters earlier that the U.N. agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.

CRICKET
Amritsar Soormas crowned champion of Sher-E-Punjab T20 League
Amritsar Soormas was crowned Sher-E-Punjab T20 League champion following its eight-wicket win over Ludhiana Lions on Sunday.
Opting to bowl, the Soormas produced an impressive bowling performance to restrict Ludhiana Lions to 142 in 20 overs.
Amritsar made an excellent start with the ball, picking up wickets at regular intervals and putting the Lions under pressure from the early stages.
Ludhiana struggled to build partnerships and slipped to 86/7, with captain Salil Arora, Abhijeet Garg and Krish Bhagat among the key batters dismissed.
Mayank Markande was the standout bowler for the Soormas. The leg-spinner bowled a disciplined four-over spell and finished with figures of 3/17, making important breakthroughs and keeping the scoring rate under control.
Ludhiana looked to steady the innings when Harish Kumar and Jassinder Singh came together. The pair started rebuilding and gave the Lions some hope of reaching a competitive total.
However, Shubham Rana broke the partnership by dismissing Jassinder for 14 off 12 balls.
Harish then joined hands with Sahil Bhaskar as the two staged a late fightback. They added 26 runs for the final wicket to take Ludhiana beyond the 140-run mark.
Despite their late effort, Amritsar’s bowlers had done enough damage through the first 15 overs to keep the Lions in check. Ludhiana eventually finished on 142, setting the Soormas a target of 143.
In the chase, Amritsar lost Jashanpreet Singh early, but Naman Dhir and Sahaj Dhawan quickly put the innings back on track.
The pair added 58 runs, with Dhir continuing his aggressive approach. The Soormas captain was eventually dismissed for a quick 29 off 12 balls, but by then Amritsar were firmly in control.
Dhawan continued to guide the chase and was joined by Rahul Kumar. The duo ensured there were no further setbacks as Amritsar comfortably chased down the target at the I.S. Bindra Stadium.
- PTI

Content warning: The following article has references to suicide. Please avoid reading if you feel distressed by the subject.
The semicolon, a punctuation mark often used while writing, signifies a pause -- one that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. It signifies a break and not the end. And sometimes, such a pause might just be what a person needs -- to ensure that the end can stay away, if not forever, at least for the time being. This is what prompted Amy Bleuel to use the punctuation mark as the symbol for the movement that she founded to raise awareness on suicide prevention and mental health.
Today, the semicolon tattoo is one of the most recognised symbols of mental health awareness in the world. But how and when did it all begin?
Project Semicolon was founded in 2013 by Bleuel, a suicide prevention and mental health advocate, to honour her father, who died by suicide ten years ago. The intention was to create a space for people to talk about mental health openly and without any shame. According to the project’s website, the semicolon became a symbol for the movement as it “is used when an author could’ve ended a sentence but chose not to… the semicolon became a symbol for anyone who could’ve ended their own life but chose to keep going.” The movement caught the attention of people worldwide and so did the semicolon tattoo.
People began tattooing the semicolon on their bodies, either as a standalone or by adding it as an element within other hybrid tattoos. These tattoos were used by survivors to honour their personal mental health battles. People have also embraced the tattoo as tributes to their loved ones who had died by suicide, while others don their tattoos as an expression of solidarity to the movement and raise awareness about mental health and suicide prevention. “For many, it’s a daily reminder to keep fighting, to keep writing, to keep living,” reads a quote on their site.
The placement of the tattoo is a matter of choice and people sport them on various parts of their body including on visible locations such as the neck, wrists, etc., while others place it in more intimate areas. The tattoos are not just meant to express but also serve as a means of personal affirmation.
The project deals with spreading awareness not just on suicide prevention but also on various other aspects of mental health including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and various other struggles. “What started as one woman’s act of hope has grown into a global movement — one inked semicolon at a time,” says the project’s website.
In 2017, Selena Gomez, Alisha Boe and Tommy Dorfman got the semicolon tattooed on their wrists to commemorate the premiere of their Netflix series 13 Reasons Why. The web series deals with themes of suicide and mental health and it was reported that the stars got the tattoo as a tribute to the show’s handling of the theme as well as the death of Bleuel, a victim of trauma, child abuse and rape.
Various regional organisations, projects, campaigns, etc., inspired by the semicolon project have come up in various parts of the world. India has also not shied away from embracing the movement. Semicolon (;) The Mental Health Awareness Project – India is one such initiative.
Founded by the Medical Students Association of India (MSAI) under the International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations (IFMSA), it was designed as a campaign model that could be leveraged by other local chapters. The project aims to create awareness regarding mental health and tackle the stigma associated with the same, among high school students from classes eighth to 10th.
If you are in distress, please reach out to national helpline 104 or any of these 24x7 helplines.

Telangana is exploring a proposal to make six months of robotic surgery training mandatory for postgraduate medical students, as the State looks to build a trained workforce to expand advanced robotic procedures across its government hospitals.
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said the government would approach the National Medical Commission (NMC) for permission to introduce the dedicated training period as part of the three-year postgraduate programme.
Speaking at the ‘State Level Multi-Specialty Robotic Surgery Workshop’ at the Marri Chenna Reddy Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences (MCR TIMS), Sanathnagar in Hyderabad, the Minister said training would be central to Telangana’s plans to expand robotic surgery, whether through a hub-and-spoke model or dedicated robotic surgery facilities at the district level.
The proposal comes as Telangana is already attempting to build a statewide pool of surgeons trained in robotic procedures.
MCR TIMS Director Dr A. Narendra Kumar said surgeons from 35 medical colleges and 47 hospitals, excluding speciality hospitals, are being trained in robotic surgery at two government institutions, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) and MNJ Cancer Institute.

“The idea is to ensure that robotic surgery does not remain concentrated in a handful of premier institutions in Hyderabad,” he added.
Robotic surgery expert Dr. Sudhir Srivastava said such a model could allow specialist expertise to reach patients without requiring them to travel to major cities. He pointed to the financial and emotional burden faced by families from rural and smaller communities when they have to leave their homes to access specialised treatment.
Former NIMS Director Dr N. Bheerappa said NIMS had recently completed nearly 1,000 robotic surgeries and that the government was bearing the cost of such procedures for eligible patients through the Rajiv Aarogyasri health scheme.
Director of Medical Education (DME) Dr N. Vani said government medical colleges had a dual responsibility of providing patient care while training the next generation of doctors. Introducing young surgeons to newer technologies, she said, could have a multiplier effect across the government healthcare system.
She also stressed that young surgeons should not rely solely on the technology, but must combine it with clinical judgement, human touch and compassion.
Experts at the workshop also cautioned that expanding robotic surgery is about considerably more than installing machines. Government Medical College Nagpur Dean Dr. Raj Gajbhiye said robotic surgery was no longer merely a technology available at a few high-end private institutions.
For government hospitals, however, he said “the real objective should be equitable access to advanced surgical technology. “Success of robotics is not about purchasing a robot,” Dr. Gajbhiye said, pointing instead to the need for appropriate infrastructure, trained faculty, structured protocols, multidisciplinary teamwork and institutional support.

Abbott Laboratories will pay $385 million to resolve claims tied to an investigation of contamination at a baby formula factory in Sturgis, Michigan, the largest in the country, which led to the supply shortages in 2022.
Problems at the facility prompted a lawsuit by the Justice Department and recall of powdered infant formula at the facility.
The recall covered several infant formula brands, including Similac, and squeezed inventory that had already been strained by supply chain disruptions and stockpiling during Covid-19 shutdowns.
The settlement, which Abbott says does not represent any finding of fault or liability, also pertains to lawsuits filed by certain relators and the Attorneys General of several states.
Abbott said on Monday that tests by government regulators of unopened product from the homes of the infants under investigation at the time of the 2022 recall were negative for Cronobacter sakazakii, a bacterium that can cause illness in infants. The company also said that no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive for Cronobacter sakazakii.
The Justice Department under President Donald Trump closed its criminal investigation into the matter.
The Biden administration eased import rules for foreign manufacturers, airlifted formula from Europe and invoked federal emergency rules to prioritize U.S. production during the supply shortage.
Abbott closed the Sturgis facility in February 2022 after the Food and Drug Administration began an investigation. The plant was reopened by June of that year.
— Michelle Chapman

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

Imagine a pharmaceutical company spends nearly four years touting a ground-breaking new medicine that will cure all diseases.
Early evidence supporting those claims is limited, and massive questions remain, but the company continues to make progress. Criticism and concerns, while addressed, don't slow its aggressive push.
After all, investors believe this is the real deal. (Or at least a really good bet.)
And then right before the pharma company unveils its fancy new drug, it gives a shocking update: It turns out the medicine could also be a poison. So, for the safety of all involved, progress in the space needs to be slowed to ensure things don't go off the rails.
That's basically the big debate going on in AI land these days.
After years of telling us how groundbreaking their tech will be, AI leaders like Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and xAI's Elon Musk are saying we need to slow the development of their most advanced models or risk a very dark future for humanity.
Is it about safety, or self-preservation?
A tumultuous 2026 for AI
Silicon Valley has been warning about the downside of AI for years. But this weekend was the type of coordinated response the industry has rarely seen.
The calls for an AI slowdown aren't happening in a vacuum. The industry's facing pressure on multiple fronts these days. Data centers, for one, have drawn the public's ire. AI's biggest supporters have even said the industry needs to do a better job of pitching itself to people.
The business case for AI remains an open question. Tired of hearing about its potential, investors and analysts are increasingly pressuring public companies to show their returns on these massive AI bets that are burning cash.
Open-weight models, a cheaper alternative to pricey frontier models, are causing headaches for companies trying to make money from model development.
Two of the biggest players in the space — Anthropic and OpenAI — are also preparing for their public debuts. That means opening up their books and themselves to even more scrutiny.
And while both have previously acknowledged the risks of AI, that hasn't slowed them down. Even Amodei, one of the biggest proponents of AI safety, has a habit of simultaneously warning about the risks while advancing new models.
This time, Amodei's concerns don't seem to be slowing its IPO plans. On Sunday, my colleague Katie Roof reported that Anthropic tapped Nasdaq for its public listing.
The benefit of a delay
Pacing AI development solves a lot of those problems.
Let's take the AI leaders' proposal at face value. In that light, it's easy to see how creating more guardrails would capture the goodwill of the general public, something it's definitely lacking.
Behind the scenes, adding any regulatory framework benefits the people already ahead. The biggest players can help write the new rules, leaving smaller players on the outside looking in.
Compliance also tends to be a costly endeavor — lawyers aren't cheap! — which is another hurdle for upstarts in the space hoping to catch up.
And then there's the biggest advantage a slowdown provides: a built-in excuse.
How come you didn't hit your Q4 targets? Safety concerns required us to take a more measured approach. Why isn't that new enterprise product out? We are choosing to innovate at a pace we are comfortable with. Why haven't your costs come down? There are built-in expenses we cannot cut if we want to stay committed to building safe models.
Those safety concerns are already affecting OpenAI. Sam Altman said it's an "ill-advised" time to IPO.
Students have dogs that eat homework. AI companies now have the fate of humanity to worry about before they can hit analysts' estimates or investors' expectations.
But what if the risk is real?
I'm not suggesting there aren't real issues with the pace of AI development. The tech does seem capable of eventually doing some pretty terrible things if not kept in check.
But choosing to take a coordinated approach to this issue now, after billions of dollars have been raised and valuations have skyrocketed, is very convenient.
What if something truly changed that scared AI leaders into wanting a pause?
I've heard this theory floated for a while. Models can make big leaps in a short amount of time. Something could be happening behind the scenes that has them all worried.
If that's the case, the most likely solution will be … more AI.
But even if this is about how humans fit into that equation, the AI apocalypse debate raises another important question. One that AI giants probably won't want to answer.
If the tech is so powerful that the AI giants are unsure how to handle it, why are these company leaders the right people to handle it in the first place?

Police say it could take months to identify Philippine ferry fire victims
- Published
Philippine authorities said it could take weeks or months to identify victims of a ferry fire that killed 76 people last week.
"Most of them are already in a charred condition," Richard Allan Mangalip, a forensic specialist from the Philippine National Police, told reporters on Sunday. Family members have been asked to help identify victims with personal items or DNA samples.
The MV June Aster was heading from Manila to Coron in Palawan province, a popular holiday destination, when a fire started in its cargo hold and spread rapidly throughout the vessel.
Forty-three people survived the disaster, while 13 people remain unaccounted for, authorities said.
Mangalip said they were "trying [their] best to collect the possible identifying marks" from victims' remains.
But it was hard to give a clear timeline on how long the identification process would take because of the volume of specimens, he said, adding, "It could be weeks, or it could be months."
A coast guard official said on Saturday that the priority was identifying victims and determining the cause of the blaze.
The fire continued burning for more than a day, releasing heat and toxic fumes that impeded search and rescue operations. It took more than 40 hours before rescuers could board the ship in search of survivors.
The MV June Aster had set off last Tuesday from Manila to Coron, a popular destination among both local and foreign tourists, known for its beaches and WW2 shipwreck diving sites.
Besides tourists, there were also passengers on the ferry who had been travelling to Coron for work or to visit family.
Survivors recall hearing a loud explosion before seeing smoke and fire. When fire engulfed the ship, chaos erupted on board, they said.
One told the BBC that he had been trampled after falling on the floor. He jumped off the boat into the sea before being rescued hours later.
But many burned to death on the ship. Mangalip said at the press conference on Sunday that some victims' remains were found clustered together in parts of the vessel.
"Our thoughts are also with the survivors and families still waiting for news of their loved ones," the Philippine Coast Guard said in a statement on Sunday. "We recognise the pain and uncertainty they continue to endure as recovery and identification efforts remain underway."

Jammu, Sep 14: The Jammu and Kashmir National Health Mission Employees Association (JKNHMEA) has extended its ongoing peaceful protest/strike for another 72 hours across the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, beginning September 15.
In a formal communication addressed to the Mission Director, National Health Mission, J&K, the Association said the decision had been taken due to the continued pendency of its long-standing demands and the absence of a concrete, time-bound resolution from the authorities.
The Association said the extended protest would remain completely peaceful, democratic and constitutional, with participating employees directed to maintain discipline and uphold public order.
The employees also reiterated their willingness to engage in dialogue with the government and expressed hope that meaningful and time-bound measures would be initiated to address their genuine grievances.
The communication, issued by the Joint Coordination Committee of the J&K National Health Mission Employees Association, said the extension would remain effective for 72 hours from September 15.
The Association has also forwarded the communication to senior authorities, including the Union Ministers for Health and Family Welfare and Labour and Employment, the Lieutenant Governor of J&K, the Chief Minister, and the Ministers for Health and Medical Education and Labour and Employment in the Union Territory.
The continued agitation is expected to further affect health services, particularly in rural and remote areas of Jammu and Kashmir, where NHM employees form an important part of the healthcare workforce.

This is what women in sport look like - Hunt
- Published
British sprinter Amy Hunt is among the female athletes to speak out against a controversial sports gambling advert starring actress Sydney Sweeney.
The advert has gone viral online and features American Sweeney naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.
It has sparked a strong reaction, with many female athletes criticising its sexualisation of women in sport, and how they are being defined by their appearance rather than their achievements as sportswomen.
Hunt, who became a four-time European champion earlier this summer, referenced the advert after she ran a season's best 22.10 seconds to finish fourth in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday.
"Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt said in her post-race interview with BBC Sport.
Referring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, she added: "21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening."
American actress Sweeney, 29, starred in the television series Euphoria and her films include Anyone But You and The Housemaid.
The backlash has included many other athletes from a range of sports posting videos of themselves competing or training, and describing the frustrations and struggles they have faced throughout their careers.
The trend was started by American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted a montage of herself training with the caption, "I don't know what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what women in sport look like."
Australia's four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus said: "Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is.
"How do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing?"
British cyclist and Olympic champion Sophie Capewell MBE, rugby players Lisa Neumann and Ellie Boatman and Australian water polo Olympian Tilly Kearns also shared their stories.
Sweeney has not commented in response but she took to social media to post a range of photos of other athletes posing naked or in limited clothing, appearing to suggest hypocrisy.
The photos were a series of ESPN covers featuring the likes of tennis star Serena Williams and MMA fighter and wrestler Ronda Rousey, alongside male athletes including NFL player Myles Garrett and basketball player Karl-Anthony Towns.

Since the days immediately following the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, U.S. President Donald Trump, a native of New York City, has made numerous claims about what he saw that day and his involvement in the recovery efforts.
One such claim Trump has repeatedly made is his assertion that he was at Ground Zero within days of 9/11 and that he sent workers to the recovery effort at the site of the World Trade Center.
In September 2026, multiple X users debated the veracity of the claim. For example, one user (archived) wrote, "There's no proof Trump sent a large group of construction workers to Ground Zero."
Other popular (archived) posts (archived) said there was no evidence Trump, himself, went to Ground Zero and helped with recovery efforts.
Another X post (archived) alternatively claimed, "President Trump is dropping VIDEO PROOF for every Fake News outlet lying to millions that he was nowhere near Ground Zero after 9/11."
(X)
Many Snopes readers searched the site to find out if Trump's claims were true.
A couple of days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Trump told multiple news media outlets that he sent at least 100 workers to Ground Zero to help pull people and bodies out of the rubble, with 125 to 150 more on the way. However, Snopes has never been able to identify any public evidence that crews he hired helped in the immediate recovery of the 9/11 attacks. Since we cannot independently confirm with certainty whether Trump had crews on site somewhere, we are leaving this claim unrated.
Footage of interviews Trump conducted in the immediate days after 9/11 placed him within blocks of Ground Zero. Trump said in those interviews that he visited Ground Zero to encourage the workers he said he brought to assist with clearing rubble at the site. It was not possible to find evidence showing Trump helped clear the pile of debris at Ground Zero, as some posts disputed.
In a phone call with a local news media station immediately after the planes crashed into the Twin Towers, Trump said he watched the towers fall from the window of one of his buildings.
Trump's September 2026 remarks
On Sept. 8, 2026, in a post on Truth Social (archived), Trump continued to maintain that he was at Ground Zero with construction workers after 9/11, clarifying that it was "obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter":
The Failing New York Magazine wrote a story that I wasn't down at the World Trade Center after the Tragedy of September 11th, because nobody saw me there. Well, I don't think I would be the first thing on anyone's mind but, I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers.
He then added he "was there as soon as the Law allowed."
The president was referencing a New York Magazine article disputing his comments about where he was on the day of, and the days following, the attacks.
Trump also made this claim (archived) in a Fox News interview two days prior, in which he added the additional context that he was constructing a new building in New York City. This is the reason, according to Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event on Sept. 8, why he had workers who he could bring to the rubble of the World Trade Center:
I was building a big building in New York and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened and they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me. We went down as a big group of people. It wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest.
What Trump told the media in 2001
Trump spoke to the media multiple times a few days after 9/11. On Sept. 13, he told a German news channel, that he had more than 100 men down at the site of the World Trade Center and more than 125 on their way. According to the German-speaking reporter, the interview was conducted a few blocks from Ground Zero.
That same day, NBC News interviewed Trump at what appeared to be the same location as his interview with the German news channel. Trump said he had "hundreds of men inside working right now" and was bringing down another 125.
PBS has a recording of another Trump interview from Sept. 13, in which Trump said he had 100 workers helping to dig people and bodies out of the rubble at the World Trade Center, with another 100 to 150 workers "coming." He told PBS that those workers were "digging out" at the site.
In another interview from that day, Trump told reporters his workers had been at Ground Zero "for about a day and a half." He said they were men from his company and that a couple had gotten hurt while working at the site. He also said he was just down at Ground Zero and was there to support them.
The evidence
When Snopes first researched this claim in 2018, we spoke to Richard Alles, a retired deputy chief with the New York City Fire Department, who later served as director of 9/11 community affairs for the law firm Barasch McGarry Salzman and Penson. Alles said that in all his time he spent at Ground Zero as a New York City Fire Department battalion chief, starting 20 minutes after the buildings collapsed, he never saw a large group of workers whom Trump had hired at the site assisting with search and rescue efforts. "This is the first I'm hearing of it," Alles said via phone call. "There would have been no need for that. Between police, fire and the construction crews, we had it all covered."
Alles added that the construction crews he saw at Ground Zero helping rescue workers were from the trade unions and were not hired by Trump.
John Feal, founder of the 9/11 first responder health advocacy nonprofit the FealGood Foundation, told Snopes at the time that he responded to Ground Zero on Sept. 12, 2001, as a construction demolitions expert and that he didn't see evidence of hundreds of workers hired by Trump at the site.
The Trump Organization was building in New York City in 2001, according to the Skyscraper Center database on skyscrapers. In fact, it finished a series of residential buildings in the city at Trump Place between 1998 and 2004. He was also building the Trump World Tower residential building near the United Nations Headquarters that year.
However, it was not possible to find verifiable information about how many people, either directly employed by Trump or contracted to work on one of the Trump Organization's projects, were working on these buildings and in New York City at the time.
A New York Times fact-check from July 2019 referenced Timothy O'Brien, the author of "TrumpNation: The Art of Being the Donald," who reportedly said the Trump Organization numbered "a little bit over a dozen people" at the time of the attacks, making it impossible to send as many workers to the relief effort as Trump claimed.
Neither the White House nor the Trump Organization responded to Snopes' requests for corroborating evidence in 2018. This lack of response is consistent with past attempts by Politifact, The Washington Post, The New York Times and Politifact again to reach out to the White House and/or the Trump Organization to corroborate evidence of Trump's claims.

In early September 2026, as Repulican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn campaigned for governor of Tennessee, many people online claimed she announced a plan to bring segregation back to schools in the state if elected.
For example, a Facebook post stated:
BREAKING: Marsha Blackburn has announced that if she wins her bid for governor she will bring segregation back to Tennessee schools with the pilot program being in Chattanooga. "The supreme court will side with President Trump and I on this. The way we see it kids feel more comfortable with other kids that look like them."
(Facebook user, Chattanooga Enquirer)
Snopes readers emailed us to ask whether the claim was true.
The claim originated from an account that was satirical in nature. Blackburn did not say she would bring back school segregation in Tennessee. As such, this claim is labeled satire.
The post came from the Chattanooga Enquirer, a Facebook page that describes itself as a "Satire/Parody" media company. The introduction to the page states: "The one stop shop for Chattanooga's fake but maybe real news."
We searched for the purported quote featured in the post on Google, DuckDuckGo (archived), and Bing, and found no evidence of Blackburn ever making this announcement.
Blackburn has long been an opponent of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, and critical race theory in schools. On her Senate website, Blackburn calls CRT "a radical school of thought used by the political left to assign racial significance to objectively neutral concepts like history and mathematics." She adds, "This dangerous agenda insists that America is a racist country and teaches that all individuals are either oppressors or victims."
As Snopes previously reported, CRT looks to the law for answers as to why racial inequality persists even as American founding documents and aspirational ideals vaunt equality, and after the Civil Rights Movement brought about landmark legislation aimed at ending racism de jure.
According to data from the 2023-2024 school year collected by Stanford University, Tennessee is ranked sixth among the most racially segregated public schools in the country.
For further reading, Snopes previously reported on the false claim that Blackburn flashed a "white power gesture" during a Senate hearing.

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.
Additional reporting by Ahmed Bahajj
