Earlier this year, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) which affects one in eight women worldwide, was renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) by the Endocrine Society.
A global consensus article published in the Lancet in May, led by Professor Helena J. Teede, argued that the name reduced a long-term hormonal and endocrine disorder to focus on ovaries and cysts, leading to inadequate treatment, or fewer people getting diagnosed with the condition.
Professor Terhi Piltonen, president of International Androgen Excess and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Society (AE-PCOS Society), and also one of the co-leads of the Lancet publication, from Oulu University Hospital, Finland, in conversation with The Hindu speaks about the name change, and its implications on patients, treatment plans, and research.
Excerpts from the interview:
Can you tell me about the process of renaming the syndrome from PCOS to PMOS?
It was sustained work over 14 years that eventually led to the name change. Earlier, there were some individual opinion papers. There were fifty-six societies were invited to be part of the whole process. And about one hundred persons represented these organisations, the patient organisations, and healthcare professionals.
We had meetings where we narrowed down on the different opinions, and we had to take into consideration many different aspects; cultural aspects, acceptability, and adaptability to understand how is it that we want it to change the life of these women. It's been a long process, but the last bit of the process took around two years.
How would the name change impact existing treatment protocol?
We are now thinking about it in a more holistic way; not only looking at the ovary, but also looking at how it affects the mood, the psychological profile, the metabolic profile and also the menstrual cycles. And I think I'm hoping that with the new name, we will now understand that this is a whole-body syndrome.
We know how to manage it, but the name change emphasises how we need to listen to the patients and take a more holistic view and invite other disciplines to play their part.
The women need the opportunity to be asked about their mental health issues, weight management, their skin, their quality of life, how they manage at work, and when they would like to conceive so that we can anticipate how they can have overall good health.
Does the name change impact the research that is being conducted?
There is a three-year overlap period where we are going to put in the codes for PCOS and PMOS while researching and eventually we will transition to using PMOS.
But of course, I am hoping that we'll see more diverse studies, for example my colleague who is an endocrinologist or in internal medicine, or a dermatologist, might take an interest in researching certain parts of the condition. So far, it was only OB-GYNs who were diagnosing it. But I think that others might acknowledge their work in seeing PMOS.
Is it also monetarily challenging to conduct research in an area that impacts women, and not men?
Yes, it is. This is only a fraction of the money that goes into erectile problems or diabetes. , In terms of funding, I think it is not proportional to the prevalence. I'm hoping that there will be more grants and that the industry would get involved as they now know that it is a condition that needs a lot of different approaches.
PMOS is often seen as a ‘modern’ condition. How true or untrue would you say that is?
When we think about nutrition, our bodies haven't been developed to be capable of dealing with very high energy foods. In our evolution, there has been a problem of not having enough food, and we had been moving around and collecting things, and having low-calorie food for thousands and millions of years. And now in a very short time, we have entered a period where food is available, that too, food with high-energy content. So, I think it kind of became a disadvantage for this type of genotype that women have.
And in society now, we have lots of pressure with hectic work lives, and with social media, and other stress factors. This sort of environment does not really serve any of the people who are sensitive to stress. And women are especially sensitive to stress altogether. I think it is linked to modern society in one way, but it does not mean that it's not relevant or that it is not meaningful.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): On the day when Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi is scheduled to interact with Gen-Z in Indore, the state government will hold its own programme for young achievers in Bhopal.
Gandhi’s Chhatron ki Goonj programme is scheduled for September 19 in Indore, while the state government has set the same date for the distribution of Scooty assistance to meritorious Class 12 students in Bhopal. Both the events are aimed at drawing Gen-Z to their fold.
The school education department’s programme has seen several changes in dates and venue over the past few days. It was initially scheduled for September 11 in Indore.
The programme was later cancelled and shifted to Bhopal. It was to be held on September 16 but has been postponed again and will be held on September 19.
Over 7,500 students to get Scooty assistance
Under the programme, meritorious Class 12 students will receive financial assistance for purchasing a Scooty.
Over 7,500 meritorious students will receive scooters under the state government’s Scooty Yojana, for which Rs 200 crore has been allocated.
Eligible students will receive Rs 1 lakh to Rs 1.25 lakh to buy petrol or electric scooters, with e-scooters gaining preference this year.

The Global Fintech Festival (GFF) 2026 came to a close today with three days of conversations, launches, and partnerships. Following a day focused on partnership announcements between traditional financial institutions and fintech and AI startups, the ecosystem continued to capitalise on the momentum to roll out another wave of new developments. Here are some of the top launches from the final day of GFF 2026… BharatPeX Launches Enterprise Payment Gateway with Dynamic Routing BharatPe’s enterprise payments division BharatPeX launched a payment gateway targeting ecommerce and fintechs enterprises. The platform offers a single integration supporting over 100 payment options, including UPI, cards, net banking, and bank transfers via IMPS, NEFT, or RTGS. It consolidates checkout, settlements, refunds, payouts, and automated reconciliation into a unified operational dashboard. It also features a dynamic routing engine that directs transactions to acquiring bank partners based on real-time success rates, card BIN performance as well as service availability. Additionally, the BharatPeX Payment Gateway offers capabilities like native OTP, tokenisation and CVV-less payment experiences, as well as EMI options, recurring payments, and virtual account tracking. PayU Rolls Out Agent HQ for SMB Merchants Prosus-owned fintech startup PayU launched Agent HQ, an AI agent storefront designed to help small and medium business (SMB) merchants deploy autonomous agents across sales, marketing, and operations. As search traffic transitions toward GenAI platforms, Agent HQ enables merchants to make their product catalogs discoverable and transactable directly on AI search systems like ChatGPT and Claude. The no-code tool integrates directly into existing PayU dashboard without requiring additional developer integration. It is built on historical platform data from PayU’s network of over 4.5 Lakh merchants. “By putting a personalized team of AI agents to work across the business - from improving discoverability and driving growth to managing chargebacks, reconciliations, refunds, settlements, etc. - we want to put control back in merchants' hands, enabling them to focus on their growth,” said PayU’s CPO Manas Mishra. Union Minister Nitin Gadkari Launches OneTag To Enable FASTag Portability Union Minister of Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari launched OneTag, a portability solution for FASTags jointly developed by the Indian Highways Management Company (IHMCL) and the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). As it currently stands, vehicle owners looking to switch their issuer bank must replace the physical windshield tag and undergo onboarding again. OneTag reduces this friction by enabling users retain the same tag, bringing down reissuance costs. NPCI provides the underlying central architecture to update issuer records across the toll network. Meanwhile, users can avail the service through NHAI’s Rajmargyatra mobile app. Existing issuer banks manage customer verification, wallet closures, refunds, and pending settlements, while the user’s selected new bank will complete the onboarding and provide services after the tag is ported. The new tag will retain the same Tag ID linked to the same vehicle registration number.

Sundays this time of year mean only one thing:
Football.
As a New York Giants fan, with a new season underway, I can’t wait to see how Jaxson Dart, the young quarterback, and Malik Nabers, the young wide receiver, will perform in 2026. I’m not suggesting the duo will remind anyone of Montana and Rice, but as pitiful as the Giants have been the last three years, there is finally reason for hope in the Big Apple.
Yet I’m disturbed by the eventual cost to many players I root for and against. A number of them will suffer dementia. Some will die by suicide.
I wonder: Am I a hypocrite for still loving the sport?
The most recent evidence: According to a study by the British Medical Journal, close to 25% percent of the nearly 900 former players who died between 2016 and 2021 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease that often leads to dementia and suicide. The actual figure may be much higher, as the study relies on brains donated by athletes or their families.
Was I shocked by the study? Absolutely not.
I’ve known about CTE for close to two decades, even co-writing a book with sports agent Leigh Steinberg (the inspiration for the 1996 film “Jerry Maguire”), who had referred to the concussion issue as a “ticking time bomb.”
And did this knowledge prevent me from cheering when one of my Giants creamed an opponent carrying the ball?
Again, absolutely not.
So, what’s different now? Why the sudden guilt?
Maybe as I’m inching — sometimes it feels like speeding — toward the big 7-0, I recognize the cost to everything in ways I didn’t before.
In sports and in life.
One thing was certain: I needed to talk to those who have spent their lives around the game. To find out if I was, indeed, a hypocrite.
I first reached out to Bill Courtney, a high school football coach in Memphis and a good friend. I worked on a book with Courtney, the subject of “Undefeated,” which won the Academy Award in 2012 for best documentary.
Courtney, 58, also has deep concerns.
“I now know what I didn’t know as a young man and a young coach, and that is the game, as we play it today, can kill people.”
Nonetheless, he’s convinced he wouldn’t be as successful as he is now — he runs a lumber company in addition to coaching — if not for the lessons he learned as a player in high school. He also, like others, sees ways to make football safer.
One way is to not allow kids to put on a helmet and shoulder pads until sixth grade. Another is to change tackling techniques starting in junior high, as well as train and certify coaches who can teach them. “Any headfirst tackle would be a 15-yard penalty,” he said, “and the second time, you can’t play anymore.”
Courtney makes sense. Except, even if the changes in tackling are implemented — and that would require a ton of will and cooperation from coaches around the country — any effects wouldn’t be noticeable at the professional level for many years.
I then spoke to Everson Walls, 66, a former defensive back for the Giants, Dallas Cowboys, and Cleveland Browns.
“I feel like a hypocrite as well,” he told me. “I don’t know how to back out of this. It [football] is a big part of who I am.” He said he wasn’t aware of the risks to his long-term health when he played in the 1980s and ’90s, but even if he had known, he is quite sure he would do it again. “Once you find out that you are really good,” Walls said, “I wouldn’t say ‘damn the consequences,’ but you are going to eagerly take that on.”
Is he worried about dementia?
Of course he is.
“My wife looks at me side-eyed all the time,” he said. “All [professional football players’] wives should. It would be foolish of them not to.”
Finally, I went to Steinberg. I knew from our talks years ago that he, too, had questioned his involvement with football. “I tortured myself with it,” he reminded me recently.
Ultimately, though, he decided it would be better to advocate for player health from inside the system instead of “drop out and feel morally superior.”
He said that with the players themselves now aware of the risks, that should be good enough for me. “They would be angry that because of the blows, people were turned off by the game,” he added.
Steinberg assured me progress has been made on several fronts with regard to concussions.
I felt more hopeful. Until he said something that is obvious and yet easy to forget:
“At the end of the day, it is a collision sport. There’s a traffic accident on every play.”
So, where do the three conversations leave me?
In the same spot as before: Rooting for my Giants. Yet troubled by the toll the game takes on the men who play it.
Michael Arkush has written or co-written 18 books, including New York Times best-sellers with Phil Jackson, Sugar Ray Leonard, and Scottie Pippen.

Actor Tatyana Ali is advocating for Black and Indigenous maternal health
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Actor and singer Tatyana Ali has become an important voice in a growing movement to improve maternity health outcomes for Black and Indigenous mothers and babies by addressing systemic racism and inequity in maternity care. Ali has been calling for reproductive justice since experiencing what she calls "obstetric violence" during the delivery of her first-born son Aszi in 2016.
Ali, 47, says being a mother is the most important role of her life, as she embarks on the latest chapter of her Hollywood career. She will compete on the new season of Dancing with the Stars on ABC, starting Tuesday, September 15. Ali is perhaps best known for her role as the lovable Ashley Banks on the NBC sitcom The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air in the 1990s. Since then, she has acted in TV and digital series, movies and released an album.
Ali and her husband Vaughn Rasberry are raising two sons, Alejandro and Aszi. In an interview with NPR, she said it was the birth of her oldest, Aszi, that eventually made her want to speak out for Black and Indigenous mothers.
Ali described having a normal pregnancy with Aszi and the days of waiting for his birth as filled with joy.
"So excited and just waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting. My mother's song when she was waiting for me was 'cuando, cuando, cuando – when when, when? When are you coming?' I sang that song. I thought we were prepared," she said.
But during the delivery at the hospital, Ali says her birth plan was immediately ignored. And she was physically restrained.
"It went from a small group of people in the room to many people in the room screaming, yelling at me," she said. "I was held down by about four people."
Ali described chaos and aggressive and dismissive behavior by the doctor and nurses.
"Faces, screaming, terror, panic. I needed somebody to help me," she said.
Ali says her hospital records detail the doctor using a high-risk emergency procedure that is rarely used. The Zavanelli maneuver is a last-resort procedure performed when a baby is stuck inside the birth canal. Ali says in her case, her son was already crowning when the doctor pushed him back inside of her. "After they pushed him inside me, and I remember roaring. I convulsed after that. Like my body – I can hear the bed just go buh-buh-buh-buh," she said, describing the sound of the bed shaking. "And I was out."
The doctor then performed an emergency c-section to deliver her son.
Aszi became strong enough to go home after several days in the neonatal intensive care unit. Ali says at the time, the hospital's head urologist told her the infant was in shock from his traumatic birth. Ali says it took some time for her to realize she had experienced "obstetric violence." She blames systemic racism in healthcare, after hearing similar stories from other women of color.
"It wasn't just me. I was just one tiny drop in a very, very large bucket that has been overflowing for a very, very long time," she said.
Black maternal health in America
The United States is arguably the most dangerous country in the developed world to give birth to a baby, with a much higher rate of maternal deaths compared to other wealthy nations. 649 women in the U.S. died of maternal causes in 2024, according to federal data.
But there is a huge disparity in the numbers: Black mothers were more than three times as likely to lose their lives from pregnancy-related causes than white women.
Many in the maternity care field are concerned by stories like Ali's and the statistics. Dr. Tamika Auguste is chair of women's and infants' services at MedStar Washington Hospital Center.
"I can't tell you how many Black women have said to me: 'Hey Doc, don't let me die,'" she said in an interview. "The poor rates in outcomes of Black maternity patients is something that rocked us to our core."
Auguste says important work has been done in the maternal healthcare field to improve protocols and guidelines to address conditions like cardiac issues, hemorrhaging and hypertension, which are more prevalent among Black women. But she says there's still the problem of bias.
Auguste points to the dangerous misconception among some in medicine that Black patients have a higher threshold for pain. She believes it's key for medical teams to acknowledge that disparities exist and communicate intentionally about bias to prevent it from affecting patient care.
"We are very purposeful in looking at outcomes with a lens of demographics of different racial breakdown of different types of data," said Auguste.
She says those discussions are moving the needle slightly. Her hospital in Washington, D.C., employs about a dozen midwives.
"Physician, midwife, doula, nurse, anesthesiologist, working together as a team. That is critical," said Auguste.
But access to maternity care is a barrier. Dr. Auguste's own hospital recently closed one of two postpartum units, citing financial pressure. More than 500 hospitals closed maternity wards between 2010 and 2022, according to a study published in the medical research journal JAMA.
Nationwide, more than half of counties don't have hospital-based labor and delivery services, according to the non-profit organization March of Dimes. The group calls these maternity care deserts.
In the South, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to live in areas without adequate access to maternity care providers, according to KFF Health News. People of color are also more likely to be uninsured.
Healing journey
Ali says, through her own healing, she has found beautiful relationships and support in the Black and Indigenous maternal health community. She travels the country speaking at conferences and other events, sharing her personal story and talking about solutions.
Ali founded a business called Baby Yams to fund grants to Black and Indigenous birth workers and students. Her team makes heritage baby quilts in vivid ankara and batik fabrics. Each quilt has a special name and represents protection and strength.
"They're this storytelling machine of the possibility, the hope," explained Ali.
Baby Yams donates part of the proceeds to the Birth Future Foundation, which provides grants to midwives, doulas and student birth workers.
"There are solutions. The solutions exist now," Ali said. "There are birth centers, there are midwives educating themselves, doulas going into practice."
A midwife in Alabama is one of many birth workers who has benefited from Ali's financial support. Nadia Gramby says she completed her licensing requirements to advance from a doula to a midwife thanks to a Birth Future Foundation scholarship funded by Ali.
Gramby, 41, says her work helping families across Alabama is especially important because nearly 40% of counties in the South are maternity care deserts, according to March of Dimes. Gramby says her practice is an important option, especially for Black families that may not otherwise have immediate access to care.
"It is an amazing joy to see families who feel safe and know that they're seen, and they made decisions to make sure that their children are born in safe environments, where they feel comfortable, and they feel cared for and they have been educated and they are empowered," she told NPR.
Black midwives and doulas have had a rich history in African American life and communities for centuries.
Midwives are medically trained to perform many of the same functions and procedures as doctors when women are having babies in low-risk situations. They deliver in hospitals alongside physicians, birth centers and in homes. They also frequently collaborate with doulas, who provide non-medical support. Research shows midwife births lead to lower rates of complications.
A report released this year by March of Dimes finds midwives are critical and part of the solution to expanding access to maternity care, especially in rural and under-resourced communities. The group is calling for policies to remove requirements for physician supervision and increase reimbursement rates from Medicaid and private insurance.
But some physicians and policymakers worry about the safety of giving birth outside of hospitals, especially when there's an emergency. Midwives can't perform surgery for example, so that can mean delays to getting emergency treatment. Some states have laws making it harder for midwives to practice.
When Ali became pregnant with her second child, she and her husband searched carefully for the right midwife and found one. She says that time around, her birth plan and desires were acknowledged.
"We deserve to be cared for. We deserve to have choices. We deserve to have control over our own bodies," she said. "We are beautiful. We are deserving of loving hands."

The United States is in the throes of the largest tax revolt in a generation, and the revolutionaries are winning.
Since 2020, nationwide home values have climbed roughly 50 percent, leading property-tax bills to increase 19 percent and contributing to a 71 percent increase in the cost of homeowner’s insurance. At the same time, the price of gas, utilities, food, and everything else has risen, stamping out entrepreneurship, dimming the fertility rate, and making even six-figure earners feel financially strained.
Homeowners have had enough, and grassroots groups have mobilized to turn private kvetching into public policy. Over the past four years, nearly two dozen states have slashed property taxes: Alabama by capping annual assessment increases, Colorado by lowering marginal rates, Indiana by creating credits, Nebraska by setting a limit on local collections, New York by sending checks to homeowners, Wyoming by carving out loopholes for seniors. My back-of-the-envelope accounting suggests that the measures have reduced property-tax revenue in those states by 7 percent, saving homeowners as much as $45 billion a year.
This November, voters will consider a spate of similar proposals, the most radical one coming from legislators in Tallahassee, Florida. Amendment 3, popularly known as “Save Our Homes,” would raise the “homestead” exemption on owner-occupied properties in the state from $50,000 to $250,000, meaning a couple with a condo with an assessed value of $400,000 would pay their county’s property-tax rate on $150,000 of their home’s value, rather than on $350,000. The amendment would eliminate levies on more than half of dwellings. In time, Florida legislators want to phase out property taxes on owner-occupied homes entirely.
Amendment 3 would give property owners a giant tax cut: $12 billion a year by one estimate. It would ease the local cost-of-living crisis too, its proponents argue. “Affordability is a problem for all Floridians,” Byron Donalds, a Republican congressman and the front-runner in the governor’s race, said on the stump last month. “It doesn’t matter what your politics are. It doesn’t matter what the color of your skin is. Because when taxes and insurance are more than principal and interest, you got a problem.”
Yet what is being framed as a populist fight for affordability is in reality a form of class and generational warfare. Property-tax relief gives to the rich and takes from the poor. It aids seniors and harms children. It puts homeownership even further out of reach for many Americans, and it makes daily life even more expensive for low-income Americans.
To be fair to the amendment’s supporters, these arguments are not exactly intuitive. The annual cost of owning a home has climbed precipitously. Millions of working-class and middle-income families own their home. If you cut property taxes, you reduce their costs. This much is true.
Yet homeowners’ insurance and property taxes don’t function on a family’s balance sheet in the same way that rent, groceries, gas, cars, child care, and airfare do. Their cost goes up when familial wealth goes up. In Florida, real-estate appraisals have increased 83 percent since 2019, according to the state’s revenue department, suggesting that homeowners’ net worth has increased by trillions of dollars. Does public policy really need to solve the problem of rising taxes due to rising valuations? Is it even a problem at all?
If retirees on fixed incomes can’t afford their insurance payments and families can’t figure out how to cover their tax bill, maybe. Yet the number of Florida homes and buildings that are delinquent on their property taxes has fallen slightly since 2020. The number of foreclosures has increased a bit, but remains low. The state’s housing market is fraying and distressed sales are increasing, but that’s because of climate change and mortgage rates, not tax assessments. Floridians may not like paying a higher tax bill, and carrying costs might be spurring some of them to downsize. But in general, property taxes are levied on people who can afford them. The typical homeowner earns twice as much as the typical renter, and has 43 times the net worth.
Tenants are “the loser in all this,” Ken Johnson, a professor of finance at the University of Mississippi, told me. Many cities and counties offset lower taxes on owner-occupied properties with higher taxes on commercial residential properties. Landlords pass those costs on to their renters. The policy will also benefit longtime homeowners at the expense of prospective homebuyers. Low property taxes increase home prices, making it harder for people without a lot of money in the bank—such as new parents and just-married couples—to get approved for a mortgage. Then they remain tenants, subject to never-ending rent increases.
In addition to distorting the housing market, Amendment 3 will devastate public finances. Property taxes provide 43 percent of revenue to Florida’s municipal general funds, the bank accounts that cities and counties use to finance day-to-day services. Amendment 3 will cut collections by as much as 30 percent, and will hit hardest in areas with a lot of homes and not a lot of commerce. To cover the $12 billion budget hole, cities and towns will likely raise or impose sales taxes and sin taxes; increase fees at the DMV, permit offices, registrars, and courts; charge more for waste removal and water; and put additional taxes on tourists. The state will trade out a solidly progressive, uniformly applied tax for an obscure, regressive mishmash of charges.
But municipalities aren’t expected to make up all of the lost revenue. They’re expected to cut. Amendment 3 explicitly protects tax financing streams for schools, meaning that cities and counties are contemplating draconian budget reductions for public-safety offices, libraries, after-school programs, summer camp, day care, flood prevention, public transit, roads, parks, senior services, homeless shelters, legal-aid clinics, domestic-violence shelters, and many other things. Austerity will be regressive too, harming the poor more than the wealthy. Rich Floridians aren’t relying on the bus to get to work. They’re not picking up free meals, taking adult-literacy classes at the library, or seeing a dentist at a pop-up clinic in a middle-school gymnasium either.
In the worst-case scenario, State Senator Tina Polsky told me, cities and counties “wouldn’t have enough money to keep going, even to pay their elected officials.” They would need to merge, or “come begging in Tallahassee, and those with the best lobbyists and the best connections are going to get the money.”
Add the possibility of a recession to that worst case. In a downturn, Florida would have no revenue from individual income taxes. (Florida voters banned them in a 1924 constitutional amendment.) It would have less income from property taxes than it did before. Yields from sales, corporate, and tourist taxes would fall. The state’s revenue base would collapse, meaning cuts to public services and layoffs and a secondary decline in consumer spending, leading the revenue base to shrink even more.
Despite these risks, Amendment 3 is expected to pass, as are many similar measures on the ballot in November. Voters have approved 78 percent of statewide property-tax measures in recent years. No wonder: Americans hate inflation and love homeownership. They believe in higher taxes, but also think other people should be the ones paying them. They may not perceive the connection between slashing property taxes and cuts to services, rising sales taxes, and increasing fees. They don’t understand that slashing property taxes means gutting the most effective wealth tax the country has, or taking from the poor to give to the rich. “It is an intellectual challenge to figure out ways to talk about these things, if you even have the guts to talk about them at all,” Texas State Senator Nathan Johnson, the solitary holdout on a property-tax relief measure that passed last year, told me.
Maybe California could convince them. Back in 1978, state residents revolted against a brutal cost-of-living crisis, a miserable housing market, and ever-increasing tax bills. By a two-to-one margin, they passed Proposition 13, which capped most property-tax rates at 1 percent, reset assessments to their 1976 level, and barred assessments from increasing more than 2 percent a year, unless a property changes hands or a new structure is built.
Prop 13 broke California. It nudged homeowners to remain in their properties for as long as possible, freezing neighborhoods in amber and trapping would-be buyers in rentals. (One recent study found that raising California’s average property-tax rate from 0.8 percent to 2 percent would increase the state’s homeownership rate by 4.6 percent.) It starved towns and cities of revenue, prompting them to rely on less progressive, less reliable, less equitable, and more distortionary taxes. It helped Boomers and it hurt younger generations. (I would say, “It helped Boomers and hurt their grandchildren,” but that would not be literally true. In California, Pappy and Gamma can bequeath their home to Junior without triggering a property-tax reassessment, meaning the state directly subsidizes dynastic fortunes.) Perhaps most salient: Prop 13 made California less affordable, radically so. It stymied real-estate development and created a trillion-dollar incentive for property owners to fight against reform.
What California did two generations ago might be the best argument against what Florida and other states are doing today. With these property-tax measures, well-off families are helping themselves now and hurting everyone else tomorrow.

Is the Premier League already a two-team title race?
- Published
Four games is far too soon to be talking about who is in or out of the title race... isn't it?
And yet Arsenal and Manchester City, who have been the top two in three of the past four seasons, look a level above everyone else so far.
Is it already a two-horse race?
With new (or newish) managers, Manchester United, Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham were all looking for better things this season.
But so far their starts range from shaky to shambolic.
How good have top two been?
Arsenal and Manchester City are the only two teams with 12 points from four games.
They are already four points above third-placed Hull City - who despite their brilliant early form may not consider themselves in any kind of title equation - and five above the rest.
Arsenal are the defending champions and pre-season title favourites.
Under manager Mikel Arteta they ended a 22-year title drought last season with what was often perceived to be an attritional style of play.
They started this season with a hugely impressive 3-0 victory over Manchester City in the Community Shield.
And they have carried on with victories over Coventry, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Sunderland - plus Napoli in the Champions League.
Including last season, they are now on a nine-game winning run in the league - and last lost in any competition in 90 minutes to City on 19 April.
Unlike Arsenal, City do not have the continuity this season with boss Pep Guardiola leaving after six titles, including a Treble, in 10 years.
Enzo Maresca, once his assistant, has taken over and led them to four wins from four in the league after that loss in Cardiff to the Gunners.
They have beaten Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Coventry - plus Porto in the Champions League - before their controversial 1-0 success at Manchester United on Sunday.
Erling Haaland scored the only goal, with the Premier League's refereeing body later admitting a mistake as it should have been ruled out for offside.
Despite their 100% starts, the underlying numbers behind Arsenal and City's starts do not imply total dominance.
Brighton (13) and Chelsea (10) have scored more goals than the eight that the top two have both netted.
For shots, Arsenal and City rank 10th and 11th and touches in the opposition box they are sixth and fifth respectively.
Arsenal have only conceded once and City have let in two goals - two of the best records in the league.

How about the rest?
The next three favourites to win the title with most bookmakers - in order - were Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester United - with Tottenham some way back.
Chelsea and Liverpool both sacked their managers, bringing in Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola respectively in the summer.
United and Spurs both changed manager earlier in 2026, with Michael Carrick and Roberto de Zerbi having their first pre-seasons.
Last season, Chelsea finished 10th, Liverpool as defending champions were fifth, and Spurs came 17th - with United ending up third after turning things around under Carrick.
So for all four hopes were high this was going to be a better season.
Chelsea are fifth, with only one defeat so far, and have scored 10 goals... but conceded nine - the fourth worst record in the division.
They have conceded two or more goals in each of their first four matches of a Premier League season for the first time since 2015-16.
Liverpool are down in seventh, unbeaten after four games - but three of those are draws.
It is just the third time in the last 63 seasons they have failed to win either of their first two home league games.
United are 13th with four points - equalling their worst start to a Premier League season since 1992-93... level with last season.
They have had more shots than anybody else in the league - 84 - and the second fewest shots conceded (41).
Despite that they have conceded as many as they have scored - seven.
Spurs would not have considered themselves in the title race after two 17th-placed finishes but would have hoped for a better start as they currently sit... 17th.
And even worse than that, it was the first time in the club's history they have failed to score in their first four league games.

What does history tell us?
Prior to this campaign, 80 teams in the English top-flight have won their first four league games of the season.
Of those, just 24 went on to win the title, proving that early dominance does not necessarily mean a side will last the pace.
In the Premier League era, nine of the 28 sides to win four on the bounce at the start of a season have gone on to lift the title, most recently Manchester City in 2023-24.

'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
- Published
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.
"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.
His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.
Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.
At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.
He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.
On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.
In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
I came to realise it was not true"
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.
Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."
Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.
Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.
Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.
Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.
The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.
After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.
He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

In August and September 2026, a rumor circulated online that Keiko Mori, a 22-year-old teacher in Japan, defied orders to lead 30 students to their deaths with hand grenades rather than allow them to surrender to American forces during the Battle of Okinawa in June 1945.
For example, on Sept. 3, a post on Facebook (archived) read:
WOW: In June 1945, a 22-year-old teacher named Keiko Mori in Okinawa was ordered to command her 30 students to commit suicide with hand grenades rather than surrender.
She refused. And she said to her students, "Live. No matter what they say, you must live." While Japanese soldiers, who were forcing death for the sake of honor, searched for them, she hid her students in a cave for 12 days.
Even when food ran out, she sang songs and taught arithmetic using stones. When American soldiers eventually discovered the cave, she stepped out first, holding up a white shirt to protect her students.
(David J Harris Jr., accessed via Facebook)
The post included an image that allegedly showed Mori holding a white garment in the air while leading a group of children out of a cave.
Other examples of the claim appeared on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and TikTok (archived), and Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the rumor was true.
The rumor was fictional. We found no credible reports about the claimed monument in Okinawa honoring Mori (archived, archived, archived). Such a monument would have come up in online searches if it existed. According to Pangram, a highly regarded artificial intelligence detector for images and text, both the text and image accompanying the story were created by AI. Given the above, we've rated this claim false.
Snopes could not determine the rumor's source.
Fake image and article helped spread false rumor
According to Google Gemini's chatbot, "most or all" of the image that claimed to show Mori and her students that circulated alongside the story's text had been generated using Google's AI tools. Google's AI tools add SynthID, an invisible watermark, to their creations, and tools like Gemini can identify if the watermark is present.
Let us note here: AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Additionally, one post that spread the false rumor about Mori and the students included a link in the comment section to a long, advertisement-filled article about Mori's alleged actions.
Pangram also identified a section of this article as having been generated by AI. The article was written almost entirely in short, one-line sentences and the same page also contained an article about singers Dolly Parton and Miley Cyrus. It's unlikely an authentic news outlet would have put those two stories together on the same page.
Rumor reflects grim WWII history
Despite evidence that the story about Mori was false, the tale could have been inspired by real events. According to an article in the peer-reviewed Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus, Japanese authorities disseminated "disinformation about the motives and behaviour of the invading Americans" during 1945, which led people in Okinawa to believe it was better to die by their own hands than be killed or captured by American soldiers.
The journal article included the eyewitness account of Miyahira Haruko, who reportedly told a Japanese newspaper that a Japanese soldier on an island that is part of Okinawa Prefecture gave her a grenade and told her to take her own life rather than be captured by American forces in early 1945.
Haruko reportedly said her mother and sister committed suicide together during this period. The journal article said that some Japanese people committed suicide in "dugouts and caves."
Ultimately, the fictional story about Keiko Mori resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
Creators of such content capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
For further reading, Snopes often investigates rumors to do with World War II.

Wired vs wireless gaming mouse: is there really a difference in performance?
It's time to ditch the cable.
If you're looking to improve your gaming setup, the mouse is one of the best places to start. The right mouse can both improve your performance and feel much more comfortable during longer sessions, but with such a vast market of mice it can be difficult to know which is best for you. Arguably one of the biggest debates is wired versus wireless, but does it really make a difference?
There used to be a stark disparity between wireless and wired mice, particularly when it came to latency, but the gap between the two has become much less drastic in recent years. In our picks for the best gaming mouse in 2026, most of our choices are wireless. When it comes down to the finer details of what you're looking for, it will depend on the sort of games you play the most and how much you're looking to spend, but it's easier than ever to see a wireless mouse as a dependable option.
What makes for a good gaming mouse?
Two of the biggest factors to look at in a gaming mouse are input latency and polling rate, two closely related stats that determine how responsive your device will be while gaming. Latency is how long it takes between taking an action (clicking and movement) and when it appears on screen, and polling rate is how often your mouse is communicating actions to the computer. Polling rates are measured in Hz — your average office mouse may operate at 125Hz, communicating every 8 milliseconds; a high-end gaming mouse can often reach 8,000Hz, communicating every 0.125 milliseconds.
Dots per inch (DPI) and inches per second are two other features to consider, though the former is generally less important to the pros. Dots per inch is essentially how sensitive your mouse is, measuring how much the cursor will move with every real-life inch the mouse travels, while inches per second (also called tracking speed) is how quickly you can move the mouse before it's unable to accurately keep up. A high tracking speed is very important, ensuring any fast movements can be communicated with precision, but an overly-high DPI can actually be more of a hindrance, picking up even the slightest unintentional hand twitches and interference from the mousepad due to oversensitivity.
The final consideration is more down to personal preference: the actual build of the mouse. Things like weight, ergonomic mouse structure, and how many extraneous buttons it has are all factors that determine the perfect device. Those who play games with lots of hotkeys will appreciate a mouse with a selection of side buttons, while a gamer primarily focused on first-person shooters might value a feather-light mouse more for quick movements.
What mice are the pros using?
In a 2025 survey of 2,420 e-sports players by ProSettings, all of the top ten mouse picks were wireless, a trend likely due to a combination of major technological improvements and the movement freedom from being cable free. Many of the best wireless mice now use 2.4GHz dongle connections, which allow for much faster polling and latency than Bluetooth.
This means that wireless mice are capable of generally reducing latency to between 0.5 and 1 milliseconds (sometimes lower), compared to wired mice at 0.3 to 1 milliseconds — a very negligible difference even to the most hardcore gamer. Similarly, DPI and tracking speed are generally identical between a wired and wireless mouse of the same tier.
The two main drawbacks of high-end wireless mice have nothing to do with performance: price and battery. Most wireless gaming mice tend to cost more than their wired counterparts, since they require extra tech like a dongle and other additional charging peripherals.
Though many wireless mice do boast an impressive battery that's capable of lasting over 100 hours, they still eventually require charging, which can be seen as a hindrance for some gamers. This is a hurdle easily overcome by remembering to charge it — often using a bundled USB cable — when not gaming or while away from the computer.
Although prices may be higher, if you're looking to play like the pros, wireless is the way to go.

Trump’s ‘first-look’ at interior of White House ballroom reveals signature detail dominating room
President shows off detailed concept art illustrating the inside of his $600 million pet project, revealing a cavernous space with marble flooring, chandeliers and more than a hint of Mar-a-Lago
President Donald Trump has released new detailed renderings of the interior of his controversial White House ballroom, revealing it to be decked out in his beloved gold trim.
“First interior renderings of the magnificent new Ballroom at the White House,” the president posted excitedly on Truth Social late Sunday after returning from watching the Irish Open at his golf club in Doonbeg.
“Massively expensive, but free of charge to the American Taxpayer — On budget, and ahead of schedule!” the president claimed.
The attached artwork revealed the $600 million ballroom to be a cavernous space lined with shiny golden-brown-tinged marble flooring and ornate gold detailing dominating its walls and ceiling, from which several chandeliers hang.
One of the images suggested it would have imposing wooden doors like those at the Kremlin but, overall, the impression was much more Mar-a-Lago than Moscow, more Liberace than Lenin.
The president has already stuffed the Oval Office with as much gold as possible and paved over the Rose Garden to make a patio like that providing the centerpiece of his Florida residence, just two examples of the many, many tweaks and changes he has made to the White House since returning to power in January 2025.
In another post Sunday, Trump promised his “spectacular” ballroom “will be the GREATEST of its kind anywhere in the World!” and again stressed: “It is a Gift to the U.S.A. from me and other American Patriots – No Taxpayer Dollars will be expended in its Construction.”
And, in another, he claimed the White House had been “a dump” before he began redecorating it, having been neglected by his predecessors, and boasted that it is “now in better shape than when built in 1792.”
The president caused shock and outrage last year when he unceremoniously had the East Wing demolished to make way for the ballroom, a complex he insisted has been badly needed for decades.
He has also claimed the ballroom is necessary because of the security enhancements it will bring – an argument undermined by the prior existence of a secret bunker, built after 9/11, which is capable of withstanding a nuclear blast.
However, his project has been tangled up in legal challenges since its inception, with the Supreme Court recently ruling Trump can continue building – for now at least.
Chief Justice John Roberts allowed the administration to temporarily press on with construction while his justices weigh whether or not to intervene in an ongoing lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argues Trump must secure congressional approval before proceeding.
The president hailed that development last month by posting a picture of the 90,000 square foot construction site and declaring: “Presidents have wanted this for 150 years, and so has everyone else.”
Other projects he has commenced as part of his “beautification” agenda in Washington include the construction of a new helipad on the South Lawn and, most disastrously, his makeover of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool in “American Flag Blue,” which became one of the defining scandals of the summer.
All of which has carried on despite voters repeatedly telling pollsters they would rather Trump focus on matters of more acute concern to them like taming inflation or ending the Iran war, which has led to the blockading of the Strait of Hormuz, a pause on oil deliveries and therefore higher gas prices at home.
A July poll from The Washington Post/Ipsos found that 65 percent of American adults said they were dissatisfied or upset with the president’s renovation undertakings, the total cost of which has been pegged at $927 million so far.

Brands v country - Kerr ramps up kit battle after latest victory
- Published
After Josh Kerr became Great Britain's first ever Ultimate Champion with a dominant victory in the 1500m in Budapest on Sunday evening, he celebrated in customary fashion - Union Jack draped around him, beaming smile, arms raised before the cheering crowd.
But he also did something less traditional, ramping up a battle over funding at the top of athletics in the process.
The 28-year-old made a clear point of obscuring the Nike sponsor's logo on his Great Britain kit by tying his Brooks-branded running spikes over his shoulder, meaning that the video footage and photographs of his trophy lift highlighted his own personal sponsor rather than his nation's.
After praising the inaugural running of the Ultimate Championship, a new biennial event run by World Athletics with a focus on big names, Kerr explained the meaning behind the move in his interview with BBC Sport.
"There is one last thing that I think we can get right, which is allowing the athletes to represent their own brands versus their country," Kerr said.
"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make any money from that sadly. We don't have the pay cheques that other sports do yet. So that would be an opportunity to grow."
BBC Sport has contacted World Athletics for comment.
- How did the first Ultimate Championship go? 
  - Published7 hours ago
- This is what women in sport look like - Hunt 
  - Published49 minutes ago
Different rules for different competitions
Edinburgh native Kerr has won medals representing Great Britain at both the Olympics - picking up bronze in 2020 and silver in 2024 - and World Championships, having taken gold in 2023.
At those events, Kerr is directly representing his country - there are national medal tables in which the triumphs achieved by compatriots are tallied up together.
But at the Ultimate Championship a much smaller field of athletes are competing for individual titles in their respective events. There is no country medal table, and the new event is billed as a season finale for individual athletes after the conclusion of the Diamond League campaign.
In the Diamond League, athletes are free to show off their own sponsors who provide them with funding by wearing their own kits.
Kerr, and the other athletes who were crowned Ultimate Champions during the three-day competition in Hungary, earned $150,000 (£111,111) for winning.
But his pointed comments made plain the position athletes find themselves in.
How athlete funding works and why kit dispute is relevant
Whereas players in sports like football earn a salary based on a contract with the team that employs them, and athletes in individual sports like tennis and golf can earn a great deal from prize money at major tournaments, athletics competitors rely much more heavily on personal sponsorships and endorsements.
That is because they are paid no direct annual salary, and the only standardised prize money on offer is $50,000 (£37,000) for winning gold in one of the 48 track and field events at the Olympics.
That prize money was only introduced at the 2024 Games in Paris, and is paltry compared to the potential millions in winnings on offer in other major sports.
Some nations - including the USA - also choose to pay athletes who win medals from their own resources, but Britain does not.
Instead, athletes are awarded funding and grants by UK Sport, with the majority of the money coming from the National Lottery.
UK Sport ranks athletes by how likely they are to win medals at major events, and gives more funding to those whose chances it believes are better.
Athletes typically use that funding to pay for training camps, equipment, travel and, in some cases, personal support staff like physiotherapists, nutritionists and chefs.
So why would athletes be instructed to wear national team kit at the Ultimates?
The Ultimate Championship is billed as three fast-paced evenings with a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot on offer for the biggest stars in athletics.
The condensed schedule and focus on star names is designed to appeal to viewers on television and social media - the latter likely playing a role in the focus on short, sharp bursts of action which can capture attention online.
Most viewers of athletics are used to watching athletes compete while wearing national kit at the Olympics and World Championships. Put simply, the use of a national kit makes it easier for the casual viewer to quickly spot who they should be rooting for and feel invested in the action.
But Kerr's comments have highlighted the fact that something which may well improve the viewing experience can be felt as a direct financial negative by the athletes themselves.
With the next edition of the Ultimate Championship set to take place in September 2028, shortly after the Olympics in Los Angeles, the battle between brands and country could continue to heat up.

ఆల్ఫాజియో (AlphaGeo) సంస్థ నిర్వహించిన అధ్యయనం ప్రకారం, ప్రకృతి విపత్తులను ఎదుర్కోవడంలో తెలంగాణ రాజధాని హైదరాబాద్ ప్రపంచంలోనే రెండో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన నగరంగా నిలిచిందని, పెరుగుతున్న ఉష్ణోగ్రతలు, తీవ్రమైన వర్షాలు, వరదలను తట్టుకునే స్థాయిలో నగర మౌలిక వసతులు లేవని పేర్కొంటూ ఓ పోస్టు సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఈ కథనం ద్వారా అందులో ఎంత నిజముందో చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఆల్ఫాజియో అధ్యయనం ప్రకారం, ప్రకృతి విపత్తులను ఎదుర్కోవడంలో తెలంగాణ రాజధాని హైదరాబాద్ ప్రపంచంలో రెండో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన నగరంగా నిలిచింది.
ఫాక్ట్(నిజం): ఆల్ఫాజియో అధ్యయనం భారతదేశంలోని హైదరాబాద్ను ప్రకృతి విపత్తులను ఎదుర్కోవడంలో ప్రపంచంలో రెండో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన నగరంగా పేర్కొనలేదు. ఈ అధ్యయనంలో పాకిస్తాన్లోని హైదరాబాద్ నగరం 41 రెసిలెన్స్-అడ్జస్టెడ్ రిస్క్ (RAR) స్కోరును పొందింది, ఇది విశ్లేషించిన ప్రధాన నగరాల్లో ఆరు అత్యంత తక్కువ ప్రకృతి విపత్తును తట్టుకోగల నగరాల్లో ఒకటిగా నిలిచింది. కావున పోస్టు ద్వారా చెప్పేది తప్పు.

అత్యధిక ప్రమాదం ఉన్న నగరాల జాబితాలో RAR స్కోరు 41తో అహ్మదాబాద్ (భారతదేశం) మొదటి స్థానంలో, 41తో హైదరాబాద్ (పాకిస్తాన్) రెండో స్థానంలో, 38తో ముల్తాన్ (పాకిస్తాన్) మూడో స్థానంలో, 36తో ఢాకా (బంగ్లాదేశ్) నాలుగో స్థానంలో, 35తో కోల్కతా (భారతదేశం) ఐదో స్థానంలో, 35తో లాహోర్ (పాకిస్తాన్) ఆరో స్థానంలో నిలిచాయి. మరోవైపు, RAR స్కోరు 8తో చికాగో అత్యంత తట్టుకునే సామర్థ్యం ఉన్న ప్రధాన నగరంగా మొదటి స్థానంలో నిలిచింది.
చివరిగా, ఆల్ఫాజియో అధ్యయనంలో ప్రకృతి విపత్తులను ఎదుర్కోవడంలో రెండో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన నగరంగా నిలిచింది  పాకిస్తాన్లోని హైదరాబాద్, తెలంగాణ రాజధాని హైదరాబాద్ కాదు.

India spinner Varun Chakaravarthy suffered another injury setback on Monday as he was ruled out of the ongoing Afghanistan series in New Delhi.
The 35-year-old had just returned after a hamstring setback and had completed a lengthy rehabilitation at the BCCI Centre of Excellence.
According to news reports, Chakaravarthy suffered a side strain during the first T20I in New Delhi on Monday. If this new injury rules him out for a lengthy period of time, India will have to name a replacement for him at the Asian Games.
Who are the other spinners in Asian Games squad?
India had named three other spinners apart from Chakaravarthy in its Asian Games squad. Axar Patel and Washington Sundar are the all-rounders who bowl spin while Ravi Bishnoi is the only frontline spinner besides the Tamil Nadu bowler.
Who could replace Varun Chakaravarthy?
With India playing ODIs against West Indies, an India-A side playing multi-day games, and injuries to a Shahbaz Ahmed and Harsh Dubey, finding a direct replacement for Chakaravarthy might not be easy.
Kuldeep Yadav
The most obvious choice to fill in is Kuldeep Yadav. The left-arm unorthodox bowler has been out of favour in the T20I setup and played just one game through the T20 World Cup campaign. But he had a decent run in the ODI Cup in England last month and has enough experience to strengthen the Indian side.
He is likely to be named in the ODI squad to face West Indies but could be moved to the Asian Games squad by the selectors.
Vipraj Nigam
The Uttar Pradesh leg-spinner has been named in the India-A squad for the One-Day series against Australia A, which begins October 6. This makes him a likely candidate to fill in.
He has been part of the India-A sides over the last year and his leg-spin could be a go-to option for the selectors for the Asian Games.
Krunal Pandya
Krunal’s solid IPL numbers and economical impact for Royal Challengers Bengaluru over the last two seasons have made a case for his selection.
However, since India already has Axar Patel as a sure-shot starter, Krunal is only an outside contender for the vacancy.

New Carlo Rovelli book challenges science's understanding of reality and the universe
I have a book on my shelf called Physics and Ultimate Reality. The title perfectly expresses the dream many physicists like me have when we begin our studies as young students. We yearn for perfect, objective knowledge of a perfectly knowable universe.
This "God's-eye view" is also what's claimed as the purpose and promise of physics in many popular books on the subject. But, now, comes a new book by physicist Carlo Rovelli that explicitly rejects any path to an ultimate reality. The force with which Rovelli -- one of the leading researchers and popularizers in the field – argues for this seemingly heretical view is what makes his On the Equality of All Things such a compelling, exciting and important read.
Rovelli begins with a simple and compelling point: We humans have access to a very limited set of experiences when it comes to the universe. Because we live on the solid surface of a planet, we think there are solid objects. Because that solid surface offers fixed reference points like mountain tops, we think solid objects can have fixed locations in space. And if those objects do move, we think we can use our fixed reference points to give us an absolute measure of that motion. In each case, however, modern physics has shown these assumptions to be illusions.
Albert Einstein's relativity revealed that measurements of time and space (including our sense of when two events are simultaneous) are relative. Quantum mechanics, our best theory of matter at the atomic level, showed us that the properties we can ascribe to things cannot be disentangled from how we measure them. In this way, Rovelli argues, modern physics began to erode the sense that physics gives us a perfect access to a world as seen from the outside (i.e. the God's-eye view).
What we get instead is the world as viewed from within.
Rovelli dedicates considerable space to a view of quantum mechanics called the relational interpretation. When quantum physics appeared in the early 20th century, it came as a shock to the physicists who were creating it. In the 250 years since Newton introduced his famous laws of motion, physicists had come to believe their equations described a reality that was entirely independent of human action or interpretation. The "stuff" described by Newton's laws, and the laws themselves existed "out there" in the "Ultimate Reality" that the book on my shelf points to. But in quantum mechanics it became difficult to speak of objects having properties before those properties were measured. This is the source of the famous Schrodinger's Cat parable where a cat in a box can be both dead and alive before the box is opened and a measurement is made.
For some physicists, it was so important to get that Ultimate Reality back that they invented interpretations of quantum physics that claimed the universe splits into separate parallel versions of itself when the box is opened. Rovelli thinks these attempts are nonsense. For him, the lesson of quantum mechanics is relationality. Everything exists only in relation to everything else. That means the properties of a system – any object – are always relational properties. There is no way to see them from an ultimate or absolute perspective because there are no ultimate or absolute perspectives. And in the absence of an ultimate perspective the power of physics to ultimately "explain everything" also falls apart.
As Rovelli puts it in his latest book, "Physics is often credited with a power it does not have: that of exhausting what can be known about the world. This is nonsense. Knowing the physical laws of the world does not amount to knowing the world."
This is a radical claim about physics, particularly for one of the world's most well-regarded physicists. Not only does it directly contradict the scientific triumphalism that one finds in many popular books about science, it's also a view that crashes against the perspectives of many contemporary philosophers of science. But as Rovelli writes, "we never leave the circle of perspectives." For him, this irreducibility of relationship is the central lesson of relativity and quantum mechanics.
One of the most original aspects of Rovelli's argument is to draw on philosophical sources beyond the usual suspects in the Greek or European tradition. He relies heavily on the classical philosophies of India and Asia. Thinkers like Nagarjuna (from the 2nd century) or Zhuangzi (4th century BC China) appear many times in the book. In this way, Rovelli recognizes them as the equals of Plato, Aristotle and others in their ability to penetrate difficult questions of reality but doing so from a different perspective.
What's particularly compelling in this book is how lyrically Rovelli still vehemently defends the power and promise of physics (and science in general). Rather than unworkable claims of an absolute certainty about an absolute reality, Rovelli sees science as an invitation to the great creative effort of seeking knowledge. And, indeed, science does produce knowledge that is both profoundly beautiful and useful. Rovelli argues for a change in view that is not a defeat but a new kind of humility in the face of the universe's vast complexity. For him it's an invitation to a new kind of wisdom and intimacy.
On the Equality of All Things is a bracing book with a bracing perspective. There are places to disagree with Rovelli, such as his neglect of the primacy of experience in considering how science is even possible. In some places Rovelli dismisses this view with a wave of hand, like in his treatment of the great philosopher Henri Bergson, who emphasized that lived time is essentially different from time represented in science. This, however, is the stuff of creative and useful future arguments. For a short book aimed at a broad audience, Rovelli has created a powerful argument for a new way to understand ourselves and our place in the universe.
Adam Frank is a professor of physics and astronomy at the University of Rochester and co-author ofThe Blind Spot. Why Science Cannot Ignore Human Experience

Jadavpur University (JU) saw night-long rampage and vandalism on August 20, when a mob, armed with sticks and rods, allegedly stormed the campus.
The violence followed a heated altercation late on August 19 between activists from the Akhil Bharaitya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) from the university’s engineering department and members of the Left-wing student outfit, Democratic Students’ Federation (DSF), and other student organizations. The ABVP alleged that its members were assaulted and that several workers required hospitalisation. Students from the engineering faculty disputed the claim and offered a counter-account of the incident.
By midnight, an armed mob allegedly entered the campus, apparently seeking to avenge the earlier altercation. The attackers tore down and set fire to placards, festoons and flags belonging to various student organisations active on the campus. The mob also surrounded Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building, trapping students inside.
The violence was captured by CCTV cameras installed across the university campus. Students and journalists also recorded several videos of the incident. Alt News accessed multiple such recordings and analysed them to establish the identities of those involved in the ruckus.
What happened at JU: A Blow-by-Blow Account
Around 9:30–10:30 pm on August 19, the DSF-run Faculty of Engineering & Technology Students’ Union (FETSU) held a general body meeting on the campus. The meeting had been announced through the union’s social media account.
ABVP and the allied Right-wing student outfit, Nationalist Students’ Front (NSF), opposed the meeting, citing a Calcutta high court ruling that no activities could be undertaken from student union offices until fresh student union elections were held. According to students present, ABVP and NSF members were outnumbered and were forced to leave the spot. A few DSF members were also injured in the ensuing scuffle.
Ayantik Pal, a third-year B Tech student who attended the meeting, said the GB meeting had been convened to elect signatories for the union’s email ID, Facebook account and bank account. Since the last FETSU election was held in 2020, he said, the meeting was intended to allow the union to continue its functioning.
According to Pal, ABVP activists at the meeting repeatedly objected that it was illegal. He said they nevertheless participated when names for the signatories were being proposed, before becoming agitated as the meeting progressed. They allegedly abused some students, calling them “Naxals” and “Maoists”, following which a scuffle broke out.
Accounts diverge over what happened immediately afterwards.
According to students, Nikhil Das, an ABVP research scholar and president of the organisation’s JU unit, attempted to enter the undergraduate and postgraduate students’ GB meeting and allegedly tried to provoke a confrontation. Students said they intervened to stop him, escalating the situation. They alleged that three DSF workers were injured in the assault by ABVP activists and that one was taken away towards the Sulekha Crossing. ABVP denied these allegations.
ABVP, meanwhile, claimed that Das was assaulted during the GB meeting and subsequently had to be hospitalised at KPC Medical College and Hospital. BJP MLA from Jadavpur Sarbari Mukherjee visited him at the hospital. Students alleged that during the visit, she threatened that ABVP and BJP workers would retaliate if those accused in the assault did not surrender. She later repeated this on camera.
Around midnight, a crowd of approximately 50–60 people gathered outside Gate 4 of the university, which is the only entrance that remains open at night. By around 12:30 am, the group entered the campus.
Pramita Basu, an undergraduate Philosophy student, said that after 7 pm, everyone entering the campus is required to show an ID card, including hostel residents. However, according to her, the crowd entered without being stopped by the guards stationed at the gate.
The group moved from Gate 4 towards the Science-Arts crossing, where some wall graffiti was allegedly damaged, before turning towards Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building. Videos from the night accessed by Alt News show some members of the group carrying saffron flags.
Meanwhile, students who had remained on campus after the earlier confrontation gathered inside Aurobindo Bhavan. According to them, they had decided to stay back until morning because they had heard that ABVP activists were looking for them outside the university.
Pal said an all-faculty GB meeting was also convened that night, with students from the arts, science and engineering faculties discussing what to do next. Around 12:30 am, he said, a university staff member alerted them that a mob had entered the campus and advised them to protect themselves.
“Within minutes, we saw a stream of mobile flashlights coming towards Aurobindo Bhavan from the side of the green zone. A few students present at the green zone were thrashed by this mob,” Pal said.
The students then woke the guards at Aurobindo Bhavan, obtained the keys and locked themselves inside, according to Pal.
The crowd that reached the building tried to break through its collapsible gates but failed. It then tore down red flags, festoons and posters belonging to student organisations and set them on fire outside the administrative building. Students trapped inside alleged that members of the crowd abused them verbally, threw stones and eggs at the building, and attempted to throw burning flags inside. Footage of the episode was broadcast live on television and recorded by students and journalists.
The violence continued until around 2 am. Around the same time, another group gathered outside Jadavpur police station and allegedly attempted to breach the entrance to the university’s main hostel, located next to the police station.
At the protest, ABVP West Bengal leaders were reportedly heard telling the media that the organisation was “putting the last nail in the coffin” of the “Dimagi Naxals” and would carry out “surgical strikes” at Jadavpur University to suppress them.
By around 2:30 am, the crowd had dispersed. The students who had taken shelter inside Aurobindo Bhavan began leaving the campus at around 5 am.
Alt News procured a third CCTV footage from University sources, where several persons of interest can be spotted as present on the campus on the night of August 20.
The confrontation did not end with the dispersal of the mob.
Around noon the following day, the Student Federation of India (SFI) and other Left student organisations held a protest near the Lenin statue at Jadavpur 8B bus stand. Kolkata Police barricaded the area and stopped the protesters from proceeding towards the university. Around 2 pm, an ABVP rally that began from Golpark reached Gate 4 of the university. Students inside the campus also gathered in response. As Gate 4 was kept locked to prevent outsiders from entering, a face-off between the two groups on either side of the gate ensued.
During the confrontation, members of the ABVP crowd were seen standing on the historic university emblem designed by artist Nandalal Bose as they attempted to cross the closed gate and enter the campus.
Visuals of Rajyeshwar Sinha, a professor of Bengali at JU, holding the partially damaged University emblem went viral.
