North Korea says its recent live-fire drill demonstrated 'huge destructive power'
North Korea says it has conducted a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones that it claimed demonstrated “the huge destructive power of concentrated fire.”
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea said Monday it conducted a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones that it claimed demonstrated “huge destructive power.”
The official Korean Central News Agency said Saturday's drill was meant to get familiar with the procedure for the operation of the integrated firepower control system. South Korea’s military earlier said it detected short-range ballistic missile launches from North Korea’s eastern coastal Wonsan area on Saturday morning.
After observing the drill, Marshal Pak Jong Chon said the drill would “improve the level of specialization to bring down the enemy’s armed forces organizationally and structurally once an order is issued.” He added that the weapons systems mobilized demonstrated “the huge destructive power of concentrated fire,” according to KCNA.
It’s extremely difficult to independently verify North Korean claims on its weapons tests. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said several missiles fired Saturday each flew about 250 kilometers (155 miles) toward North Korea’s eastern waters. The flight distances signal the weapons are designed to strike targets in South Korea.
The firing drill marked North Korea’s first public ballistic missile launches in about three weeks.
Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump scaled back a major bilateral military drill with South Korea, citing what he called a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. That’s an apparent effort to revive diplomacy between them, but North Korea rebuffed Trump’s overture, saying that shortening the drill didn't change its “provocative, aggressive nature.”
Buoyed by his advancing nuclear arsenal and deepened ties with Russia and China, experts say Kim likely thinks he has greater leverage in possible diplomacy with the U.S. than when he first met Trump in 2018-2019.
Kim said earlier this year that he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
- Published
US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts.
"You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.
One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.
Coxon – who has also worked at OpenAI – welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.
On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".
The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.
The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.
On one hand, the sector is seen as huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.
But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.
In August OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.

And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.
The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

Although the photograph recirculated in 2026, it dates back to at least December 2018.
"In 1973 Japan planted trees in concentric circles as part of an experiment in forestry spacing. This is what they look like today from above," one Reddit post (archived) captioned the photograph.
(Reddit u/Impressive_East_)
That image and other photographs showing the same formations have circulated online for years, appearing on platforms such as Instagram, 9GAG, Facebook, Pinterest and X.
In short, the photograph was real, and the claim about the forest was also accurate. It showed two experimental plots of Japanese cedar near Nichinan, a city in Miyazaki Prefecture on the island of Kyushu. According to the Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office, the experiment was established in fiscal year 1973 to study how different planting densities affected tree growth and wood quality. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The photograph circulating in 2026 was not new — we traced it to at least December 2018.
The same forest has attracted attention before. We previously investigated similar photographs of the experimental plots in September 2024. One of the images circulating at the time was also available in The Associated Press' image archive.
Origin of the photograph
The photograph first gained attention when Japanese news outlet Sankei News published it in a story about the forest.
(www.sankei.com)
The outlet credited the image to Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office, a regional office of Japan's Forestry Agency. Its caption (translated from Japanese via Google Translate) read, "A circular pattern visible in the mountains of Nichinan City, Miyazaki Prefecture."
The image later appeared in numerous social media posts and articles.
What the photograph shows
The photographs circulating online show Japanese cedar trees arranged in two groups of concentric circles in a national forest near Nichinan, in Miyazaki Prefecture. An AP caption describing the forest said the trees in the outer ring were approximately 20 meters (66 feet) tall, about 5 meters (16 feet) taller than those near the center.
The circular forest was also discoverable on Google Maps and Google Earth, as the Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office gave its location as 31°43'50.0"N, 131°23'05.0"E.
According to the office, the experiment was linked to changes in the local timber industry. Obi cedar was planted sparsely in the area for shipbuilding timber, but demand later shifted toward wood for general construction.
Researchers created the experiment to study how different planting densities affected tree growth and wood quality. It was established in fiscal 1973, with the cedar seedlings planted in March 1974. The trees were arranged in concentric circles at different distances from one another, creating planting densities of about 377 to 10,027 trees per hectare. Seen from above, this produced the circular pattern that earned the site the nickname "mystery circles."
Later surveys showed that planting density affected the trees' size and growth. A 2011 study concluded that around 2,000 to 2,800 trees per hectare was suitable for lower-cost forestry. The experiment's final report, completed in fiscal year 2023, concluded that planting densities of 1,500 trees per hectare or fewer could be effective in terms of financial returns and afforestation costs.
For further reading, in January 2015 we investigated whether a law in Japan makes it illegal for citizens to be fat.

Intensifying vaccination of dogs and ensuring that people bitten by dogs receive timely and complete rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) could save far more lives in Keralam than routine pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) vaccination of children, according to a new modelling study on the cost-effectiveness of rabies interventions.
What the study found
The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia, estimates that routine childhood PrEP—vaccinating children against rabies before any animal exposure — would prevent only about 10 additional deaths over 10 years, while adding an estimated $10.5 million to $36.5 million to healthcare costs.
In contrast, comprehensive vaccination of dogs, combined with improved post-bite treatment and efforts to close gaps in PEP, could reduce rabies deaths by 83% compared to the current strategy, the study says. Scaling up vaccination of both owned and free-roaming dogs to 70% coverage could potentially bring human rabies deaths down to zero in Keralam within three years, according to the model.
The research was led by the University of Glasgow in collaboration with researchers from the Directorate of Medical Education, Kerala University of Health Sciences, the School of Public Health, the Directorates of Health and Animal Husbandry in Keralam, and the London School of Economics and Political Science.
Rabies in Keralam
Rabies prevention is already one of Keralam’s most intensive public health interventions, with more than 9,00,000 people receiving free treatment every year following animal bites. The State also has a PEP completion rate of over 90%. Yet human rabies deaths continue to occur, with 33 deaths reported in 2025, including among children.
The findings add a new dimension to the ongoing debate over whether Keralam should introduce routine PrEP for children as a rabies prevention strategy. Paediatricians and several public health experts have advocated childhood PrEP because children are particularly vulnerable to severe bites, including injuries to the face and hands, which could become fatal, despite post-exposure treatment.
The study does not rule out PrEP. Instead, it argues that PrEP may be more appropriate for specific high-risk populations who face difficulties in reaching healthcare facilities quickly after exposure, including some geographically dispersed tribal communities.
It argues that given Keralam’s relatively strong access to PEP, universal childhood PrEP may produce relatively little additional mortality reduction for the huge resources required, whereas improved dog vaccination and better wound management and timely PEP may produce greater population-level gains.
Cost effectiveness
“The study is a comparison of the cost effectiveness of PrEP against other interventions as a population-level strategy to reduce rabies. It points out that, as a public health strategy, investing in dog vaccination is more cost effective because it stops virus transmission in the community, and takes us closer to rabies elimination,” said Zinia T. Nujum of the School of Public Health, KUHS, who led the research in Kerala.
According to Martha Luka, researcher at the University of Glasgow’s School of Biodiversity, One Health & Veterinary Medicine and lead author, PrEP for children is unlikely to be the best use of public health resources in Keralam, where access to post-bite vaccination and completion of the regimen are already high.
Canines are the reservoir of the rabies virus and accounts for 70% of the rabies cases. Vaccinating the dog population interrupts transmission before people are exposed, whereas PrEP mainly protects vaccinated individuals while the wider risk remains.
The researchers modelled 12 different combinations of dog vaccination, post-bite treatment and PrEP over a 10-year period from 2026-2035. The study’s sensitivity analysis underlines the importance of improving access to PEP. Raising the proportion of bite victims who seek medical care from 70% to 95% could prevent more than 1,100 additional deaths—over 20 times the mortality reduction achievable even with maximum PrEP coverage in the model.
Vaccination of domestic dogs
The researchers also found that increasing vaccination coverage among domestic dogs alone could produce substantial health gains. “About 70-80% of dog-bite cases in the State are due to domestic dogs. Mandatory licensing and vaccination of domestic dogs, can help improve coverage. We could focus on completing domestic dog vaccination and then move on to vaccinating strays,” said Dr. Nujum.
However, she pointed out that the population of free-roaming dogs in Keralam could be at least five times the official estimate, highlighting the need for better data to plan vaccination programmes. The researchers argue that the State’s priority should therefore be a sustained One Health-based dog vaccination programme targeting at least 70% coverage, involving local bodies, Animal Husbandry and Health departments, veterinary teams, NGOs and communities.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

A photograph featuring Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS Summit drew widespread attention online. But another Indian official in the frame soon became a talking point of his own. The officer is Sidharth Babu, a 36-year-old Indian Foreign Service (IFS) diplomat currently serving as Deputy Secretary in the East Asia Division of the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). His role, along with his Mandarin skills and experience in China, has put him in proximity to several high-level diplomatic engagements. Babu belongs to the 2017 batch of the IFS and has built his career around international relations, particularly India's engagement with East Asia. Babu is originally from Kochi, Kerala. According to his LinkedIn profile, he studied mechanical engineering at Mar Athanasius College of Engineering between 2008 and 2012. Before entering the civil services, he worked in the e-commerce industry. His first attempt at the Civil Services Examination did not result in a selection. He returned the following year and secured All India Rank 15, eventually choosing the Indian Foreign Service. He began his diplomatic career in New Delhi as an officer trainee in December 2017. His first overseas posting was particularly relevant to his subsequent career. Babu moved to Beijing in August 2018 as a Third Secretary and was later promoted to Second Secretary, serving there until July 2022. The four-year China posting gave him first-hand experience of the country and its political and diplomatic environment, while also strengthening his Mandarin language capabilities. After China, Babu moved to the US. Between August 2022 and June 2024, he served as Consul in Monterey County, California. During the same period, he pursued a Master of Arts in Language Interpretation and Translation at the Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey. Babu returned to New Delhi in June 2024, initially working as an Under Secretary. In January 2025, he became Deputy Secretary in the East Asia Division, the position he currently holds. The BRICS Summit was not Babu's first appearance at a major engagement involving Modi. During India's 77th Republic Day celebrations in January, he was positioned on the VIP podium and interpreted a conversation between Modi and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. His latest appearance has since made him a viral figure online, with social media users discussing both his role at the summit and, in some cases, his appearance. The attention, however, has brought renewed focus to the behind-the-scenes diplomatic officials who help facilitate conversations between world leaders. Pakistan was fined 50 per cent of its match fees and deducted 11 World Test Championship points for maintaining slow overrate during the third and final Test against England in Birmingham on Monday.
The Babar Azam-led side was found 11 overs short of the target “after time allowances were taken in consideration,” the ICC stated in a release.
“In accordance with Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to minimum over-rate offences, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for each over their team fails to bowl within the allotted time, with the maximum penalty capped at 50 percent of the match fee.”
“In addition, as per Article 16.11.2 of the ICC World Test Championship playing conditions, a side is penalised one point for each over short. Consequently, 11 World Test Championship points have been deducted from Pakistan’s points total,” the ICC said.

The sanctions were imposed by ICC match referee Ranjan Madugalle, on-field umpires Paul Reiffel and Chris Gaffaney, third umpire Allahudien Palekar and fourth umpire Russell Warren.
Pakistan had lost the series opener at Leeds by an innings and 103 runs, the second Test at Lord’s by 194 runs and the third Test at Edgbaston by 8 wickets.
“It means Pakistan lose ground at the bottom of the World Test Championship standings as a result, with the side now sitting in ninth place with a 4.63 points percentage,” the ICC said.
Pakistan is currently bottom of the WTC points table with only two wins and seven losses in nine Tests so far.

September is typically the time when television gets serious again. The summer’s biggest TV shows have aired their finales, the fall schedule is kicking into high gear, and streamers are rolling out everything from high-concept sci-fi to prestige dramas. There’s plenty of familiar IP in the mix, but also some genuinely original shows worth putting on your “to watch” list.
While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Reacher), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.
From returning favorites to ambitious new series—and at least one show that might rekindle your love of traditional anime—these are the TV shows we think you should make time to stream this month.
The Paper
What happens when a newspaper attempts to not just survive, but thrive, in a world where digital media has become the norm? The Paper, a spinoff of The Office from Greg Daniels and Michael Koman, follows the staff of a struggling Midwestern paper as they attempt to revive it.
Ultimately, its idealistic new editor-in-chief Ned Sampson (Star Wars and Harry Potter alum Domhnall Gleeson) and his hungry young reporter Mare Pritti (Chelsea Frei) end up grappling with what journalism looks like in the digital age. Season 2, which arrived on September 9, finds their Toledo Truth Teller newly revitalized and searching for its next big scoop, making the show a surprisingly sharp comedy about the future of journalism—and who gets to shape it.
Lego Star Wars: The Mandalorian
Though this summer’s The Mandalorian and Grogu (which is streaming on Disney+ now) seriously underperformed at the box office, Lucasfilm is partnering with Lego to take another stab at the fan-favorite Star Wars series—which might be exactly what the franchise needs right now. Lucasfilm and Lego are going back to the beginning, reimagining all three seasons of the Pedro Pascal-starring live-action series as a 49-minute animated comedy.
For anyone who somehow managed to miss Mando and Grogu until now, the story follows Din Djarin (Pascal in the live-action series, Gavin Hammon in this iteration), a bounty hunter known as the Mandalorian, who takes a job transporting a mysterious Force-sensitive child. That child, of course, is Grogu, aka Baby Yoda. What starts as a simple assignment turns into a galaxy-spanning adventure as the pair become unlikely partners. Consider this version an entertaining way to play catch-up.
South Park
It’s hard to remember a time when the world didn’t have South Park. For nearly 30 years, audiences have watched as four potty-mouthed fourth-graders—Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny—navigate life in the bizarre mountain town of South Park, Colorado, in this very much adults-only animated comedy. Along the way, they’ve encountered alien life forms, celebrities, and Elon Musk (yes, the real one). They’ve also watched Kenny die on at least 100 occasions.
Last year, the seemingly never-ending comedy reinvented itself as a particularly pointed political satire by taking aim at figures including JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem, Donald Trump, and Donald Trump’s manhood. The White House, unsurprisingly, had thoughts. And so did the Emmys; the show just took home the 2026 award for Outstanding Animated Program. Clearly, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have no plans to take their foot off the gas; they just announced they’re taking a page out of Trump’s renaming book and rechristening the show South America for its 29th season, which premieres on September 16.
Slow Horses
What if television’s best spy show was also one of its funniest? If John le Carré and (the original) The Office had a baby, it would look and sound a lot like Slow Horses, which returns for a sixth season on September 16.
Based on Mick Herron’s Slough House book series, the series follows a dysfunctional team of MI5 misfits who are banished to the infamous Slough House unit, where they work under the notorious Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), a foul-mouthed, flatulent, chain-smoking wreck of a man who also happens to be the most brilliant operative in the room. It’s a prestige spy thriller that doesn’t take itself too seriously, bouncing effortlessly between shoot-outs and the kind of droll office banter you’d expect from the best workplace comedies. In a career full of memorable performances, and an Oscar to show for it, Slow Horses just might be the role Oldman is best remembered for. It’s also the project that has made Jack Lowden oddsmakers’ top pick for the next James Bond.
City of Blood
In City of Blood, an eight-episode miniseries from Germany, climate change has turned Berlin into a sweltering city teetering on the edge of collapse—and vampires are ready to take advantage of the chaos. While the privileged few live beneath a climate-controlled dome, the rest of the city’s denizens are left to battle the heat, crime, and corruption that have become part of everyday life. But when estranged sisters Bea (Lea Drinda) and Phoebe (Soma Pysall) reunite, they uncover a nefarious political plot and learn that, thanks to that aforementioned undead population, blood has become the city’s most coveted commodity. It’s a perfectly strange mix of climate dystopia, family drama, and vampire thriller. And it arrives on September 16.
MobLand
Season 2 of MobLand is almost here—whether Tom Hardy likes it or not. (Despite all the recent headlines surrounding the Oscar winner’s behind-the-scenes drama, he has already signed on for Season 3.) The highly underrated, or perhaps just underseen, crime drama returns with the Harrigan family’s criminal empire under threat from rival forces, forcing their street-smart fixer Harry Da Souza (yep, Hardy) to navigate increasingly bloody internal tensions.
As Harry works to keep the fractured family from tearing itself apart, he’s aided by his trusty sidekick Zosia (Jasmine Jobson), a tech specialist who brings a distinctly 21st-century skill set to their old-school criminal enterprise headed up by Conrad (Pierce Brosnan) and Maeve Harrington (Helen Mirren). Meanwhile, rival forces close in, loyalties shift, and violence spreads through every corner of the family’s world. Expect more bloodshed, shifting allegiances, poor decisions, and one of television’s most kickass theme songs (Fontaines D.C.’s “Starburster”) when Season 2 premieres on September 18.
Outlander: Blood of My Blood
Before there was Jamie and Claire, there were their parents. Like its predecessor, this Outlander prequel follows two separate timelines as it details the courtship of Jamie Fraser’s parents, Brian Fraser (Jamie Roy) and Ellen MacKenzie (Harriet Slater), in 18th-century Scotland, alongside the story of Claire Beauchamp’s parents, Henry Beauchamp (Jeremy Irvine) and Julia Moriston (Hermione Corfield), in World War I-era England. Their two love stories unfold across different time periods, weaving together romance, family drama, and the time-traveling forces that kept Outlander fans enthralled for eight seasons. The series’ second season arrives on September 18.
American Horror Story
Season 13 of Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk’s horror anthology is shaping up to be what has at various points called an Avengers-esque “endgame-level event” of “greatest hits.” While the details, as always, have been kept rather quiet, what we do know is that the new season of American Horror Story will pull bits and pieces from each season of the series, with a heavy emphasis on its witchcraft-laden “Coven” and “Apocalypse” storylines.
We also know it is reassembling an all-star cast of past stars, some of whom will play double—or even triple—character duty. Among them: Murphy mainstays Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters, Jessica Lange, Kathy Bates, Emma Roberts, Billie Lourd, and Angela Bassett. The new season arrives on September 26, which gives you plenty of time to brush up on your AHS lore.
Neon Genesis Evangelion
Before Netflix gave it a new English dub—and, depending on who you ask, stirred up a lot of feelings—there was the original Japanese-language version of Neon Genesis Evangelion. The landmark anime, released in 1995, follows a group of teenagers recruited to pilot giant biomechanical weapons called Evangelions, or Evas, as they defend a post-apocalyptic Tokyo (now known as Tokyo-3) from mysterious creatures, aka Angels. But what starts as a fairly straightforward battle-for-humanity story soon becomes something far stranger, delving into trauma, loneliness, identity, and human connection.
The Criterion Channel is bringing all 26 episodes of the classic (pre-Netflix) English dub to streaming for the first time, alongside the original Japanese-language version for all you purists. It’s a fitting return for one of anime’s most boundary-pushing series.

Power House is the title of Tamil star Vikram’s upcoming film with director Anand Shankar, the makers announced on Vinayaka Chaturthi, Monday, September 14, with a title announcement teaser. The film, which was previously called Chiyaan 63, will release in 2027.
The title teaser introduces Vikram as the man who runs Nalla Thambi Catering Service with his family, which includes his sister (played by Riya Shibu) and mother (Urvashi). After overseeing the preparations for a wedding, he steps into a dark passageway at the back of the house. In a classic Vikram-esque moment, we realise that in a storage room at the back, he has tied up a man to a chair while another is hung upside down from the ceiling. When the latter grunts and struggles upon seeing Vikram, the hero calms him down and says, “I have just started cooking, haven’t I? I promise to send you back after a full meals. 100% guarantee.”
The teaser, like the previous teasers of Vikram’s films, doesn’t give out any details about the plot. Interestingly, ‘Power House’ is a phrase that’s been popular in Tamil pop-culture since the release of Rajinikanth’s 2025 film, Coolie. The cast of Power House also features MS Bhaskar, Shammy Thilakan, VTV Ganesh, and Samyuktha Hegde. Sendhil Thyagarajan and Arjun Thyagarajan produce the film under the banner of Sathya Jyothi Films.
Notably, this is Vikram’s second collaboration with director Anand Shankar after Iru Mugan (2016). Apart from this, Vikram also has a film with Bodi Rajkumar in the pipeline. Vikram was also set to work with Madonne Ashwin of Mandela and Maaveran and Prem Kumar of 96 and Meiyazhagan fame; however, reports state that both the films have been shelved.

How did the first Ultimate Championship go?
- Published
As poster boy Armand Duplantis performed the Ultimate Championship's official song and fireworks lit up the sky above the newly crowned winners, athletics had taken its first strides in a new direction.
Across three fast-paced evenings the inaugural event played out in Budapest, where a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot was distributed among the sport's biggest stars.
It looked different. It felt different. And, after three successive sell-out crowds and positive feedback from the athletes, it appears it is here to stay.
"It's a good first step towards changing track and field for the better," said Usain Bolt, event ambassador and the greatest sprinter in history.
"The athletes are loving it. It's a different energy, a different vibe."
World Athletics and its president, Lord Coe, worked for three years to tackle the absence of a season-ending pinnacle event.
Rather than keeping to an established formula, the Ultimate Championship was a bold, innovative undertaking - and it is hoped it can exist as a testing ground to help shape the sport's future.
"We walked out, we came through the little starlights and we all looked at each other and said, 'this is unbelievable'," Britain's four-time global relay medallist Imani-Lara Lansiquot told BBC Sport.
"It's so rare that things really live up to the expectation, the hype. I'm so, so glad, having been in this sport for many years now, to actually see us be put on a platform and celebrated in this way."
Athletics has long grappled with the issue of maintaining the interest and excitement which it generates at the Olympics throughout the rest of those four-year cycles.
The structure of the season has not always been clear for occasional viewers, while showdowns between the world's top athletes can be inconsistent. From a storytelling perspective, that is far from ideal.
They are all issues World Athletics has sought to begin addressing with the biennial Ultimate Championship, while also compensating the athletes with record prize money.
The premise is accessible: condensed, fast-paced sessions, with the best competing against the best for a global title and significant prize money.
A striking new appearance and several innovative features ensured the Ultimate Championship provided a notably different feel to that of the sport's established global championships.
An infield painted black sought to focus attention on the illuminated live events, while the horizontal jumps were decided in a bright pink sandpit.
A new trophy waited for the winners on a plinth, with their crowning moment marked by sparklers and celebratory music.
New features for TV audiences attempted to enhance the viewer experience, with athlete headshots, win probabilities and projected finishing positions flashing up on screen.
They did so with varying success.
Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen was unimpressed by his predicted finishing position of 12th before winning the 5,000m title, while Britain's 1500m champion Josh Kerr was expected to finish last - a result of both athletes racing lightly over recent seasons.
There was a notable athlete-centric feel to the event beyond the increased financial rewards.
The world's top athletes arrived on the eve of the championship for a red carpet event featuring photoshoots.
Athlete videos were played inside the stadium before events and winners held centre-court style interviews before being escorted to a champions' enclosure, where they joined Bolt and master of ceremonies Noah Lyles.
On the videos, Britain's Georgia Hunter Bell said: "I do like the fact that it builds personality and character for, hopefully, people to connect with the athletes. That storytelling is something that's really interesting.
"If you think of superstars like Carlos Alcaraz, Serena Williams or Tadej Pogacar, obviously they're great athletes, but it's their personality coming through that makes it fun."
BBC commentator and former 1500m world champion Steve Cram said: "The key is the exposure of it. It's good for the sport. It's really good for the profile of the athletes."
But the championship did not avoid criticism - the biggest its exclusion of certain events.
World Athletics took the decision to include events based on viewer behaviour, including pulse rate and sweat response.
That meant that distance track events, including the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, were omitted, while only selected field events were included. Shot-putters and discus throwers were excluded entirely.
The event format was also altered. Round progression in several field events meant increased jeopardy, with the competition whittled down to the top four athletes by the fourth and final round.
British long jumper Jazmin Sawyers told BBC Sport: "Some field events didn't get any attention because they're not here. The championship is worse off for not having them.
"It looks amazing in stadium and broadcast. It's dynamic. It's exciting. There's a place for it alongside regular championships.
"I don't think I would like to see it replace regular championships, but I like the idea that this is something that exists alone."
On the long jump competition format, she added: "I would love to see all eight [athletes] get all four jumps. It makes it more interesting.
"I was able to come from fourth to second. What if the person who was eighth could go from eighth to first? That's more exciting."
On the matter of the excluded events, Coe said the disciplines held at the Ultimate Championship were "not in tablets of stone".
Looking ahead to the next edition in 2028, the Ultimate Championship will be positioned at the end of a season which is headlined by an Olympics.
It remains to be seen how it will fit alongside the Diamond League - the sport's season-long series - in the schedule of the athletes.
Former Olympic heptathlon champion Denise Lewis told BBC Sport: "People have wanted to see something that looked different and felt like a different product. World Athletics has delivered.
"I don't think we know what it will do to the global calendar of athletics.
"The overall picture and the landscape isn't clear. There is place for this, but I do think it is unclear what yet."
Coe accepted before the weekend that there would be "no guarantee we're going get everything right" and said a "slightly different format" might be considered in future.
But, regardless, the competition was a statement of intent as the sport seeks to engage with new, bigger audiences while ensuring its star names are rewarded with prize money closer aligned to that of other sports.
Speaking after become Britain's first Ultimate champion in the 1500m, Josh Kerr said: "I welcome anything that can push this sport on to make it more entertaining for people to watch and athletes to go out and compete.
"There is one last thing that we can do to get it right and that is to let athletes wear their own brands versus their country.
"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make money from that. We don't have the pay cheques other sports do just yet.
"My $30,000 pay cheque just came through from winning the World Indoors, so $150,000 is a huge jump and I'm massively appreciative."

Swedish left-wing bloc edges ahead in knife-edge election results
Final results are not expected before Wednesday, when local election boards count postal votes that arrived too late for polling day, along with ballots cast from abroad
Sweden's centre-left opposition has edged ahead of the ruling right-wing government in a knife-edge general election, with days of uncertainty expected before a final result is confirmed.
The left-leaning bloc, led by Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson, was projected to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, based on votes counted from 6,195 of Sweden's 6,312 electoral districts, the country's election authority said.
The right-wing governing bloc of prime minister Ulf Kristersson trailed with 173 seats, separated by roughly 20,000 votes, with around 94 per cent of the vote counted on Monday morning.
Exit polls from public broadcaster SVT had initially shown the left-wing parties ahead by several percentage points, prompting jubilation at the Social Democrats' election night gathering in Stockholm, though the mood shifted to quiet waiting as the closer preliminary results came in.
Sweden elects its parliament through a proportional representation system, with parties needing at least 4 per cent of the vote to win seats. More than 8 million of the country's roughly 10.6 million people were eligible to vote.
The country's political landscape is split between two four-party blocs, on the left and the right, meaning the outcome hinges less on any single party's result and more on which side can assemble a majority.
Final results are not expected before Wednesday, when local election boards count postal votes that arrived too late for polling day, along with ballots cast from abroad.
Speaking early on Monday, Mr Kristersson said the outcome remained genuinely uncertain, though he pointed to what he described as a broader ideological majority in parliament.
"There is a very clear non-socialist majority, or non-left leaning economic majority in the Swedish parliament," he said.
"When we have the final result it's a good idea to look at possible combinations. I will actually take note of that and at least figure out whether there are any possibilities."
No major media outlet had called the result. Ms Andersson urged her own supporters to wait for the final count.
"We must wait for the final election result," she said. "Right now we are leading, but we have to wait for the final result."
Mr Kristersson has governed Sweden since 2022 at the head of a three-party centre-right coalition, relying on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, a party with far-right roots that has moved toward the political mainstream, to secure a parliamentary majority.
The Sweden Democrats had been promised cabinet posts this time had the governing coalition been returned to office. In a break from a longstanding taboo, Mr Kristersson pledged before the vote to bring the party directly into government as he seeks to build a majority right-wing coalition. Since taking office, his government has abolished permanent residency for refugees, tightened welfare rules and stepped up expulsions of people without the right to remain in the country.
Ms Andersson, who served as prime minister from 2021 until losing power at the last election, would need to secure a coalition agreement with other parties to return to office, and her own bloc faces internal tensions of its own, with disagreements over migration policy, a proposed tax on billionaires and the construction of new nuclear reactors. Her Left Party and Centre Party partners, in particular, differ sharply on economic policy, which could complicate efforts to pass a budget even if her bloc secures a majority.

Kharif sowing has nearly caught up with last year, although acreage under several key crops remains lower, agriculture ministry data showed. Farmers had planted 109.6 million hectares as of 11 September, about 1.6 million hectares below the area sown during the year-ago period. The acreage is also close to the ministry’s normal benchmark of 110.4 million hectares. The headline figure masks sharper declines in rice, maize, oilseeds, sugarcane and cotton, which are critical to India’s food, edible oil and fibre supplies. Rice acreage stood at 42.6 million hectares, down 1.7 million hectares from a year ago. Pulses offered some support, with acreage rising 167,000 hectares to 11.8 million hectares, led by gains in Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh. Coarse cereals and oil seeds increased marginally, while cotton and sugarcane remained below last year’s levels. The uneven monsoon remains a concern. India has received 15% less rainfall than normal between 1 June and 13 September, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), with significant regional variations. The rainfall deficit and prolonged dry spells could affect crops at critical growth stages. “The latest kharif sowing figures present a mixed picture for Indian agriculture. While the total sown area is marginally lower than last year, the real story lies in the regional variations, where rainfall patterns, soil moisture, crop economics and local agro-climatic conditions continue to shape farmers’ sowing decisions," said Uday Raj Anand, chief executive, domestic business, agrochemical company Parijat Industries. Area under Shri Anna and coarse cereals stood at 18.3 million hectares, marginally up from 18.2 million hectares a year ago. The increase in area was mainly due to higher acreage in Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand. Oilseed acreage declined marginally to 19.39 million hectares from 19.4 million hectares last year. Lower acreage under soybean and groundnut offset gains in crops such as sesame and sunflower. Cotton acreage was also marginally lower at 10.9 million hectares, compared with 11.0 million hectares a year ago. The decline in cotton area coverage is mainly attributable to substantial reductions in Rajasthan and Haryana, with declines in Punjab and Andhra Pradesh that have more than offset the gains recorded in Telangana and Gujarat. Sugarcane acreage at 5.84 million hectares was marginally below the 5.88 million hectares recorded a year ago. The narrowing sowing gap comes despite a deficient monsoon season. Also, rainfall distribution has remained uneven. Russian drone hits train near Ukraine-Poland border soon after dignitaries passed through
KYIV, Ukraine — A Russian drone struck a train near the Ukraine- Poland border on Sunday shortly after senior visiting officials — including the former prime ministers of the U.K. and Sweden -- passed through, Ukraine's state rail operator said.
According to Ukrzaliznytsia, a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson, Carl Bildt and security advisers from several European Union states had purposely left the station at Yahodyn ahead of schedule. The visitors were on their way back from a security conference in Kyiv.
"It is highly probable that the Russian drone 's intended target was in fact the diplomatic train, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled," the company said in a Telegram post.
Bildt, the former Swedish PM, shared a video on X of the attack at Yahodyn station, near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland.
"This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing," Bildt said. "It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was hurt. Very good safety system. Our train just had an evacuation warning."
Bildt, Johnson and fellow passengers had been in Kyiv for the Yalta European Strategy conference, which is an annual gathering of leaders and experts across politics, business, security and media.
Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to Ukrzaliznytsia.
There were no immediate reports of casualties on any of the trains.
Ukrzaliznytsia said it "constantly adjusts train schedules" to guard against strikes.
"I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning," Johnson wrote in a post on X.
"What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day — even on civilian railways," he added.
Earlier on Sunday, a Russian drone hit a truck less than a mile from Polish territory, according to border guards, forcing the temporary closure of the Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing.

There are many, many strange things about the stew of conspiracy theories that fall under the umbrella of “9/11 Truth”—the false, often antisemitic worldview purporting that the US government had inside knowledge of or even actively participated in the September 11 attacks. But perhaps the strangest is that the seed of these theories was planted three months before the attacks themselves.
It was June 28, 2001, when Milton William “Bill” Cooper took to the air on his national radio show after watching a news report on CNN. “Supposedly, a CNN reporter found Osama bin Laden, took a television camera crew with him, went into Osama bin Laden's hideout, interviewed him and his top leadership, his top lieutenants and colonels and generals in their hideout,” Cooper told his listeners. “He came out and told everybody, ‘Within three weeks, Osama bin Laden is going to attack the United States and Israel.’”
Cooper had part of the story right—a reporter had indeed just reached the inner sanctum of al Qaeda in the mountains near Kandahar, Afghanistan, but he was actually a correspondent for a Middle Eastern broadcaster. And that reporter, the MBC correspondent Baker Atyani, had actually interviewed al Qaeda’s military chief, Mohammed Atif, not bin Laden. “In the coming weeks, there will be a big surprise; we are going to hit American and Israeli installations,” Atif told Atyani. “The coffin business will increase in the United States.” According to Atyani, bin Laden—who was present for the interview—smiled and nodded.
To Cooper, speaking on the radio that day, the interview represented either a major embarrassment for the US government, which had been hunting bin Laden for years, or it was evidence that the government was lying about the threat from bin Laden.
“Now, don’t you think that’s kind of strange, folks?” Cooper said. “The largest intelligence apparatus in the world, with the biggest budget in the history of the world, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and can't find him. The FBI, also under the leadership of Louis Freeh, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and years and years and many years and can’t find him. Some doofus jerk-off reporter with a camera crew waltzes right into his hideout and interviews him?”
“Now that tells us two things: Either everyone in the intelligence community and all of the intelligence agencies of the United States government are blithering idiots and incompetent fools, including the entire apparatus of the FBI and all of their personnel—or they're lying to us. They're not looking for him at all.”
Cooper went on to say that “the CIA created Osama bin Laden” and that “they're now using him to help bring about world government by making him the big boogeyman because they can't use [Iraqi dictator] Saddam Hussein anymore.”
Cooper argued that the whole threat from bin Laden was a farce—what would now be called a “false flag” operation. “If you believe it, you are one of the stupidest jerks that ever lived on the face of this earth, and whatever’s going to happen they’re going to blame on Osama bin Laden.”
About 10 weeks later, Cooper’s comment would come to be seen as a prophecy.
The events and aftermath of 9/11 altered almost every aspect of American society: from the ever-present security theater of daily life—the 3.4-ounce liquid bottles at airports, the defensive bollards that now dominate so many urban landscapes—to the expansion of the surveillance state, to 20 years of war in Afghanistan, to the backdrop of fear and anxiety that permeates the culture. Few, though, rightly recognize one of the most important and pernicious impacts of 9/11: how it changed our society’s very understanding and relationship to facts and truth.
It’s a story that not many people fully understand, one with roots in the UFO conspiracies of the 1980s and with tentacles that stretch to the National Mall on January 6, 2021—and one that helps in particular to explain the transformation of Alex Jones from a fringe Austin, Texas, talk show host to one of the most important (and disruptive) political forces of the 21st century. This transformation began in the first minutes after the September 11 attacks.
Cooper first came to prominence in the 1980s, among the first of a group who would come to be known as “UFO whistleblowers,” former military or intelligence veterans who purported to have insider knowledge about the government’s cover-up of alien civilizations, captured spacecraft, and recovered alien life-forms. It was the first golden age of modern conspiracism, as trust in government cratered following Vietnam, Watergate, and the revelations of dark assassination plots by the Pike and Church committees; books about cover-ups and urban legends like the Bermuda Triangle and the “Philadelphia Experiment” became bestsellers.
Cooper claimed to have been a naval intelligence officer in the 1970s and said that, as part of his work with a high-ranking admiral, he’d been able to covertly paw through the contents of the admiral’s cabinet of classified material. As Colin Dickey wrote in a review of a Cooper biography, the cabinet became “a repository of secrets known only to Cooper, whose contents seemed to change and evolve over the years, fitting whatever need Cooper’s current conspiracies had.” In early iterations, Cooper hinted it contained the truth about the JFK assassination and the government’s contact with aliens.
In the 1990s, amid the rise of far-right talk shows like that of Rush Limbaugh, Cooper became a national radio figure as well; his shortwave The Hour of the Time focused on a witches’ brew of sinister government conspiracies, alternate histories, warnings about the New World Order and secret societies, and a healthy dose of general-purpose skepticism; Cooper often exhorted his audience, “Wake up, sheeple!” (Much of his conspiracism contained thinly and not-so-thinly veiled antisemitism.)
For a brief period, Cooper was one of the nation’s most famous “UFO-ologists,” but few believed him—he feuded frequently with others in the field. He eventually laid out a grand conspiracy account in his 1991 memoir/fever-dream of a book, Behold a Pale Horse.
Behold a Pale Horse is a wacky piece of writing—there’s almost no other word for it. At one point it quotes the entire text of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated antisemitic screed from the early 1900s that alleged a secret Jewish plot to overthrow Christianity. Cooper’s work was basically QAnon three decades early, outlining a vast global conspiracy, decades-long and all-encompassing, to steal America and our freedoms from real Americans, all to serve some global super elite. The book became an underground bestseller—it still is today—and took off particularly within the militia movement.
This newfound fame coincided with the start of his talk radio career on WWCR, World Wide Christian Radio, in January 1993. With a 100,000-watt signal, he could reach huge swaths of the country from his home in Arizona. And over time, Cooper developed two important—and later infamous—superfans. One was a young Gulf War veteran named Timothy McVeigh, who in the early spring of 1995 journeyed with a companion—their exact identity is disputed—to Arizona to try to talk to Cooper at his home. “The last thing he said before they left in their green Mercury Marquis station wagon with a puke-yellow interior was, ‘Watch Oklahoma City,’” Cooper would later recount. Soon after their meeting, McVeigh attacked the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, killing 168 people and injuring nearly 700.
Then there was Alex Jones, a local public-access talk show host in Austin, Texas, who first came onto the national radar for his fundraising work to rebuild the church at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas. The site had burned down in 1993 at the end of a 51-day siege by the US government, as federal agents tried to arrest the leader of the Branch Davidian cult, David Koresh. In the end, agents in armored vehicles tried to fill the compound with tear gas; the buildings caught fire—it was never clear how the fires started—and most of the Davidians who remained in the compound died in the blaze. There were 75 fatalities, including about two dozen children. The Waco siege was a key flashpoint for the far right in the 1990s.
Jones saw inspiration in Cooper’s model, and Cooper became something of a mentor to the budding radio host, calling in for an interview on Jones’ early shows. Jones’ show on KJFK-FM lasted until 1999—he was even voted “Best of Austin” radio host by a local newspaper, which called him “either Austin’s great exposer of truth or a black helicopter conspiracy nut, depending on your worldview.” But his conspiracism made getting sponsors difficult, and KJFK fired him in December 1999. Jones quickly latched on to a new venture on the expanding internet: Infowars.com.
On September 11, 2001, Cooper was outraged by the attacks and warned of what would come next. “Folks, I can assure you that 72 hours from now, we will be at war. We will be bombing two or maybe three countries … Because that’s how it works. When governments are attacked, they lash out. Thousands of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with what is happening at the World Trade Center and the Pentagon are going to die,” Cooper said. “Nothing will be the same after today.”
Broadcasting that day on Infowars and about 100 syndicated stations, Jones did one better: “I went on the air and said, ‘Those were controlled demolitions,’” he later told Rolling Stone.
In the weeks ahead, Cooper and Jones diverged politically. Cooper had come to see Jones as a copycat, a fearmonger, and a liar. (On September 26, 2001, Cooper’s show was titled simply “Alex Jones—Liar.”)
Amid the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Jones dove deeper into budding 9/11 conspiracies, and Cooper—who had stopped paying taxes, was drinking heavily, and was engaged in sometimes violent disputes with his neighbors—began prophesying his own death. In November 2001, law enforcement arrived at his Arizona compound to arrest him on an outstanding warrant on suspicion of aggravated assault; Cooper opened fire, shooting one deputy in the head, and was killed in the returning police gunfire.
The field was clear for the rise of Alex Jones.
In the years that followed, Alex Jones became a key force in the spread of 9/11 conspiracies. The movement, which came to be known as “9/11 Truth,” encompassed a host of different theories: that United Airlines Flight 93 had been downed by US fighters; that the Pentagon had been struck by a missile, not a plane; that the World Trade Centers had been brought down by space weapons.
By even the first years after 9/11, the ideas had become so widespread that the government’s 9/11 Commission took pains to document in careful factual detail the impossibility of some of the conspiracies, hoping to avoid the ambiguities that dogged the Warren Commission’s report into the JFK assassination. Popular Mechanics devoted a special issue—later turned into a book, with a foreword by Senator John McCain—to debunking the most popular ones.
But the conspiracies took root in the early internet of the 2000s: Arguably the first viral online documentary, known as Loose Change, took the conspiracies to the broader public, becoming one of the most-watched videos on Google Video and the early era of YouTube. (Jones would even get an “executive producer” credit on one version of the film.) The DVD box promised, “What you will see inside will prove without a shadow of a doubt that everything you know about 9/11 is a complete fabrication.”
The reality is that the film offered no conclusive evidence of government involvement or conspiracy, but would be familiar format-wise to anyone online today in its “We’re-just-asking-questions” tone, cherry-picking quotes and evidence out of context to broadly hand-wave at surely sinister machinations behind the scenes.
9/11 conspiracism found a home politically on both the right, with Jones and his acolytes, and the left in the 2000s, as Democrats protested the documentable lies and mistruths that helped lead the nation into war with Iraq. Documentarian Michael Moore released a blockbuster movie in 2004, Fahrenheit 9/11, a polemic that tied George W. Bush’s administration, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq together in a sinister warmongering and corporate profiteering conspiracy; it became one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time and won the prestigious Palme d’Or at Cannes.
According to a May 2006 Zogby poll, some 42 percent of Americans believed that the US government and the 9/11 Commission “concealed or refused to investigate critical evidence that contradicts their official explanation of the September 11 attacks” and that “there has been a cover-up.”
I’ve spent much of the past decade writing about 9/11 and have spoken at hundreds of public events; rarely do I make it through an event without an audience question that’s at least conspiracy-adjacent.
Jones, in particular, found conspiracism wildly profitable. As Nicole Hemmer, a Vanderbilt professor who studies the far right, told me, “Because he was a critic of the war in Iraq, he becomes seen by many people outside of the Alex Jones universe as somebody who bridges the left-right divide. Even though he is a far-right figure, he can feast off this credibility that he has as being somebody who is above politics—and that really helps elevate him into, increasingly, a household name.”
Jones became nationally infamous for arguing that later tragedies, like the elementary school shooting at Sandy Hook, were also false-flag operations. In the first Trump term, amid the Covid-19 pandemic, Jones became a fierce voice against government lockdowns, and as the aftermath of the fall 2020 election unfolded, he and his “InfoWars Battle Tank”—an armored truck worth some $300,000—became a ubiquitous presence at Stop the Steal rallies leading up to the protests at the Capitol on January 6. Throughout Donald Trump’s rise and first term, conspiracies loomed large. Trump himself first came to political prominence amid the birtherism movement, and his supporters embraced Pizzagate and the broader QAnon conspiracy.
In recent years, Jones, of course, has suffered a remarkable comedown; his vicious lies finally caught up with him in lawsuits from the families of the victims of the Sandy Hook shooting, and after a lengthy court battle, his InfoWars.com domain has been acquired by The Onion.
But if Jones has lost his most recent battles, it’s hard not to see that his conspiracism has won the broader war. Today, as the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, it’s notable that the anti-government conspiracists have effectively taken over the US government itself—from Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Covid and vaccine denialism to President Donald Trump’s own fetid swamp of a social media feed. In news that would make Bill Cooper particularly proud, Trump has even promised to release the government’s files on the truth about UFOs. For the most part, though, we’re still waiting.

Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.
