Frequently Asked Questions
What Is Noise Canceling and How Does It Work?
When people think of noise cancellation in headphones, two things happen at once. First is passive sound isolation: headphones physically block your ears and block some sound from reaching them. Second is active noise cancellation (ANC), which uses a mix of exterior microphones and software to suppress outside sound before it reaches your eardrums.
ANC has been around since the 1970s, but has been refined to very advanced levels since then. Nowadays, it feels like magic, but the principles of physics haven't changed.
Sound moves through the air as pressure waves. The frequency of a wave (the number of times it oscillates per second) determines the pitch. We perceive low-frequency waves, like from an airplane rumble, as dull, bassy sound. We hear high-frequency waves, like a police siren, as a sharp, treble sound.
ANC uses microphones to hear incoming waves and generate the polar opposite waveform. When you add opposite waveforms together, they cancel each other out, and it's as if there is no sound wave at all, at least to our ears.
It isn't perfect because many sounds surround us at the same time—some constant, like the hum of an AC, while others are varied and sudden, like the human voice. ANC can't cancel every sound in your environment, but the best headphones get impressively close.
What Is Transparency Mode or Ambient Sound Mode?
You don't always want to block out all the sound around you when wearing headphones. That's why most models have a transparency mode (sometimes called ambient sound mode), which does the opposite of noise canceling—it filters in environmental sounds through your headphones so you can hear your surroundings more clearly.
Like with ANC, some headphones accomplish this task better than others. Apple AirPods are some of the best; it can feel like you're not wearing earbuds at all when using their transparency mode.
One limitation with these modes is outside interference, namely wind. I've tried using transparency mode while riding an ebike, and it mostly sounds like a blistering blast of artificial wind noise. If you're looking for headphones for outdoor activities like running or biking, open earbuds are a great alternative, as they leave your ears open to naturally hear the world around you.
How I Test Noise-Canceling Earbuds
I test all kinds of headphones, including noise-canceling ones, the way regular people might use them. I wear them for multiple weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I use them to take calls, listen to music, watch TV shows, scroll social media, and listen to my favorite playlists.
For testing noise cancellation, I use headphones in the real world. Luckily, I live in New York City, where loud traffic, subway platforms, cafes, and crowds of people are ever-present. When I can, I take earbuds on long flights to see how they handle jet engine noise.
For audio, I don't have a set playlist I test every single headphone with. I instead try to sample a wide variety of genres and artists. My main streaming source is Spotify Lossless, but I take time to test other lossless formats and high-resolution audio codecs when possible.

Now, Zomato To Charge A COD Fee Zomato has begun charging some customers an extra fee for paying cash on delivery. With this, it is adding another layer to its already crowded order bill. The New Monetisation Layer: For Zomato, the latest fee opens another high-margin channel that monetises its sticky customer base. The levy also penalises a specific behaviour. By making cash payment costlier, Zomato aims to recover handling costs, reduce order risk and encourage online payments. But the COD levy also adds another variable charge to a user’s food bill. Paying in cash, often a matter of preference or necessity, is now being treated as a premium choice. A Recurring Pattern? Zomato’s latest levy is not an isolated pricing tweak but part of a recurring pattern. Earlier this year, it hiked the platform fees by nearly 20% to ₹14.90 per order from ₹12.50 earlier. For a food delivery business seeking better margins, the latest levy appears to be an easy lever to pump up revenue. Rivals Close In: Zomato’s latest monetisation move comes amid intensifying competition in the food delivery space. Flipkart is piloting Eat In, Rapido is scaling its zero-commission Ownly play, and newer players such as Swish are expanding rapidly. These challengers may not yet threaten Zomato’s dominance, but they could force the Eternal-owned platform to defend users and restaurants more aggressively. So, will the latest fees make Zomato more resilient or give rivals an opening to gain users? Its IPO is likely to be worth around ₹3,000-4,000 Cr, with the startup seeking a valuation of around ₹9,500 Cr. The IPO is expected to comprise both a fresh issue of equity shares and an offer for sale (OFS) by existing investors. The fresh issue would likely constitute a larger portion of the IPO size, though the structure will be finalised closer to the listing. Delhi NCR-based InsuranceDekho was founded as the insurance arm of used car marketplace CarDekho in 2016 by Agrawal and Babbar. It was later hived off as a separate business. The startup offers motor, health, life and other insurance products. It has also been granted a composite broking licence from the regulator, allowing it to offer reinsurance services. Besides, it operates Heph, a SaaS platform for insurance distributors. Yamanashi Prefecture plans to charge climbers for helicopter rescues on Mount Fuji during the mountain’s closed season, part of a package of measures aimed at deterring reckless ascents.
According to the new plan unveiled Monday, people climbing above Mount Fuji’s 6th Station during the closed season will be required to submit a climbing plan in advance. Authorities will recommend changes when equipment, routes or other elements of a plan are considered inadequate.
Climbers who require rescue by a prefectural disaster-response helicopter after failing to submit a plan will be charged. Those who submitted one but deviated from it or didn’t take prefectural recommendations could also face charges if experts determine that their equipment, climbing method or other circumstances amounted to reckless climbing.

$5.5M daycare built with provincial funds now derelict, scavenged by thieves and damaged by flooding
74-space East St. Paul daycare completed in 2024 has yet to provide care for any kids
A $5.5-million Winnipeg-area daycare built two years ago with provincial funds sits vacant, derelict and surrounded by weeds after being plundered by scavengers and damaged by flooding.
The non-profit group hoping to operate the daycare and an advocate for not-for-profit daycares are now pleading with the province to open the East St. Paul facility, which has yet to care for a single child.
The 74-space daycare was built in 2024 on behalf of the Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust. It was one of 22 daycares built in Manitoba as part of a project started by the former Progressive Conservative government along with JohnQ Public, a company owned by 11 Manitoba municipalities.
The structure has been vacant since, even though the daycare operator waiting to use the building has 800 kids on its waiting list.
The provincial government has said this is because a change of land ownership has contravened the daycare's operating agreement.
CBC News took a tour of the daycare last week and documented extensive damage to both the interior and exterior of the building.
"It's heartbreaking and frustrating," said Patrick Ryan, the volunteer board chair for Created 4 Me Early Learning Centre, which has been stymied in its efforts to move into the building.
The tour of the daycare revealed broken windows inside the facility, broken glass on the floor and damage to the building's security system.
Two commercial fridges and a dishwasher are missing and presumed stolen. Copper wire has been stripped from inside and outside the building.
Air-conditioning units on the daycare's roof have been partly dismantled, with mechanical parts missing — presumably removed by scavengers — and rainwater has penetrated the building, damaging ceilings. The building went months without power, meaning its sump pump didn't run and about half a metre of water has pooled in the basement.
Selkirk RCMP investigated the damage but said they did not identify any suspects.
Ryan estimated the damage to the as-yet-unused daycare exceeds $1 million.
"It's frustrating from the perspective of the amount of money that the public has put into the facility to see the building in the state that it is," he said.
His organization hired staff to work at the daycare but had to let them go after making repeated attempts to get the centre open.
The executive director of Created 4 Me says the situation has been "very difficult."
"It is very difficult to plan for the unknown, without an opening date being set, or being pushed back," said Laura Van Landeghem.
"It has been emotionally draining."
Provincial funds stopped flowing in 2024
The daycare was built for Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust, an arm's-length entity formed by Manitoba's most populous First Nation to acquire real estate for investment and housing for the benefit of band members, according to its founding documents.
The daycare is built on part of a former golf course east of Highway 59 called The Meadows, purchased by the trust in 2021. The placement of the daycare on land located more than 150 kilometres south of the First Nation's main reserve led some band members to criticize the decision to build in East St. Paul.
In 2024, the Peguis real estate trust sold 75 per cent of a company that controls the Meadows land to a numbered company owned by Andrew Marquess, a former adviser to the trust, according to a purchase and development agreement obtained by CBC News.
Manitoba paid out $3.3 million of the $5.5 million budgeted for the daycare before funding for the project stopped flowing in November 2024, according to the province.
According to a letter tabled in the Manitoba Legislature the following April, former deputy minister of education and early childhood learning Brian O'Leary said the project may not have followed normal provincial or municipal procurement practices.
In January, Manitoba Education and Early Childhood Learning Minister Tracy Schmidt said the province had an agreement with Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust.
"Our understanding is right now they do not own that land," Schmidt said at the time.
"We need to ensure the long-term viability of this project, so we need to ascertain that the agreement is in compliance. Once we have certainty about the long-term viability of this product, we'll proceed as soon as possible."
Eight months later, Schmidt said the province still has not received documentation from Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust to demonstrate who owns that land.
"Until we receive documentation assuring government who owns the land, we can't proceed," she said earlier this month in an interview in her office.
"Me and my team have been in constant communication with legal counsel, and we are pulling every lever available to us to make sure we can get the centre open as soon as possible."
A lawyer for Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust did not return requests for comment.
Schmidt said she could not provide a timeline for getting the daycare open because the province is not the legal owner of the property.
"If I could walk down there tomorrow … and open it up myself, I would do that, and I think the premier would come with me. We are doing everything that we can."
Delay puzzling: advocate
The delay in getting the East St. Paul daycare open is baffling, said Gerrie Prymak, a retired teacher who now advocates for child care and helped found Little Stars Playhouse daycare in Winnipeg's North End.
Prymak said Little Stars had to enter into an operating agreement with the province before it could open, and questioned why the provincial government can't cut through the bureaucracy in this case.
"I don't know why it's taking a year and a half," Prymak said in an interview at Little Stars on Selkirk Avenue.
She urged Premier Wab Kinew to get personally involved.
"[Have] a face-to-face meeting and say, 'Children first.… We've got to get this open,'" she said.
Kinew said Thursday he is "always down to meet."
Prymak said she went to visit the daycare site herself when she heard it still wasn't open.
"When I saw the vandalism, I thought, 'what a waste,'" she said. "Why can't there be some security that they can pay for to take care of this piece of property that we invested so much money for?"
Prymak also said the province has fallen short of its 2021 promise to create 23,000 daycare spaces by March of this year.
The NDP government said in August it has created or promised to open 12,700 spaces since taking power in 2023.
Schmidt said the province is still working to create more daycare spaces.
"While I understand that every single space counts, and that families are relying on these 74 spaces in East St. Paul to open as soon as possible, Manitobans should rest assured that our government is working as hard as we can to meet that need," she said.
In the meantime, Patrick Ryan is encouraging more action from the province to get Created 4 Me daycare open.
"We're really calling on the provincial government and the Rural Municipality of East St. Paul to step up and do what it takes to get this place open," he said, adding he has had reasonable conversations with all parties involved.
"Everybody has an interest in getting this place opened. Call on everybody to sit down together and figure out a plan to get it open."
With files from Cameron MacLean

Pakistan will be among the six countries that would compete in next month’s Men’s Asian Champions Trophy hockey tournament here, Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said on Monday, citing the union government’s policy which allows the archfoe to play on Indian soil during multi-lateral engagements.
The Asian Champions Trophy, to be held from October 27 to November 5, will feature India, Pakistan, China, Japan, Malaysia, and Korea and will be played at Jalandhar and Mohali’s hockey stadiums.
Two reserve teams -- Oman and Bangladesh -- have also been named for the tournament in case of pullouts. The event, which is held under the aegis of the Asian Hockey Federation, is an annual competition but was not held last year.
India enters the competition as defending champion, having won the title in 2023 (Chennai) and 2024 (Hulunbuir, China).
“There is no problem in multi-national tournaments. May be individual series (India and Pakistan) cannot take place,” Mann said when asked about Pakistan’s participation and whether the requisite clearances have been taken for it.
Also read | Devajit Saikia on Women’s Asia Cup trophy boycott: Women’s team has shown solidarity with 2025 Men’s team
The central sports policy with regards to Pakistan bars any bilateral engagement with the country against which India launched a brief military offensive just last year after the Pahalgam terror attack killed 26 people.
However, adhering to the Olympic Charter, the Sports Ministry has stated that the two countries can compete against each other in multi-lateral events and India would not stop athletes from across the border to play here for such engagements.
Despite this, Pakistan had withdrawn from the Junior World Cup of hockey in Tamil Nadu last year, citing high tensions between the two countries in the aftermath of Operation Sindoor.
Mann said league stage ACT matches will be played at Jalandhar, while the semifinal and the final will be played in Mohali stadium.
Assuring full support for hosting the event, Mann said Punjab is committed to ensuring the successful organisation of the first-ever tournament in the state’s history.
Hockey India secretary general Bhola Nath Singh, who was also in attendance at Monday’s event, said the relationship between the hockey federations of India and Pakistan is “excellent”.
“I want to say this on record that we share very good relations between the hockey federations of India and Pakistan.
“You must have noticed that whenever I go, if the Indian team defeats Pakistan, I meet the Pakistani team first. The boys (players) there also show immense respect,” said Singh.
The Asian Champions Trophy will commence on October 27 in Jalandhar and the final match will be held in Mohali on November 5.

Here at WIRED we’ve been trying to make sense of at least two incidents in the AI industry this week: First, the major fight over a million-dollar math problem and whether OpenAI surreptitiously borrowed the work of other researchers to solve the problem first. A day later, an Anthropic researcher—who had previously worked at OpenAI—very publicly quit his job, citing concerns about how both companies were handling AI safety. Another technical staffer at Anthropic said in response that people at the company “really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” (Note the exclamation point.)
The internet erupted into a debate about whether these fears are very legitimate, totally overblown, part of a regulatory capture strategy, or self-aggrandizement on the part of the AI labs that make the tech. Or some combination thereof.
One prominent technology and AI researcher, Timnit Gebru, has been especially fiery, posting on X and Bluesky about the overlapping ideas and ideologies that she thinks led us to this bizarro moment. Previously, Gebru was most known for her highly publicized departure from Google. Hired in 2018 to evaluate biases within the company’s fast-advancing AI tools, she and her fellow researchers presented a paper on the potential dangers of probabilistic large language models. Google rejected it. Gebru wasn't at the company much longer. She’s written an upcoming book about her experiences, titled Deep Unlearning: The Rise of AI and the Radicalization of a Tech Idealist (expected to ship early next year).
Gebru has many thoughts on the AI-related events of this past week. While her work is essentially rooted in AI safety, she rejects phrases like “safety and alignment” and thinks those who are warning of our impending doom are trying to distract from the actual harms the tech industry might perpetuate.
LAUREN GOODE: What do you think all the attention on the “math fight” says about the current state of AI?
TIMNIT GEBRU: Well, first I would ask, why are they heavily investing in solving math problems? Why are they choosing certain disciplines? Somehow these subjects, like programming and chess and math, were elevated to mean, OK, you solved this and thereby you’ve solved intelligence. It’s so they can say, “We solved it.”
The story that OpenAI wants you to hear is, this AI did this incredible thing, and it’s super intelligent. That’s why they chose math, this open $1 million question. But if it had gone through the whole process by which the math community vets the significance and novelty of claims and who contributed to them, and we had all waited until the dust settled, we would have gotten a better sense of whether OpenAI was framing this breakthrough accurately.
There’s something called the Leiden Declaration that I think is really good, which warns about what happens if the field of mathematics is used by corporations in this way. Policymakers start to rely on press releases and popular media, when they should be talking to mathematicians themselves. The amount of time it takes now to go from companies claiming an AI breakthrough to Bernie Sanders proposing a bill is really short, and that’s not a good thing.
It’s all just cutthroat right now leading up to their IPOs. Generally, researchers are supposed to be collaborative. When I was at Google, we were collaborating with researchers at Microsoft, at Amazon. You do that all the time. Now, the researchers are all frenetic about the problems they think they’re solving because of their pending IPOs.
How do you interpret the resignation of that Anthropic engineer, who’s saying the companies are reckless and gambling with our lives? On the one hand, you seem to agree that the companies are being reckless; on the other hand, you’ve made clear that you think the “AI will cause the end of civilization” debate is senseless.
My whole career, I’ve been trying to say the same thing from different angles. We wrote our stochastic parrot paper in 2021 for this reason. OpenAI had claimed GPT-2 was too powerful to release. It was so hyped up. And we were saying, you’re asking the wrong questions.
In my book I write, “Can a bridge decide to collapse?” The whole “Oh no, our models went rogue” thing … When a bridge collapses, you don’t analyze whether the bridge was ethical or sentient or why it decided to collapse. You ask, who is the person who built this bridge to be so flimsy? There are permits you have to acquire. There are supposed to be tests. When you ask about the bridge collapsing itself, you’ve lost the thread.
Meanwhile, what’s really existential is AI powering autonomous weapons, killing machines, that are actually being used in warfare. The climate catastrophe is a real thing that could be exacerbated by what these tech companies are building. Bosses are using AI as an excuse to get rid of their pesky workers. This machine-god narrative is, in my opinion, meant to distract us from these. The industry has become a mix of cults, a mix of people who are true believers, just like a preacher who says the end times is coming. The singularity has been coming for decades now.
Take me through, step by step, how “AI extinction” might happen, if it were real. I’m thinking of this post where someone said, Does an angry GPU just show up at my house or something?
I can’t really envision it, but a lot of those scenarios seem to be that you ask the machine to optimize for some other task, and then the machine decides that the way to get to that goal is by killing everyone in the world. Does the AI hypnotize you so that you don’t unplug it? I don’t know! Other people say, well, the AI can infect your machines. Yes—and we already have malware, so…
What about floods and fires? What about a major disruption to the global food supply chain? There are real threats coming to us, like people being able to create and use chemical weapons. [Note: Not long after we spoke, Anthropic revealed that it had blocked several potential malicious attempts by scientists to build biological weapons.]
There’s another element where you’re so privileged that you can’t imagine other things harming you. Like if you’re not worried about police brutality, or floods, or warfare—things that can actually kill you—then you can obsess over the machine-god.
Why are we spending so much time talking about this idea of AI that people have been talking about since the ’40s and ’50s? I have this game I play sometimes where I read quotes to people about artificial intelligence that I’ve gathered in my research, and I ask, What decade was this statement made in? Sometimes people get it right, but a lot of times they do not, because it all sounds the same.

It’s been quite the couple of weeks for Formula 1. First, its annual visit to one of the oldest tracks on the calendar, the Italian temple of speed that is Monza, just outside Milan. Apologies for no Ars report, but your correspondent was on the ground, on vacation, learning the hard way that attempts to call the circuit “accessible by public transport” can still involve walking several miles. The place was packed with Tifosi—the hardcore Italian superfans—dressed in red, who had their hopes dashed almost immediately as Charles Leclerc first ruined his teammate’s race, then his own, all within the first two laps.
Salvation came in the form of the first Italian title contender in my lifetime, Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli. Opting to take a new engine and other power unit components meant Antonelli would start the race from 19th. But the kid is in fine form right now, and Monza’s long straights and slow corners make for several good overtaking spots. I declared to my race companions that morning that “he’s going to podium, easily,” but if anything, I was too cautious. By the time Leclerc’s heavy crash at Parabolica had stopped the race, Antonelli was already up to 12th.
From the second standing start, on fresh medium tires and still needing a second pitstop, he made short work of the rest of the grid, including his teammate George Russell, who spent much of the race in the lead, on a theoretically faster one-stop strategy. Even a mistake from Antonelli that saw him make an excursion through a gravel trap as he tried to pass Russell couldn’t stop his charge, and he became the first Italian to win the Italian Grand Prix in 60 years—fairy tale stuff, surely.
The contrast with this past weekend could not be starker.
The sport traveled from Italy to Spain to race on the new Madring, a temporary circuit built around a sprawling exhibition center near the Spanish capital’s airport. The 3.3 mile (5.4 km) circuit had a troubled gestation, with construction setbacks caused by heavy rain, among other issues. Like some other new street circuits, a highway passes over the course, constraining the track design somewhat, and its most notable feature is a long banked corner meant to generate IndyCar-like passing. At least, that was the idea.

Lenskart has increased its stake in extended reality (XR) startup AjnaLens’ parent Dimension NXG with an ₹8 Cr investment to deepen its bet on smart eyewear and wearable technology. In a regulatory filing, Lenskart said it acquired an additional 1.8% stake in AjnaLens for ₹8 Cr. Following the transaction, its holding in the startup increased to 9.01% from 7.21% earlier. The latest acquisition follows two earlier purchases this year. Lenskart acquired an additional 0.68% stake in AjnaLens in February and 1.69% in July. Together, the three transactions increased Lenskart’s stake by 4.17% from its earlier holding of 4.84%. The aggregate consideration for these three acquisitions stood at ₹18.5 Cr. Lenskart said the investment is aimed at strengthening its strategic association with the XR, AI and smart wearable technology ecosystem, while supporting technology-led opportunities in smart eyewear. It first invested an undisclosed amount in the startup in July last year with an aim to develop AI-powered smart glasses. At the time, Lenskart said the partnership would combine its expertise in frame design and engineering with AjnaLens’ XR technology capabilities. Founded in 2014 by Pankaj Raut, Abhijit Patil, and Abhishek Tomar, AjnaLens provides hardware and software solutions using XR technology. It uses XR to provide learning solutions and claims to cater to defence, enterprises, and more sectors. The startup reported a turnover of ₹10.4 Cr in FY26, down 19% YoY from ₹12.8 Cr in FY25. Lenskart has since steadily expanded its smart eyewear play through the launch of its Phonic audio glasses and its upcoming AI-powered smart glasses. The company has also partnered with Qualcomm for its smart-glasses technology stack. The continued push toward smart eyewear comes as the company said its B by Lenskart smart glasses crossed 30,000 users on the waitlist at the end of FY26. Globally, smart glass shipments jumped more than 1,000% in 2025 despite a slowdown in smartwatches and hearables, as per IDC data. Founded in 2010 by Peyush Bansal, Neha Bansal, Amit Chaudhury, and Sumeet Kapahi, Lenskart is an omnichannel eyewear retailer serving customers in India, the UAE, Singapore, and Japan. It operated 3,459 stores across India as of June 30, 2026. In the first quarter of FY27, its net profit surged 273% to ₹228.4 Cr from ₹61.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue jumped 43% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,714.2 Cr.

Stoke City centre-half Luke Graham and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure will receive their first full Scotland call-ups on Tuesday when Sebastien Pocognoli names his first squad as head coach.
Graham was part of Scotland's pre-World Cup training camp in May after a breakthrough campaign with Dundee, winning the Scottish Premiership club's players' player and young player of the year awards.
The 22-year-old was an unused substitute in the country's send-off friendly win against Curacao, which was also Steve Clarke's last game in the dugout at Hampden Park.
The defender, who has three caps at under-21 level, has started strongly for The Potters in the Championship, who are unbeaten in their last four games, with Graham an ever-present.
Former Rangers academy product Ure was in demand across Europe after a free-scoring spell - 20 goals and three assists in 20 matches - that took Sirius to the top of the table in Sweden and it resulted in a £5.5m summer transfer to La Liga with Sevilla.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.

A Pennsylvania woman has died from complications associated with measles, the third death in the state this year involving the virus.
The 40-year-old woman died Saturday, Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said in a Facebook post in which he called the death “measles-related.”
The post did not identify the woman other than as a resident of Jefferson County, a rural area about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northeast of Pittsburgh.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said in the post.
The post did not say whether the woman was vaccinated against measles. No more information about the case would be released, it stated.
Pennsylvania’s two previous measles-related deaths involved infants. Both occurred in August and a coroner reported that the virus itself caused one of the deaths.
One infant, a boy, died shortly after birth of a ruptured spleen. The boy had measles that did not contribute to the rupture, according to Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.
Rather, measles was listed as a “significant condition” at the time of death.
The other infant, a 6-week-old girl with a genetic defect that left her highly vulnerable to infection, died due to measles, Diamantoni told The Associated Press.
The girl was born with a condition called Amish lethal microcephaly that causes an unusually small head and underdeveloped brain. Children with the condition typically live 6 months or less.
The first dose of measles vaccine is typically given to infants around 1 year old, meaning neither infant was old enough to be vaccinated.
As of Friday, Pennsylvania had 676 measles cases in 37 of the state’s 67 counties. Of those cases, 124 involved hospitalizations and four people who were vaccinated against measles, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
The three measles-related deaths reported by state and local officials as of Sunday did not square with figures of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which showed no such deaths this year.
“The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause,” read the CDC website Sunday.
Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and Republican President Donald Trump’s administration have clashed over details of the two previous deaths in the state.
— Mead Gruver

What It Means for a Woman to Shout ‘No’
It’s not just about denial or self-protection. It’s about living a bigger life.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
On the first day of self-defense class, I learn to say “no.”
We’re in a Southern California martial-arts studio not far from an In-N-Out Burger. The space smells faintly of cooked meat. I’m one of six students, all women: four nurses, one flight attendant, and me. In this introductory session, we’re supposed to get a taste of what it means to protect ourselves—and, if necessary, to fight back.
For the longest time, I had wondered what it would be like to hit someone. Like, really hit them. I had grown up understanding that women aren’t supposed to engage in fantasies about violence, which is to say that we aren’t really supposed to think about it. But many of us do. All the time.
Violence can, of course, affect anyone. It is in our homes and neighborhoods and in the news; it is experienced person to person, nation to nation, directly and indirectly. But for women especially, even when violence is not an immediate physical reality, what is real is the constant threat of it.
In my experience, this sense of threat doesn’t change as time goes on. So in late 2023, I signed up for self-defense classes with a training program called Impact Personal Safety. I was working on a book exploring the ways in which women and girls are socialized not to say “no,” even to people who threaten them. But I also just wanted to understand what it is for “no” to be expressed in the body—what it means to feel the “no.”
Our lead instructor, Dawn Hofmeister, is in her 50s and petite. She stands straight and appears to glide through the air, and although I’m much larger than she is, I feel submissive in her presence. She teaches alongside a couple of female assistants and a male sparring partner, Matt Harris. A middle-aged man with doe-like eyes, Harris tells the assembled group that he will be playing the role of our assailant that day, a character named Billy.
Everyone likes Harris. Nobody likes Billy. Billy emerges after Harris slips on a padded suit and helmet. In the scenarios we’re thrown into, Billy is aggressive. He walks right at us, his voice raised. He can also be sneaky: Sometimes, he’ll sidle up in a bumbling, faux-friendly way before lunging. Other times, he appears to be severely mentally ill, or under the influence of drugs, or perfectly sober but intensely pushy. He asks for things (the time, a cellphone) or whether we need something—help with our groceries? A ride? When we rebuff him, he starts toward us with purpose.
“No!” we yell. This is supposed to come after some effort at placating him—I don’t need a ride, thank you; I think the person you’re looking for went the other way—a tactic that, in these scenarios, does not work, in that it does not thwart Billy from approaching, bull-like, with apparent malicious intent. Hofmeister explains that she teaches students to say “no” repeatedly and often because it helps strengthen a woman’s resolve to assert her boundaries and puts a potential assailant on notice that what he’s about to do is undesired. She adds that the word can increase the power of a physical blow and disrupt a freeze response, keeping the woman breathing through her counterattack.
Along with saying “no,” we’re taught the palm-heel strike—heels of the hands up and together, palms facing outward, ready to hit—the first line of physical defense in a sequence of moves and postures meant to end with Billy on his back or side, writhing. The second move is a strong knee to the groin. The third, once he’s down, is a knee or stomp to the head.
Billy takes a fair amount of abuse. Sometimes I worry about Harris, the human being inside the padded suit, especially when he is slow to get back on his feet. But feeling bad for Billy, I realize, is part of what I’m trying to undo: the internalized empathy response that can make people, especially women, afraid to hit another person, or lead them to give bad actors the benefit of the doubt even while the voice in their own head is saying danger.
When Billy advances toward us, my first “no” is the weakest. But then my hands go up and I yell “No!” with more force. Billy falls, and I jab my heel into his chin. My knee goes to his groin—another “No!” Soon the no’s are coming quickly and easily, and by the time Billy is splayed on the ground, I’m hovering over him—like Muhammad Ali standing over Sonny Liston in that famous 1965 photo—and practically screaming.
Contemporary self-defense courses recognize that protecting oneself involves a lot more than elbowing an assailant in the neck. As Susan Brownmiller put it in her 1975 book, Against Our Will: Men, Women and Rape, telling women to kick a man in the groin or stick a thumb in his eye is not enough—because first, women must overcome an aversion to hitting. Describing her time learning self-defense, she wrote that this inhibition “was so strong in each of us that on the first try none of us could make physical contact.” What women need, she argued, “is systemic training in self-defense that begins in childhood, so that the inhibition resulting from the prohibition may be overcome.”
What many people think of as women’s self-defense tends to go by the designation Empowerment Self-Defense, or ESD. Also known as “feminist self-defense” and “holistic self-defense,” ESD posits that teaching nonphysical strategies is as important as teaching physical ones—because if a woman can recognize and thwart an attacker’s verbal intrusions early in an encounter, she is less likely to need to get physical. Impact Personal Safety, Southern California, the program I trained under, says that it has taught assertiveness, boundary-setting, deflection, and de-escalation to tens of thousands of students—plus the skills necessary for what the organization’s late founder, Lisa Gaeta, described as “causing a scene.” (Essentially: raising your voice and shouting things such as “Get away from me” and “I don’t want this,” which is harder to do than you might think.)
That makes ESD different from mainstream self-defense, which “tends to be stranger-focused, sometimes fear-based, rather than empowerment-based,” Jocelyn Hollander, a University of Oregon sociology professor and self-defense instructor, told me. ESD’s emphasis on “internal” skills—emotional, psychological—is aimed at subverting behaviors that students might have adopted based on their gender or personal history, or in response to political and cultural messaging. Basically, Hollander said, the method gives women the tools they need to say no “to whatever someone wants to do to or with you.”
ESD is applicable not only in extreme interactions but also in what some might call the more routine situations that many women experience, such as being coerced into sex. In Hollander’s classes, she has students turn to each other with a simple question—“Can I borrow your pencil?” or “Do you want to go have coffee?”—to which the other person then has to respond “No.” Usually, there’s a lot of nervous laughter, Hollander told me. Many students realize that they never say “no” to anybody. Or, when they do, they qualify it, soften it, make excuses. But once they discover that the world won’t end when they say “no,” Hollander observed, it can be a “huge epiphany.”
Such training, Hollander’s research suggests, pays tangible dividends. Women who take ESD classes are less likely to be the victim of rape or sexual assault than women who do not. In a 2020 study of female college students involving nearly 300 women, Hollander found that those who had taken an ESD class had about 50 percent lower odds, on average, of experiencing any sort of assault over the one-year period following the course than those who had not taken a class. “I just have to point out that 50 percent is a huge decrease for an intervention,” she said. “Psychologists are usually happy if they get a few percentage points’ difference. Fifty percent is immense.” Her research has also found that many students experience increased “self-efficacy”—a sense that they can be effective in the world. And other research has found that this sort of self-defense training can reduce feelings of anxiety, depression, fear, and self-blame.
Hollander’s results have been echoed in the work of other academics, including Charlene Senn, a University of Windsor psychology professor whose research focuses on male violence against women. Senn was inspired by the academics Patricia Rozee and Mary Koss, who in 2001 published a paper titled “Rape: A Century of Resistance,” which synthesized decades of research on sexual violence. They translated their analysis into a series of recommendations, such as giving women cognitive and emotional education to defend themselves against assault. Senn took those recommendations and set out to make them come alive.
First, she created a program for university women called Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act—a 12-hour, evidence-based training that, among other things, teaches women how to recognize a risk of sexual assault and then resist it. Then, from 2011 to 2013, she and a group of academics conducted a study of 893 female college freshmen in Canada, to test the program’s efficacy. Of the students, 451 were assigned to a “resistance group” and took EAAA classes, and 442 were put in a control group, which meant that they basically “went to a room,” Senn said, and read sexual-assault-prevention pamphlets distributed by their schools.
After the EAAA courses, Senn said, the resistance and control groups were given follow-up surveys at intervals of one week, six months, 12 months, and 18 months. The researchers found that one year after the EAAA training, the women in the resistance group were 46.3 percent less likely to have been raped and 63.2 percent less likely to have experienced attempted rape than the women in the control group. A later study by Senn and her colleagues, which looked at a broader, more diverse cohort of university women who took EAAA classes from 2017 to 2021, had similar findings: a 57.3 percent reduction in reports of rape and a 32.9 percent reduction in attempted rape six months after the training.
To me, these results were nothing short of stunning. I wondered why data like these hadn’t been publicized more widely. Jill Cermele, a psychology professor at Drew University, told me that this was partly because of ideology. Cermele co-authored a 2022 paper with Martha McCaughey, an academic specializing in women’s studies and the author of Real Knockouts: The Physical Feminism of Women’s Self-Defense, about the ways in which the efficacy of self-defense has been neglected or ignored by both public-health officials and anti-rape activists—some of whom contend that emphasizing the need for women to learn self-defense serves only to put the onus on them, rather than on men.
Cermele said she believes that this logic is misguided—that no matter people’s views on blame, anyone who cares about women’s safety has “a professional and a moral obligation to pay attention to the data.” That said, “one of the things that psychology tells us is that people are not convinced by data—they’re convinced by stories.”
During my next set of self-defense classes, things take a darker turn.
The 16-hour “basics” training unfolds over the course of two weekends, with a new cohort of students. Our lead instructor is Dani, a young woman who took her first Impact class when she was only 6. Our padded assailant is Michael Peñafiel, a middle-aged father of a young son. Like Harris, our attacker from the intro class, Peñafiel has an alter ego: Kane.
On Day 1, we hit, we kick, we send knees into Kane’s groin. Yet the stakes feel somehow lower. Partly, it’s the absurdity of Kane’s outfit—a suit of hard plastic, foam, and duct tape, with a harness-like thing slung between his legs and around his waist. His helmet makes him look like a bug. The padding forces hims to move around the studio with his hips thrust forward.
But then comes Day 2: what we glibly call “sexual-assault day.” Our instructors teach us how to fend off an assailant who approaches while we’re lying on our side, and demands that we get into positions that could—quickly, disturbingly, unmistakably—leave us open to assault. We get down on hands and knees. We lie flat on our backs. Today, our attacker is closer, the interaction more intimate. This makes everything scarier and can provoke a freeze response that feels impossible to overcome.
Kane gets behind me, clutches my arms, and pins me to the floor. He crouches on his knees, breathing heavily over me. I think: Maybe if I just lie here, he will go away. I’m surprised at how heavy he is and how difficult it is to imagine freeing myself from his grasp. He hisses instructions. “What’s going on?” I ask him. We’re supposed to say this phrase out loud, not so much to prompt a reasonable answer but to remind ourselves that we are being attacked in the first place. He merely mumbles. Dani tells me to roll onto my back, which is the last thing I want to do. “Be patient,” she says. “He’s going to make a mistake.”
And make a mistake he does. As Kane tries to position himself directly on top of me, he releases one of my arms and up it goes, my fingers in a beak-like shape, directed at his eyes. “Eyes! Eyes! Eyes!” everyone yells. I stab at the netting on his padded helmet, and Kane falls backward. Then I get into a kick position, leg in the air and ready to strike—his head, his torso, his groin, wherever I can find a target. After a few kicks, Kane finally goes down, at which point I pull myself up and run around to the top of his head to assess that he’s indeed knocked out. Finally, I run away, keeping in mind the final step: go get help.
I should acknowledge that self-defense techniques may not help in situations when it is impossible or dangerous for a woman to fight back—such as when she is incapacitated, or when an assailant is armed and threatening deadly force. And it is fair to argue that the potential perpetrators of violence, not their victims, should be the ones subject to intervention and training. But Impact’s founder, Gaeta, who died last year, had no patience for the argument that to avoid victim blaming, women should not be taught to defend themselves. People say, “Well, we should make men be better,” she once told me. “How the fuck am I going to make men be better?”
The point about responsibility is not a new argument. In the ’80s and ’90s, for instance, some feminist activists began to express concern that teaching women self-defense was akin to engaging in victim blaming—so the practice became “unfashionable in a way,” Hollander told me. She added that yes, ideally, more men would move through life with the explicit understanding that they should not assault women, “but from a researcher’s perspective, we have no clue how to make that happen.” No intervention has been shown to meaningfully reduce perpetration. “And what are we supposed to do in the meantime?” Hollander said. “Just sit around and wait for the revolution?”
Some researchers argue that when it comes to men, self-defense training for women can move the needle in an important way—by shifting men’s own understanding of their place in the world. “Changing men does not necessarily entail intervening directly with men,” Hollander wrote in a 2018 article. Quoting a paper by the masculinity researcher Michael Flood, she added, “Empowering women may transform gender relations by ‘shifting the wider conditions within which men make choices about violence and non-violence.’”
The third day of basics class is the day I start crying.
We’re learning how to react defensively and offensively: Many of the techniques involve moving toward our assailant, not away from him. This is counterintuitive—instinctively, one wants to retreat from danger—but being able to inflict real damage and disable an attacker means having to get up close.
The disabling doesn’t go well for me. About three hours into the class, I’m thrown to the mat and pinned. Kane is on top of me and feels stronger and heavier than usual, more hell-bent on restraining me. Just when I think I’ve started to get away, he grabs me again and pins me on my side, my back to him, my arms folded in front of me. I freeze. The instructors and other students yell words of encouragement—“He’s going to make a mistake!” someone calls—but I can’t move. The words are meaningless. Adrenalin is making me tremble.
After what seems like an eternity, Kane seems to ease up a bit, and I’m able to turn toward him, hit him, and stumble away. I make my way to Gaeta—present that day, watching from a table at one end of the studio—who asks, “What happened?” The question is part of the drill. After the fight, we’re supposed to describe in as much detail as possible what occurred and what our attacker looked like, to practice how, in the real world, we might give specific information about an assault to a friend or law-enforcement officer.
I’m not sure what to tell her, but I try: “He attacked me. He threw me to the ground. I tried to get up and almost succeeded, but he pinned me back down.” I feel shame and embarrassment rising, and I begin to cry. I run to the line of students assembled against a wall. One says, “Good job.” The others don’t know what to say. Neither do I. I just stand there with tears streaming, my heart thumping.
Two weeks after my graduation from the class, I’m stuck on that memory, of an encounter that felt like failure. Peñafiel has since clarified that he did not, in fact, ease up on me. He also said that my reaction—freezing, crying—is not uncommon.
Driving home from that class, shaken, I had called my friend Nancy, a documentary filmmaker whose work has focused largely on sexual assault. She tried to put what had happened to me into perspective: I got scared, she said, and felt shame and embarrassment, which came not only from being scared but also from my sense that I hadn’t fought back in the “right” way. About a week after the class, I also spoke with one of Impact’s assistant instructors, Amanda Hall, who is also a reality-TV producer. She told me that she has seen this sort of response many times. She herself cried during the opening drill in her first class. The adrenaline can be “really activating,” she said. “It’s scary no matter what.”
I try to give myself a little grace. After all, I was able to finish the fight. This reminds me of something that Cermele, the psychology professor, told me: Many people mistakenly believe that once an assault happens or starts, you have to somehow wait until the assailant is finished. This is not always the case. “Unfortunately, assaults take time,” she said, which means “multiple opportunities for resistance. And if I couldn’t organize myself to resist in the beginning, if I was too drunk, if I was too afraid, if I was whatever, there might still be a moment where I can do something with that. And I think we miss that by not talking about resistance. It’s very all-or-nothing.”
She told me about a student who, after learning self-defense techniques one semester, was assaulted by a male friend’s roommate at a college party. During the attack, the woman was able to summon her skills and fight him off. “We would call that a success story,” Cermele said. “The assault ended because of what she did, not because he decided it was over.”
I now know what it feels like to hit someone. I also can’t stop thinking about how different the world might be if more girls and women were taught to defend themselves. We might see the number of assaults against women cut in half. We might see more teenagers like a self-defense student who told me that now she knows how to use her voice: “I feel like I’m a powerful person.” We would see more women learning to shout “No!” and enjoying, with much less fear, what one instructor called “a bigger life”—the kind of life every one of us deserves.

FIDE, on Monday, confirmed the venue, format, prize fund and schedule for the World Championship match between reigning world champion D Gukesh and challenger Javokhir Sindarov.
Both Gukesh and Sindarov will be 20 when their duel begins, making it the youngest World Championship match in chess history.
India’s Gukesh had claimed the World Championship title in 2024 after he beat China’s Ding Liren. Uzbek GM Sindarov earned the challenger spot by winning the Candidates tournament earlier this year.
Here is all you need to know about the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match:
Where will the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match happen?
The Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match will take place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva, Switzerland.
Fondation Martin Bodmer is a heritage library and museum. The Fondation holds around 150,000 documents in around 120 languages, making it one of the finest private collections in the world.
When will the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match happen?
The opening ceremony will take place on November 22. The first classical game is schedule for November 24 final one on December 11. If a tiebreaker is needed, it will be played on December 12.
What is the tournament format for the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match?
The Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match will consist of a maximum of 14 classical games. The winner of each game wins 1 point, while a draw would result in 0.5 points. The first player to reach 7.5 points wins the match and the title. If the score is 7-7 after all classical games, the title will be decided through tiebreaks.
What is the time control for Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match?
Each player will have 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game. A 30-second increment is added from move 41. A draw offer would not be permitted before Black’s 40th move. But before that point, a draw may be claimed through the Chief Arbiter or Deputy Chief Arbiter only in cases of threefold repetition or stalemate.
What is the prize fund for Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match?
The total prize fund is USD 2.5 million. Each player receives USD 200,000 for every game won and the remaining balance is divided equally between the two players at the end of the match.

Deaths in India due to second hand smoke increased nearly 50% in 2023, compared to 1990, even as death rates improved by about 30%, according to a global analysis published in The Lancet Public Health journal.
The estimates also suggest that while the population exposed to second hand smoke increased from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2026 -- up by 18.4% -- age-standardised prevalence dropped from 43.2 per cent in 1990 to 30.6 per cent in 2023 in India.
Age-standardised prevalence is a statistical adjustment made to data to allow a fair comparison of prevalence across age groups.
An international team of researchers forming the 'Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 Second-hand smoke Collaborators' estimated prevalence of exposure to passive smoking and the disease burden it contributes to across 204 countries and territories.
"In 2023, an estimated 2.71 billion people worldwide were exposed to SHS (second hand smoke), including 767 million children aged 0-14 years," the authors wrote.
Globally, exposure prevalence was 33.9 per cent in 2023. China, India, and Indonesia accounted for nearly half of the world's exposed population, with 664 million, 444 million, and 142 million people exposed, respectively, in 2023, they found.
However, "age-standardised prevalence was highest in southeast Asia, east Asia, and Oceania (48.4 per cent), with female individuals in some countries experiencing nearly 1.8 times the exposure prevalence of male individuals," the team said.
In India, absolute deaths in 1990 due to passive smoking were 2,17,700, while those in 2023 were 3,25,600 -- death rates or deaths per hundred thousand population, however, fell from 46.1 in 1990 to 30 in 2023, down by 35%, the findings show.
"The numbers mean that despite a fall in the adjusted rates, the absolute number of people exposed to passive smoking is still increasing. This can have long-lasting effects across multiple organ systems, not just the respiratory system," Neetu Jain, pulmonologist and senior consultant at Pushpawati Singhania Hospital and Research Institute, New Delhi, told PTI.
"Second-hand smoke exposure is associated with an increased risk of several diseases, including cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. The effects of passive smoking can also be particularly concerning in people with conditions such as coronary artery disease," she said.
Children were found to account for more than 12% of the world's health burden from second hand smoke, with lower respiratory infections causing the greatest burden, according to the study.
"Passive smoking is avoidable if smokers take steps to prevent exposing others to tobacco smoke. Smoking outside the home and away from enclosed spaces can reduce exposure to second-hand smoke, particularly among family members and children. Children are especially vulnerable because their lungs are still developing, and exposure to tobacco smoke can adversely affect their respiratory health," Dr Jain said.
"The effects tend to be greatest among those who are least aware of what passive smoking is and the health risks associated with it," the pulmonologist said.
"However, we should encourage smokers to quit and focus on bringing down smoking across the country through effective tobacco-control measures, including higher tobacco prices and taxes," she said.

For over a month and a half, residents of Chitpur Jyotinagar Colony in Cossipore, North Kolkata, have been without regular water supply after five public taps serving the colony ran dry following pipeline work in the area. Home to around 5,000 people, the 200-metre-long stretch is largely inhabited by people belonging to the Muslim community, and from lower-income backgrounds.
Residents, whose daily lives and livelihoods have been disrupted, alleged that water supply has been deliberately cut off by the state’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to target them on the basis of their identities and force them out of the slum.
It is worth noting days after the election results were declared, local BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari had pledged not to do anything for Muslims in his constituency. “Today, in front of Baba Bholenath, I swear, I will not do one job for them (Muslims) in the next five years. Will not issue any certificate for them. I am saying this live. I do not care about what anyone else says or thinks,” he had said.
Residents of Jyotinagar this colony, around 95% of them Muslims, depend on informal jobs for their sustenance. While women manage household chores in the morning before working at nearby factories in the afternoon, where they clean glass bottles and break glass panels into shards, most men work as daily wage labourers, masons, drivers, rickshaw pullers, or at factories.
How Did Water Supply Stop?
Alt News visited the water-deprived area, located a few meters from the over 200-years-old Cossipore Gun and Shell factory. The colony has five taps, which used to supply water from 5 am to 11 pm daily. Since July 29, after water supply was cut off, all five taps have been dry, locals said.
Locals said that water supply was perfectly normal and no complaints from the neighbourhood was made to the local civic body or any authorities, and yet, pipeline work was carried out in the area by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) from July 26-28.
“Pipeline work was happening, they had dug two pits, one at the beginning of the slum and another at the end, marking the slum. On July 28, the water supply stopped around 11 pm. The next morning, we were waiting for the water supply to return. It has not been restored since,” said a resident, Mohinudeen Sheikh.
Sheikh, along with other residents, alleged that the pipelines were shut during the night while the roads were being repaired. “They used the cover of midnight to close the pipelines and mend the streets. We had no water from the early morning onwards,” he claimed.
‘They Also Took Away Electricity’
Residents said the water crisis was accompanied by a disruption in electricity supply as well. “They took away both water and electricity,” one youth said.
“They thought we were drawing electricity illegally from the main line, so they stopped the supply,” said a resident, Pinki Bibi. “All our houses have separate electricity connections and we receive separate bills. Then how can they say we are drawing electricity illegally?”
Residents claimed that electricity was restored after more than a week, following an incident during the Kanwar Yatra when poor visibility allegedly led some Kanwariyas to fall into the pothole-ridden lane. Alamgir Biswas, secretary of the Jyotinagar Colony, said that the supply was restored 10-15 days after the Basti Unnayan Samiti protested against the disruption.
Locals alleged that Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) said the main-road connection had been shut to verify whether allegations of illegal electricity tapping were true. However, electricity supply remained available in the lanes branching off the main road. After seven days, CESC was able to verify that no illegal tapping was taking place and restored the connection, they added.
‘They are Trying to Evict Us’
Residents alleged that the disruption of these essential services was a part of a concerted attempt to evict the slum dwellers. Alamgir alleged: “The plan was to cut off the basic needs of water and electricity so that we leave the area. In this area, there is absolute communal harmony. Hindus and Muslims live harmoniously together. However, this government is trying to create a rift between us.”
Morjina Begum, who works at the glass factory, also alleged, “They are trying to evict us from this colony and therefore employing these tricks of cutting off the water supply. We are not new to this place. I was born here. My grandfather had settled here years ago,” while asserting, “We are not going to leave this place so easily. We will fight.”
Begum said residents had also approached the local councillor, Suman Singh, but has received no meaningful assistance as of yet. Alt News tried to speak to Singh, but he did not answer our calls till press time.
Saraswati Biswas, a 60-year-old Hindu resident, alleged that Tiwari, the newly elected MLA, had referred to the residents as “Bangladeshis and encroachers”. “He is calling us Bangladeshis and encroachers. How am I a Bangladeshi? My forefathers used to live here. I have proper documents proving that I am an Indian. I voted this year,” she said.
Legal Entanglement With Kolkata Port
While investigating the possible reason behind the elongated water supply disruption, Alt News found an intricate legal entanglement between the residents of the colony and the authorities of the Kolkata port.
As per legal records, the entire colony is built on a parcel of land measuring approximately 3478 square metres officially belonging to the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata. On February 23, the estate officer of the port issued an eviction order for the colony.
Alt News accessed the order, and found that it was issued based on the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The notice terms the residents of Jyotinagar Colony as ‘unauthorised occupants and/or trespasser to the port property’. The estate officer ordered the residents to vacate the land within 15 days of date of publication of this notice. Before the eviction order was passed, a hearing took place, wherein, port authorities submitted that ‘there is potential threat to communal unrest’ due to the existence of the colony.
According to legal documents accessed by Alt News, the residents of the colony came to know about the existence of this eviction order on June 9. The residents alleged that after the change of government in West Bengal, local BJP supporters started to campaign for the demolition of the slum. The locals claimed that they began deeming the colony as “a den of illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”.
In order to seek legal protection from the eviction drive, residents appealed before the chief judge of the city civil court, Calcutta, however, on August 18, the court declined to grant any immunity from eviction to them.
The Port authorities in their submission before the city civil court had mentioned that ‘unlawful activities’ were ongoing in the colony. They described the premises as congested and unsafe for human habitation, citing the presence of inflammable materials and several uninsulated electrical wires that could potentially cause a fire. They also lodged two police complaints at the North Port police station on September 9, 2020 and July 25, 2022.
On August 19, the residents appeared before the Calcutta high court, seeking protection from eviction. The court granted an interim stay order on the eviction process till September 18. In the meantime, the water and electricity disruptions happened, which residents believe was done to purposely disrupt their lives to expedite the eviction.
Nine residents of the colony: Alamgir Biswas, Pinki Bibi, Mafajel Gazi, Sk Mainuddin, Rahima Bibi, Saraswati Biswas, Anita Prasad, Lima Bibi and Bonani Bibi appeared as petitioners before the high court. In their appeal, the residents had informed the HC that although the proceedings recorded before the estate officer of Kolkata Port mentioned two persons: Hafizul and Tarcina Bibi as respondents from the colony, the order does not record that any notice for eviction, under section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, was issued publicly.
It was also submitted before the HC that the order issued by the Kolkata Port does not record that the petitioners were called upon to show cause against the proposed eviction, were afforded an opportunity to produce evidence or were given an opportunity of personal hearing.
According to Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, all concerned persons, that is all persons who are in occupation of the public premises, have to be given the opportunity to show cause why they wouldn’t be evicted.
Section 4(3) of the Act clearly mentions: The estate officer shall cause the notice to be served by having it affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the public premises, and in such other manner as may be prescribed, whereupon the notice shall be deemed to have been duly given to all persons concerned. However, the order issued by the estate officer makes no mention of any such notice being issued or served. This issue was also raised in the petition before the high court.
A team of lawyers including Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, Samim Ahammed, Md Nasirul Hoque and Ivi Banerjee represented the residents legally. Speaking to Alt News, Ahammed said, “The Port authorities are claiming that the land in question is their property. But in reality, it is public property. Therefore, a government body like the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, must ensure the fundamental rights of the public, in this case, their right to shelter.”
The State has the power to regulate and make sure people follow the law and cannot occupy public property illegally. They are exercising this power through the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. But while doing this, the State cannot treat people unfairly or take away someone’s home and leave them without shelter. Having a place to live and being able to live with dignity are part of a person’s inalienable rights protected by the Constitution, he explained.
Simultaneously with the HC appeal, another appeal was submitted by the residents before the chief judge of the city civil court seeking the restoration of water connection. This prayer, however, is still pending.
According to the port authorities, the total damage incurred due to the existence of the colony, starting from 1990, has reached approximately over Rs 61 crore. As per the legal records, the estimated monthly damage amount is calculated to be more than Rs 19 lakh rupees, and the port is losing more than Rs 2 crore annually in terms of revenue due to the colony.
Questions Of ‘Communal Targeting’
The geographical location of the water disruption has become a point of contention for residents, who have alleged that this is a form of communal targeting.
When one walks along Khagendra Chatterjee Lane towards the Ganges, with the Gun and Shell Factory on the right, the road turns left towards the river after two temples, and becomes Chitpur Strand Road. The Cossipore Jetty is on the right, followed by Jyotinagar Colony.
Residents showed Alt News the two points where pipeline work had been carried out. They said the entire stretch between the two points had remained without water. They also alleged that the points where the road was dug up correspond to the boundaries of Jyotinagar Colony, which has a predominantly Muslim population. According to the residents, taps immediately before and after this stretch, located in predominantly Hindu residential areas, continue to receive water.
Alt News checked the taps inside the colony and found them dry. Taps located immediately before and after the stretch where the pipeline work had been carried out, however, had water supply. We found that the tap directly opposite a temple, just before the first point where the road had allegedly been dug up, had water supply. The tap at the other end, near the second point where digging had taken place, also had water. In between, however, an approximately 150-metre stretch, had no water supply.
‘A Basic Need’
For residents, the suspension of water has led to tremendous daily struggle. “Water is a basic need. There are so many people in our colony, and there is no water. People have to stand in queues to fetch water from the taps that are present in the nearby areas. Though people are sharing their taps, they prioritise their own needs. This affects our work,” a resident said.
A woman in her mid-twenties, while cleaning utensils, showed buckets filled with water fetched from the river. “Look at the condition of the water we are using to clean. It is so muddy and filthy. At this point, all we can hope is we don’t fall ill,” she said.
The monsoon season has made it more difficult. “The water level is very high in Ganga now, so it becomes dangerous to bathe in the river or fetch water. The river water is muddy and unfit for consumption. But we are left with no option,” an elderly woman said. “We are scared that our children will develop skin infections. There are already a few cases,” said a woman in her thirties, while standing in queue to bathe her children.
Residents have to walk some distance from their colony to a functioning tap to fill water, which they then transport back on vans.
Locals Allege Administrative Apathy
Alamgir elaborated that after water and electricity supply was cut off on July 29, the following day, locals reached the corporation office and complained. “They took my number and told us that they would look into the matter. But nothing happened. On the following day, we submitted a written complaint at the main corporation office in Hatibagan. They also told us they would try to look into it. However, as everyone can see, nothing has changed as of yet,” he said.
Several residents had approached the local police station, the councillor, and MLA Tiwari, seeking their intervention, but no official visited the colony to inspect the reality so far, they lamented. Residents also said that when a group of women approached Tiwari, he dismissed them stating he was not responsible for the disruption of water supply and refused to restore it.
Further, Pinki Bibi alleged that Tiwari had used communal slurs and threatened the locals with eviction. “While talking to the people, he threatened them, ‘If I want, I could demolish the mosque that was built in the colony. And evict the entire colony with it,’” she said.
Morjina Begum told Alt News that residents believe they are being purposely treated this way because of their Muslim identities. Asked why they felt this was the case, she referred to speeches by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the local MLA following their election victories, in which they said they would not work for Muslims because Muslims had not voted for them. “Where are we supposed to go? There are so many of us?” she asked.
Also Read: I swear I won’t do anything for Muslims, says Bengal BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari
Burdened by the uncertainties of their future in the colony, an elderly woman in her 70s, sitting on the threshold of her house, said, “I pray that in my next life I am not born as a Muslim in this country.”
On September 9, Minakshi Mukherjee, CPI(M)’s central committee member, visited the locality along with other workers and leaders, and expressed her solidarity with the residents and protested against the eviction drive. At the initiative of the party, a water tanker visits the colony every two to three days to provide residents with an alternative source of water.
MLA Ritesh Tiwari Responds
When Alt News asked Tiwari about the predicament of people in his constituency, he distanced himself from the issue, saying, “The plot belongs to the Port. The people have a feud with the Port. The Port had ordered them to vacate. Later, the high court ordered them to refrain from taking temporary coercive action. The water supply is provided by the KMC. So, what role do I play here? What can I say here? The matter is sub judice, and it is better for political leaders to refrain from making any comments.”
When asked whether he could stand by the people of his constituency and help restore their water supply, he said, “This is not my job…they [residents] have sought the assistance of established political leaders… so they should keep faith in the people they have called. Should they lose that faith so quickly?”
Upon being further prodded on why he was not helping people in his own constituency, the MLA replied (in Bengali), “Why don’t you do my part of the job!” (“Amar bhaag er kaaj ta apni kore deben”)
