A 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania has died of complications from measles, according to the county’s coroner.
It marks the third vaccine-preventable, measles-linked death in the US this year. All three have occurred in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing an explosive outbreak that has caused over 670 cases and 124 hospitalizations across 37 counties. Prior to these deaths, Pennsylvania had not reported a measles death in 35 years.
In a news release dated September 12, Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said the death in the woman was “a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease.”
The county’s chief deputy coroner, Jason Stiver, added that “this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly.”
“Many people associate measles with a childhood illness, but it can lead to severe complications in individuals of any age,” Stiver said. “Measles is highly contagious and can result in serious respiratory illness, hospitalization, and in rare cases like this, death.”
Preliminary death certificate
While the news release stated that no additional information about the case would be provided, the New York Times obtained a preliminary death certificate. It indicated the woman had several chronic medical conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and she required supplemental oxygen at all times. Her health status made her vulnerable to complications from measles.
The death certificate listed the immediate cause of death as respiratory failure “due to suspected measles.” Furlong told the Times that the woman’s measles case had yet to be confirmed by testing, but that she was unvaccinated and known to have been exposed to someone with measles. At the time of her death, she had many symptoms of measles, including the tell-tale rash, which often begins as red spots on the head or face, and spreads down the body.
The news release noted that the coroner’s office is working with the state health department, which has not yet added the death to the state’s official outbreak tally. The health department provided a statement to the Washington Post saying that it was aware of the case.

Almost 150 politicians across Europe have been included on harmful deepfake pornography websites over the last few years, according to new research seen by WIRED. Some of the politicians, who are overwhelmingly women, have had their likeness included in explicit videos, while others have names and photos listed in disturbing database-like entries that can link to deepfake creation tools.
Analysis of around 160 domains that host deepfake abuse and other nonconsensual sexual content, by researcher Benjamin Shultz, has found that at least 138 women members of parliament (MPs) from 22 European Union countries have appeared or been mentioned on the sites. In contrast, only nine male MPs were referenced in any way. By Shultz’s calculations, it is 33 times more likely for women MPs to be targeted by deepfake ecosystems.
“Deepfake porn is part of a much bigger trend of online hate and intimidation against women and female politicians,” says Suzanne Kröger, a Dutch member of parliament with the Progressive Netherlands group, who was impacted. Kröger, who expressed anger at what the research uncovered, says the findings are “really deeply disturbing” and help to reveal the scale of abuse. “We are politicians, we have a platform and speak out,” Kröger says. “But meanwhile, there are millions of women victims of these criminal acts.”
The research, which has been published by German digital democracy think tank Agora Digitale Transformation, focuses on national members of parliament from all 27 countries in the European Union. Shultz, a fellow at Agora and the lead researcher at the American Sunlight Project, compiled the details of more than 5,800 members of parliaments across Europe in July and then used custom search engines to find where they appeared across the deepfake websites. (The research does not include members of the European Parliament).
Politicians from Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, and France appeared on the websites the most, according to the findings, and the more senior a politician is, the more likely they were to be targeted. Shultz alerted all of the MPs individually and provided guidance on how the content may be removed. The websites also include depictions of celebrities, journalists, and other public figures, he says. WIRED is not naming the websites in order to not drive further attention to the abusive images.
Multiple researchers and lawmakers say that while politicians have been targeted with deepfakes for years, it can damage democratic practices and create chilling effects that may stop women and girls from becoming public figures. “This discourages women from taking office in the first place and also crowds these women out of public life,” Shultz says. “There’s so much evidence to support that this does real psychological damage. This also does reputational damage for the future if they want to fade out of politics and have another career.”
“Deepfake videos are used to intimidate politicians but also to belittle women,” says Sarah Dobbe, a Dutch Socialist Party MP, who was impacted. “It is very important that if a woman or girl is victimized in this way, she can get direct support if needed, and that the content is removed quickly.”
Across the sites he monitored, Shultz categorized multiple categories of abusive content or behavior. His results include instances where MPs appeared in content that was actively being hosted by the sites, indexed results where content had been removed, and also a number of profiles and “gateways” where potentially new content could be created.
Multiple websites hosted pages that include the names of MPs, official photos, and in some cases their social media profiles or personal information. Some included sections “rating” the women’s bodies, Shultz’s report says. Often next to these MP biographies were links to so-called nudifier apps or the websites’ own tools that claimed to digitally undress people. “It has all the images, all the information, and a direct link to the tool, and in three clicks you can generate,” Shultz says. “That’s just as bad as actually hosting the content.”
Since AI-created deepfakes first emerged at the end of 2017, the underlying technology to produce them has become much more accessible, and the output of the tools has become more realistic. Over time, millions of nonconsensual AI images and videos have been created, mostly by men and boys, and are often used to harass, intimidate, or blackmail women and girls, including at almost 100 schools around the world.
“These platforms are designed to run like businesses,” says Henry Ajder, an AI adviser and deepfake expert who has been tracking the ecosystem since 2018. He says that while it is not surprising that politicians are being targeted in this way, the findings are helpful for officials in Europe to understand the severity of the issue. “The whole infrastructure is set up to do this at scale with ease,” he says.
In general, lawmakers have been slow to introduce legislation to tackle the growing array of harms caused by deepfakes. However, in recent months, some laws have started to be introduced. Both the UK and EU are planning bans on nudify services, while under the US Take It Down Act, at least two major deepfake websites publishing thousands of images and videos of celebrities have been taken offline. Reporting by journalists unmasking those behind the websites has also led to major sites being taken offline. Ahead of this story being published, WIRED found that at least half a dozen of the domains that appear in the research have recently been removed from the web—reducing the total number of depictions of the European MPs.
Shultz, who is also researching the number of depictions of UK and US politicians, previously analyzed how many US senators and members of Congress appeared on deepfake sites in 2024. After the websites were taken down, Shultz says, there has been a “significant decrease” in the number of depictions of those American politicians that appeared on the websites two years ago.
“It’s a priority to ensure that these images are taken down, but that also there’s strong regulation on this type of technology,” says Kröger.

Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

Rainbow clouds shone over parts of Victoria over the weekend, in an unusual visual phenomenon known as iridescent clouds.
Photographs of the spectacle were taken by onlookers in the Melbourne suburbs of Mount Waverley and Caroline Springs.
Sarah Scully, a senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, said the visual phenomenon was not uncommon in Australia but was rarely captured.
“People don’t often notice them, as they’re really fleeting,” she said.
Iridescent clouds often form from cirrus clouds, which were seen over Victoria on the weekend. Cirrus clouds are made up of ice crystals and are commonly found in the higher levels of the troposphere – the level of the atmosphere where most weather occurs – where the temperatures are coldest.
The clouds get their rainbow appearance when light is diffracted – bent – around ice crystals. The phenomenon often occurs in newly formed clouds where the ice crystals are the same size.
The smaller the cloud, the more rays of sunlight can pass through and be diffracted by a single ice droplet, according to the BoM.
Iridescent clouds gain their appearance from the diffraction of sunlight, which causes the colours to spread into rings or waves.
They differ from rainbows, in which both the refraction (bending) and reflection (bouncing back) of sunlight result in colours in a specific order with neater bands.
Iridescent clouds are sometimes mistaken for sun dogs, another type of visual phenomenon with similar characteristics.
“Sun dogs are a different type of optical phenomenon,” Scully said. “They occur almost like a pillar of light that’s either on both sides of the sun or just on one side of the sun.
“That is due … to water crystals being in the atmosphere and … it sits at low levels of the horizon. You need it to sit even lower [than an iridescent cloud].”

The projected savings from a highly touted Trump administration plan to lower Medicare drug costs may be drastically reduced — by as much as 80% — thanks to secretive deals cut with more than two dozen pharmaceutical companies, according to a new analysis.
At issue is an approach known as “most-favored nation” pricing, which would tie the prices paid by Medicare to what 19 other wealthy nations pay for the same medicines. The White House has maintained the effort would save Medicare $26 billion over several years and help mitigate the long-standing problem of increasingly unaffordable prescription drugs.
To make this happen, the administration is creating two pilot programs — GLOBE for Medicare Part B and GUARD for Medicare Part D — that will require drug companies to pay additional rebates if their prices exceed the lowest international price found in those 19 countries. More specific details about the rules are due shortly.

The Best Standing Desks for People Who Are Tired of Sitting
Featured in this article
Not every standing desk is worth the investment, but the ones that are can change the entire rhythm of your workday. Switching between sitting and standing not only encourages movement and better posture, but it also breaks up the long, sluggish stretches of time that come with desk work.
Our team has been testing desks at home for years, putting each one through several weeks of daily use. Mostly, that means standard desk work, but also tasks like building Lego sets and wrapping holiday gifts. These are the models that stand out. They’re durable, comfortable, and practical (some even come with techy upgrades), and they make it easy enough to make standing a small, everyday habit.
Read our home office guides for more, including the Best Office Chairs, Home Office Gear, Best Computer Monitors, Best Computer Speakers, Best Webcams, and Best Laptop Stands.
Updated September 2026: We've deleted discontinued models, pared down and reordered the guide, and added the Vari Ergo electric standing desk to our top picks.
Tips and Frequently Asked Questions
Is a Standing Desk Worth It?
New research shows that while standing desks can potentially mitigate some health risks by limiting your sitting time, standing too long isn't all that great and can increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. I reached out to Anne-Kristina Arnold, a kinesiology expert and senior lecturer in the Department of Biomedical Physiology and Kinesiology at Simon Fraser University. She says the results from this recent study “illustrate how challenging some of this epidemiological research is."
“To say standing workstations are good for everybody in every situation all the time is never going to flow,” Arnold tells WIRED. "There are so many variables, so many varied kinds of work we do—we're varied in our body sizes, in our fitness, in the shoes we wear. It's really hard to be able to say definitively that standing workstations are good. The research is mixed."
Switching from sitting to standing doesn't solve all problems, and standing too long can cause its own problems. If you want to work with a standing workstation, Arnold recommends to use it in the standing position for 20 minutes per hour. If you have a normal desk, get up and move every 15 to 20 minutes. However, there's no definitive guideline. “The standing workstation isn't necessarily the answer—getting up and walking is better,” Arnold concludes. —Julian Chokkattu
Electric vs. Manual Standing Desks
Our guide here focuses largely on electric standing desks, which have motors in the legs to smoothly move the table up and down. However, we have a few manual standing desk recommendations, too. If you're planning on switching up how you work a few times every day, an electric desk will simply be more convenient. However, if you just want to be able to adjust the height of your desk and won't be changing it all that often, then maybe look at manual standing desks. They're often cheaper.
How to Properly Stand and Sit With a Standing Desk
The same ergonomic rules you follow when sitting at a workstation apply when you're standing. When your elbows are at a 90-degree position, you want the desk keyboard to be elbow height. Your monitor should be at eye level (a good rule of thumb is the top of your monitor should meet your eye), and if you're using a laptop, you should keep it angled with a laptop stand for a more ergonomic typing position. Be sure to adjust your office chair appropriately to the floor before adjusting the height of your desk.
Watch Your Wires!
Cable management is exceptionally important when it comes to standing desks. After setting up your standing desk, make sure you keep an eye on every single wire that's connected to something on the desk when you start raising the desktop. Otherwise, funny things start to happen: wires come undone, or scoot light objects off the desk.
WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has unboxed and set up many desks over the years, and yet he still made a rookie move. As he was raising a desk, he didn't realize his Ethernet cable was taut, and it broke cleanly off the back of his PC when the desk reached a certain height. Welp. As for me, I'm a naturally distracted person, and so I need to tack my cables down or suffer grievous consequences on the regular.
Keep an eye on the wires. Keep an eye on stuff near the wires. If you're not careful, you can even accidentally knock art off your wall. —Matthew Korfhage
How We Test
I and other members of WIRED's Reviews team test standing desks in our own homes and in our own home offices. We use desks for months at a time (even years, in some cases), jotting down every flaw we see over the course of that time and noting any highlights. We look at building materials, motor noise, motor speed, preset options, cable management, and ease of use—and of course, the simple intangibles like aesthetics.
We gauge the difficulty of the assembly and setup, as well as the difficulty of disassembling or moving each desk. Desks are a solid investment, and so we expect a desk to be with us for years, perhaps longer than we live in a city. And so we also look at both the length of the warranty and the service reputation of each company.
Sometimes a small detail can take on outsized importance when using a desk over long periods, whether the existence or nonexistence of a grommet, a rounded edge, or a bolt that gets a little wobbly over time. That's why WIRED's Reviews team believes in the value of long-term testing, and why we do so in our own home offices.
This long-term testing also means it's not easy for our small team to test every single desk out there, as these are bulky, big pieces of furniture and the setup is fairly involved. This means you may see a few missing brands in this guide, but we're always testing and adding more desks. —Matthew Korfhage
Other Standing Desks to Consider
Ergodriven Tempo Automatic Standing Desk for $629: It was only a matter of time before desks got “smart,” right? This Tempo from new-ish company Ergodriven is designed to automate the process of standing or sitting, with a Cruise Control function that will encourage you to change position during the day by, well, automatically doing so. A “wiggle” will alert you when the desk wants to change position, which you can override manually if you're eating lunch or in a meeting. A sensor will register your presence, so the desk won't move when you're away. WIRED contributor Nicole Kinning found that this all works as promised—as does a little app that registers “achievements” like standing time. But note the desk, while sturdy, is also a bit heavy, and a slight cosmetic crack formed early on the rounded edge. The 16-year warranty provides a bit of assurance.
Luxor Compact Electric Standing Desk for $200: The Luxor is a no-nonsense standing desk that does exactly what you expect and takes up minimal space. It’s perfect for students, small apartments, and anyone who needs a compact, budget-friendly setup. At 23.5 inches deep, the tabletop is shallow enough to fit into tight corners or shared spaces. The electric lift moves steadily at an inch per second, whisper-quiet, and the 154-pound weight capacity can handle a laptop, monitor, and a few textbooks with no sweat. The lift mechanism is exposed underneath, so you’ll want to leave some legroom when at sitting height. —Nicole Kinning
Simple Height Adjustable Desk for $850: The Simple Height Adjustable Desk lives up to its name. Assembly is straightforward and cable routing is tidy thanks to an integrated channel that keeps everything corralled. The T-shaped legs slide into a bracket instead of screwing or locking into place, which feels a little ambiguous, but once it’s upright, the desk is solid and sturdy. In practice, the desk became everything I needed. It’s smooth, quiet, and spacious, with four height presets. The laminate top is durable and forgiving—ideal if you’re like me and regularly forget that coasters exist. There are no fancy gimmicks, which is exactly the point. It's a dependable, fuss-free desk that prioritizes function over flashy. —Nicole Kinning
Eureka Ergonomic Opal Standing Desk for $2,250: WIRED contributor Nicole Kinning was a big fan of the, well, opaline looks of the Eureka Ergonomic Opal standing desk. It's a sturdy, milky-toned, downright fancy-looking pillar of vaguely art-deco luxe: beaded cabinets on each leg, gold hardware, marbled top, integrated drawer, hooooooey! It all makes for a quite distinctive aesthetic, and setup is a bit tricky given the heft of the desk. But unlike most standing desks, this one is outfitted quite beautifully as a full workstation, with roomy cabinets in each leg and a drawer offering ample storage. Just be sure to put grips on the bottom; it slid around on Kinning's hard floors like a curling stone, she noted. Once it's in place, bask in the stateliness. It's the rare standing desk where she could see herself writing a Great American Novel.
Autonomous Desk Pro for $600: The standout feature here is the new Desk AI, a separate control attachment that tracks your standing habits along with environmental factors like air pressure and quality, temperature, humidity, and noise. In theory, it’s meant to help you work smarter, but in practice, it mostly flags things you can’t control from the desk itself. If it came with an air purifier or fan to manage these conditions, then we’d be talkin’. Still, it’s a fun and techy bonus on an otherwise reliable desk.
Vari Solid Wood Electric Standing Desk for $829: Even though it’s solid wood, this desk never felt too precious for everyday use. Made from FSC-certified lumber, the desk is heavy and stable, even at standing height on carpet, and the motor is impressively quiet and subtle when adjusting. The ComfortEdge feature turned out to be more helpful than reviewer Nicole Kinning expected; over long typing sessions, it noticeably softened where my wrists meet the desk, a nice upgrade to a standard desk’s hard, squared-off edges. Yes, the solid wood Vari is on the pricier side, but it feels justified if solid wood and long-term durability matter to you. If they don’t, consider the traditional version.
Boulies Magvida for $760: The Boulies Magvida advertises its best feature in the name itself. This midsize desk (55 x 28 inches) is known for its EMO system, a magnetic organization setup built beneath the desktop. Instead of drilling holes or fiddling with brackets, you just snap accessories, like a cable tray, hooks, and silicone straps, into place. The add-ons feel premium and the magnets don’t budge, and there’s an optional magnetic drawer that’s also handy. Add in memory presets, a child lock, anti-collision detection, and simple color options and you’ve got a clean, clever setup.
Herman Miller Jarvis Bamboo Standing Desk for $1,325: As someone who spent years hunching over keyboards, obsessive research led WIRED reviewer Simon Hill to the Jarvis Standing Desk (now owned by Herman Miller), which has served him well for six years. With a contoured bamboo top, handy optional extras to tuck wires out of sight, and a responsive control panel for easy height adjustment (including presets), this is an excellent standing desk. The only weakness is that it wobbles slightly at higher levels. The newer touchscreen OLED control unit is not as reliable as the original, so opt for the programmable controls.
Room & Board Lincoln Desk for $5,399: Few standing desks can lay claim to true elegance. But Room & Board's Lincoln desk—designed in collaboration with design firm Gensler—is an exception. This is a dignified, sturdy, wobble-free electric standing desk that'd fit in with an executive office or a well-appointed home, made with solid wood and available in walnut, maple, cherry, ash, or oak (with a rye, salt, or charcoal stain). You can configure the desk to have integrated drawers on the left, right, or on both sides if you choose the larger 72-inch size. There's even a drawer in the center! This is what privilege looks like, where standing desks are concerned. The price is commensurately high, though take note this included white glove delivery and assembly. Also take note that the thickness of the desktop means only some clamps will mount onto its girth. This monitor arm mount will work, but for some mounts, you might have to directly screw it to the desktop. All in all, this is a gorgeous standing desk that doesn't look anything like a standing desk, but with a few quirks and a high price.
Staples Union & Scale Electric Standing Desk With Micro Movements (UN62092) for $513: Staples' house brand, Union & Scale, makes some of WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu's favorite affordable office furniture, and its standing desk is no exception—though at this middle price range, it didn't keep pace with Branch's reasonably priced desks. Still, this was easy to put together, and while the white desktop is not much to look at, the dual motors do the job. He liked the control panel, which has dedicated buttons for moving the desk up and down, as well as two height presets. He also didn't see any wobble, though the collision sensor could stand to be more sensitive. There's a cable tray at the bottom back of the desk to route cables, but there's sadly no grommet to pull them through. The Micro Movement mode moves the desk up and down over time to reduce fatigue and encourage movement, but it might be more distracting than useful.
Beflo Tenon Premium for $3,998: While incredibly expensive (and heavy!), WIRED contributor Henri Robbins found the hardwood smart desk both sturdy and well-designed. Assembly was straightforward, and once the desk was up and running, Robbins found all of the features (touchscreen controls, a built-in power strip, audio passthrough, and LED lighting) to work well, and in convenient locations. The touchscreen controls are intuitive (iOS-like), and features like a sit/stand timer and phone connectivity provide additional functionality. The desk supports over 200 pounds of stuff even when moving, and the height-adjustment motors will temporarily disable if they overheat, instead of risking damage to the desk. The table also looks fantastic, and a multitude of first-party accessories let you customize the desk to your specific needs. The largest issue with this table is the noise. While in no way loud, it was certainly more audible than the “whisper-quiet” descriptor Beflo uses in its marketing. Besides that, the lighting color adjustment had some difficulties creating specific colors using the built-in touchscreen, and the audio cable was too short to reach a desktop computer on the floor, even at the lowest height. However, the Tenon is still a great, if pricey, option to consider.
Herman Miller Spout Sit-to-Stand Table for $3,275: Herman Miller's Spout Sit-To-Stand Table is lovely to look at. Like the Branch Four-Legged Desk, it looks like a normal desk with four legs, giving it a luxe look. Those motors in the legs rise smoothly, and it’s easy to raise and lower the desktop to my preferences with the button on the right. The motor does have a high hum to it, and WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found it loud enough that she'd hesitate to use it when her husband is on a call in the same room, but not so loud it would disturb her son if he were sleeping a room away. Bizarrely, it doesn’t have memory presets, but it's pretty easy to just adjust the desk each time to sitting and standing heights. You can add a cable tray underneath the desk each time to organize cords, but it costs extra. The only other item built into the desk is a single slim center drawer perfect for pens and notebooks. It comes in three desktop sizes and three finishes: laminate white, veneer walnut, and veneer ash. You can also customize the base color, with seven different colors ranging from your classic black and white to a gentle blue and olive green. While it’s gorgeous to look at and works well, Farrell found it disappointing that such a high-priced desk doesn’t have presets and uses veneers rather than real wood.
FlexiSpot E7 Pro for $400+: Standing desks can get pricey, but FlexiSpot routinely offers similar functionality at a lower price. At first glance, the E7 Pro looks much like the Herman Miller Jarvis, but look closer, and you discover the entry-level option has a shallow 23-inch desktop, the control unit feels a bit cheap, and it emits a high-pitched whine in operation. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill had some issues fitting larger power adapters in the cable tidily, and the desk can get wobbly when fully extended. But, even when fully configured, the E7 Pro is cheaper than many rivals. Minor flaws aside, it is a perfectly decent standing desk.
Inbox Zero 47-inch Adjustable Electric Standing Desk for $196: This desk has every feature you'd expect to need at the price range less than $200, wrote former WIRED reviewer Martin Cizmar. There are rolling casters so you can not only move the desk up and down, but also shake it all around. The desk's electric controls have presets but also allow you to fine-tune the height for typing or Zooming. The split top that makes it easier and cheaper to ship doesn't hurt the performance, but is less pleasant visually, and the little motor works audibly hard (tshunk, tschunk, tshunk) while raising the desktop. Based on three months of testing, it's a decent budget standing desk with casters, but if you can spend a little more, you'll probably be happier with something else.
Standing Desk Accessories
Branch Clamp-on Power for $89: This simple and elegant clamp attaches to your desktop and adds three AC outlets, a USB-C, and a USB-A, so you don't have so many wires running down to the ground.
LumeCube EdgeLight 2.0 for $150: Why have a lamp take up valuable desk space when you can clamp the lamp to your desk? These task lights from LumeCube are great for illuminating the desktop and even your face during late-night Zoom calls. You can adjust the color temperature and the brightness.
BenQ ScreenBar Lamp for $139: Alternatively, you can place these ScreenBar lamps over your computer monitor, and it will light up your desktop, no clamping required. The ScreenBar Pro also has a motion sensor, so when you leave your desk, the lamp will turn off, and it will light up when you're back. You can adjust the brightness and color temperature, and an automatic setting makes it adjust these controls based on the room's ambient lighting.
Secretlab Premium Footrest for $89: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu been using this footrest for several years, and it's excellent. The plush memory foam is cushy and a nice respite for Chokkattu's feet, and it's easy to clean with a vacuum and a damp cloth. It hasn't shown much wear despite years of use.
Monoprice Single Monitor Adjustable Gas Spring Desk Mount for $84: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has tested a few of these WorkStream arm mounts for years, and they've reliably done the job. You can adjust the tension with a hex key and move the monitor around to your desired position. Just make sure you don't go over the recommended weight load with a big and heavy screen.
Mount-It! Dual Monitor Arm for $280: This heavy-duty monitor arm holds up my ultrawide monitor and my vertical monitor, both of which have BenQ Screenbar lamps on top, along with my webcam. It handles the weight with no effort, and the clamp is accommodating enough to even work with the 5-inch Room & Board standing desk. There's RGB lighting throughout, but it's not bright enough to splash onto the wall, so it's a little pointless, noted WIRED Reviewer Julian Chokkattu.
Harber London Professional Desk Mat for $239: Keep your desktop protected with a large desk mat like this one. I've used several mats from Harber London over the years, and this latest model is the favorite of WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu. The pebbled leather is supple and soft, and the mat stays put. It's easy to clean as well.
Avoid These Standing Desks
Corsair Platform:6 Desk for $1,400: Where do I start? I liked Corsair's standing desk because it's spacious, has a fun pegboard design to mount your tchotchkes, and even has an interesting rail system that lets you mount and slide things across the desktop, like your monitors. Unfortunately, several months after mounting two monitors on the included dual-monitor arms, this rail system has tilted forward due to the weight. (I'm also not the only one to experience this.) It doesn't help that I never really found this rail to be all that useful. The standing function works well, and you get two presets, but sometimes the little screen would throw me an error message “rE5.” Pressing and holding the down button resolved it, but none of these are issues anyone should deal with considering the crazy-high price. That's the real problem. It's just so expensive, and the five-year warranty feels like a slap in the face. This model is still listed for sale, but as out of stock last time we checked. —Julian Chokkattu
Marinamantra ‘Flow’ Sit-to-Stand Desk for $1,149: I had high hopes for this one. A desk that lets me sit crisscross applesauce while I work?! Sold. But the reality didn’t live up to the pitch. When I unboxed the desk, several screws were scattered loose in the box. That set the tone for a desk that eventually worked, but often misbehaved, sometimes refusing to move up and down. That said, I do like the cord management lip and the clever Velcro covers that keep cables and hardware neatly tucked out of sight. Unfortunately, none of that matters much if I’m spending more time flipping it over and poking around underneath the hood than actually using it. —Nicole Kinning

On the intervening night of June 18 and 19, Jalil Akhtar, an elderly Muslim man, from West Bengal’s Bagroi village in Karandighi block of Uttar Dinajpur district, was woken up from sleep and picked up by Dalkhola police from his home, his family alleged. Other members of his household, sleeping in the same home, came to know of his arrest only the next morning.
The 66-year-old man, whose name appeared in both the 2002 and 2026 Special Intensive Revision (SIR) lists, was allegedly arrested on grounds of “being a Bangladeshi”, his family told Alt News. After spending nearly three months in various holding centres and judicial custody, when Akhtar was produced before additional chief judicial magistrate (ACJM) of Islampur court on Wednesday, September 2, the investigating officer of the case gave a written declaration that identity documents submitted by Akhtar were valid. However, Akhtar has not yet been granted bail, the court is expected to hear the matter next on September 10.
During his nearly three-month-long incarceration, Akhtar was kept in two holding centres, and then lodged in Islampur jail, until, his family claimed they were told he would be deported to Bangladesh. They further alleged that during the entire duration, police failed to prove that Akhtar’s citizenship and legal documents were fake, raising questions over why the arrest was made in the first place when his name appeared in the latest SIR list.
“My brother is an Indian, we have all the documents and he has never even seen the Bangladesh border. Yet, he was arrested, kept in holding centres and jailed on a mere suspicion of being a Bangladeshi, which the police could not even prove. Was he held for so long just because we are Muslims and live in a border district with significant Muslim population?” asked Motiur Rahaman, Akhtar’s cousin.
‘Picked up at Night without Family Being Informed’
According to his family and locals, Akhtar slept on a cot in front of his single-room home. His wife, Taufa Bibi, woke at dawn on June 19 to find him gone. She initially assumed that he might have gone to offer ‘Fazr Namaz’, but began to panic when she found his kurta hanging from the family closet.
Motiur was first to launch a hunt for his cousin, a landless villager who was entirely dependent on his two migrant worker sons. Describing the long fight in detail to Alt News, Motiur said he assembled a crew of fellow villagers and they scoured through the entire neighbourhood including forest areas through the day. They were eventually informed by a local that a police vehicle had entered the village the previous night.
Upon calling one of his sources at the recently established Bazargaon police camp, which falls under Dalkhola police station, Motiur learned that the police had picked up a man from his village the previous night, allegedly identifying him as an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant. The group then reached the police outpost, and found Akhtar sitting on the floor of the lock-up, bare bodied, as the police, Motiur claimed, did not even allow him to wear his kurta while nabbing him.
Motiur further alleged that, as per Akhtar’s recollection of the arrest to his family, the police held him at gunpoint, apparently to keep him silent while taking him into custody from the densely populated area.
The Family’s Fight To Prove His Citizenship
“In the police camp we tried to reason with the officer in charge that Jalil Akhtar’s name was not only in the 2026 SIR list, but was also in the 2002 list, so he should be released. The police retorted saying ‘don’t you people dare to threaten me, those days of threatning are over…now the government has changed,” claimed Motiur.
Another officer of the outpost reportedly told Motiur to give them some time to verify the documents and if everything came out clean, his cousin would be released. However, the same morning, Akhtar was moved to a holding centre in Nizampur near Chakulia.
To establish his Indian citizenship, Akhtar’s family began gathering every document they could find. According to his family, they obtained the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list, both of which included Akhtar’s name. They also collected land deeds linking Akhtar to his father, Rousan Ali, as well as a residence certificate issued by the Bazragaon-2 panchayat, stating that Akhtar was a permanent resident of the panchayat area.
On July 9, they visited Dalkhola police station and submitted the documents for verification. Before that, they had also approached the district superintendent of police’s (SP) office. On both occasions, the police asked them to allow time for the documents to be verified and assured them that no harm would come to Akhtar if he was indeed an Indian citizen. According to his family, the police also said they were under “considerable pressure from higher-ups to identify and deport those deemed to be illegal Bangladeshi migrants”, and that they were only acting as per orders.
‘An Attempt To Send Him To Bangladesh’
However, as days went by, Akhtar remained under police custody and shifting between holding centres. Dulal Rajbanshi, organiser of the Votadhikar Surakkha Samanway Samity, an organisation formed to help those whose names were deleted in the 2026 SIR, helped Akhtar’s family. “We were able to prevent the police from sending Jalil Akhtar into Bangladesh twice. When they failed to send him into ‘no man’s land’, the police eventually filed a false FIR and produced him before the court,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, Akhtar was moved to another holding centre near Phulbari border crossing near Siliguri, allegedly to send him to Bangladesh. The state police keeps the detainees at temporary holding centres, before handing them over to the BSF for deportation into Bangladesh, Rajbanshi claimed. He said that in Akhtar’s case, first the police handed him over to the BSF, who took him towards Phulbari to apparently deport him.
“We were informed by local sources that Akhtar was moved from the Nizampur holding centre and taken towards Phulbari on July 6. The next day, we reached Uttar Dinajpur district magistrate’s office in Raiganj, who asked us to immediately contact the SP in Islampur,” he said.
“We travelled a 110-kilometre distance from Raiganj to Islampur, where again, the SP said that he needs time to investigate, as there is “immense pressure from above to deport illegal Bangladeshis”. However, we were later told that Akhtar was brought back to the Chakulia holding centre. It was unclear what happened after this, and which border they took him to in order to attempt deportation the second time.”
However, acting on the SP’s direction, the group then met Dalkhola police station’s inspector-in-charge (IC) in the following days. “The IC asked us whether we could bring any relatives of Akhtar to the police station for verification. By that evening, we had brought even his 90-year-old aunts and all other relatives to the station. But the police did not meet them, instead, they collected the death certificate of one of Akhtar’s brothers,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, the BSF often selects a favourable point along the border to ‘pushback’ alleged Bangladeshis, sometimes at gunpoint. “Currently, the Border Guard Bangladesh and Bangladeshi villagers are on high alert to prevent any pushback from India. As a result, many people are getting stranded in no man’s land, as neither country is willing to take them in. Akhtar’s family was wary of this exact fate,” he claimed.
According to Motiur, the IC also mentioned “immense pressure”, stating that the police were already “holding a list of 500 names whom they have to deport and 50 more were recently added”.
‘It Is Better If They Kill Me’
In the meantime, Akhtar’s family visited him at the detention centre. According to Motiur, Akhtar broke down completely. “My brother kept saying, what will I do if I am sent to Bangladesh? I don’t know anybody there. I have never been to that country. I can’t even beg there. It is better if they kill me than push me into Bangladesh,” Motiur said.
According to the family, a Border Security Force (BSF) team also visited their home to investigate the matter. “The BSF team came and spoke with us. They were infuriated by the state police’s actions — or lack of investigation — and told us that they would not deport an Indian citizen. At least the BSF came to the village to investigate. Nobody from the state police even cared to do that,” Motiur claimed.
On July 20, villagers organised a protest against Akhtar’s arrest in the nearby Rasakhowa Haat. However, before the programme could start, police intervened and dispersed them, they alleged. The next day, Rajbanshi alleged, the administration again attempted to send Akhtar into Bangladesh.
“On July 21, we received information that he had once again been moved from the Nizampur holding centre. We got the news around 2 pm and, by 4 pm, had organised a press conference at the Uttar Dinajpur Press Club in Raiganj. We shared information about the press conference across social media. We were worried that police might announce that he has gone missing. The next day, on July 22, police informed the family that they would produce Akhtar before the Islampur court,” claimed Rajbanshi.
Discrepancies between FIR and Police Submission
As per the FIR lodged against Akhtar by Dalkhola police, he was picked up from Nizampur around 1:05 am on June 20. Nizampur is also where, according to his family, he was subsequently held at a holding centre — the location is around 35 km from Akhtar’s home.
Motiur alleged that upon prodding the police on who lodged a complaint against Akhtar, police refused to reveal the name of the complainant. According to the FIR, Akhtar was detained at the Nizampur centre along with two other “illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”. The FIR states that all three detainees are from “AndhaRahamatpur village of Thakurgaon district of Bangladesh”. It is claimed that this was revealed by Akhtar himself during interrogation.
The FIR further states that Akhtar crossed the Hili-Malda border and entered India around 24 years ago. However, the documents submitted by his family before the court show that his name appears in both the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list. In both documents, his father’s name is the same. If the police account is accurate and Akhtar entered India only around 23-24 years ago, it would be impossible for his name to have appeared in the 1995 voter list, nearly three decades ago, and subsequently in the 2002 SIR list.
Alt News has seen the case diary submitted by police in court on August 5. It says Akhtar voted in 1982 elections as well, although it does not clarify which elections and where. The submission also mentions that during investigation, police had been told by locals that coming to Uttar Dinajpur in 1982, Akhtar worked as a rikshaw puller in Delhi and does not speak proper Bengali. These statements directly contradict the FIR claim that he entered India around 24 years ago and does not establish any link between Akhtar and Bangladesh.
According to the police’s submission, Akhtar was born in either 1959 or 1960 and first appears in official records in 1982. No records relating to him from before 1982 could be found, the police said. They also claim that he failed to establish a credible link with Raushan Ali, whom he identifies as his father, through land records or other documentary evidence.
However, Rajbanshi claimed that Akhtar was not required to produce his parents’ birth records to establish his Indian citizenship. “Under the Indian Citizenship Act, a person born before 1987 does not need to show the birth records of their parents to prove their Indian citizenship. The 2002 and 2026 SIR exercises were also meant to identify and remove illegal entries from the electoral rolls. Akhtar’s name appears in both lists. Yet he continues to be detained, merely to serve what appears to be the BJP’s political agenda,” he said.
The September 2 Hearing
As per legal records, the police postponed the bail hearing four times stating that they need more time to verify the documents. During the hearing on September 2, the additional chief judicial magistrate and the defence counsel asked the police to testify whether the documents provided by Akhtar were valid. The police ultimately confirmed the documents were legitimate.
According to Akhtar’s lawyer, Firoz Ahmed, the police deliberately avoided telling the court whether the former’s documents were genuine. “The ACJM pressed the investigating to state whether Akhtar’s documents are genuine before carrying on with the investigation. Even then, the IO remained silent,” he said.
Later, however, the police stated in a report submitted in the late afternoon that Akhtar’s voter ID and PAN card were genuine Indian documents, and that his records in the 1995 voter list and 2002 SIR list were also genuine. “They are awaiting an email response to verify the authenticity of his Aadhaar card, so they could not say anything about it,” Ahmed added.
“As his birthplace and his current residence are different, and fall under different police stations, the police are now harping on that, as if relocating to another place is a crime,” Ahmed alleged.
“The police had been given a target to identify and round up Bangladeshis, and they are targeting any vulnerable person they can find. Since Akhtar was born in another village, around four to five kilometres from ours, and is extremely poor and owns barely any land, it is easy for the administration to portray him as a Bangladeshi, citing a lack of evidence,” Motiur alleged.
Dalkhola Police’s Response
Alt News spoke to Sankha Chatterjee, IC of Dalkhola police station. Upon being asked whether Akhtar was arrested at gunpoint as alleged by his family, he said, “A lathi is enough for us to arrest a 66-year old. We don’t need a gun for it. As for the family’s allegation, tell them that we used a Bofors cannon to take Jalil Akhtar in custody.”
He further said that police had submitted their findings before the court. “Now it up to the court to decide whether Jalil Akhtar is an Indian or a Bangladeshi or a Pakistani or a Cuban citizen. According to our investigation, we couldn’t find any documents of Jalil Akhtar till the age of 21. All his documents are from the age of 22 till 66,” said the officer.
Alt News asked about the discrepancies between the FIR and the case diary submitted by the police before the court, however, the officer’s response did not clarify the aforementioned loopholes. Chatterjee simply said: “I don’t want to get political, but if you come to Uttar Dinajpur, I can show you people who have voter cards and other documents of both India and Bangladesh. It’s better not to get into how they were able to cross over to this side.”
Motiur, Rajbanshi and Akhtar’s family claim their efforts have helped prevent Akhtar’s ‘pushback’ till now. But the family’s ordeal is far from over. They still do not know when, or whether, he will be freed from detention and his name will be cleared in this ‘test of citizenship’. For the family, what began as an effort to establish his identity has become a prolonged battle against an administrative process that they believe is inherently designed against them.

Lindsay Clancy holdout juror was reportedly accused of domestic violence
Clancy, 36, admitted to killing her three children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan - in the basement of her Massachusetts home in 2023, before trying to take her life. Her case ended in a mistrial September 4
The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial was previously accused of domestic violence, according to a report.
The man, who has not been publicly identified, allegedly grabbed his wife by the throat and threw her into a dresser in September 2021, CBS News reported.
The juror’s 13-year-old nephew reportedly called 911, according to a Brockton, Massachusetts, police report obtained by CBS News. The Independent has asked the Brockton Police Department for comment.
The man was later charged with one count of domestic violence assault and battery and pleaded not guilty. The criminal charge was later dismissed, according to the report.
The holdout juror has not been publicly identified. Plymouth Superior Court has not made the jury list public.
The Independent has contacted Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office and Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington for comment.
Clancy’s case ended in a mistrial September 4 after the jury was deadlocked three times.
Clancy, 36, a former labor and delivery nurse, admitted to killing her three children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan - in the basement of her Massachusetts home in 2023, before trying to take her life. Her suicide attempt left her partially paralyzed.
Her defense attorney argued that postpartum psychosis prompted her actions. Prosecutors argued that Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her children.
After five weeks of testimony and seven days of deliberations, jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the killings.
Several jurors and Clancy’s lawyer have since suggested that the jury was split 11 to 1 in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible for the killings.
Jury foreperson Roni Carlson told NBC 10 last Tuesday that the holdout juror declared that he wouldn’t say Clancy was not guilty by reason of insanity — even though he had reasonable doubt.
“He admitted he had reasonable doubt. I started filling out the forms; I was so excited,” Carlson said.
The holdout juror then told her: “But I’m still not going to say she’s not guilty by reason of insanity.”
Other members of the jury, Paula Devlin and Kellie Farina, also told the outlet that the holdout juror didn’t seem to want to listen to instructions, including the judge’s definition of “reasonable doubt.”
“He actually said one day in the end, ‘Why don’t we have the judge come and read it again?’ and we were like ‘No, we have it in front of us,’” Devlin said.
“He was very arrogant,” Farina added. “He really did not take anything that anybody said.”
The jurors noted they were trying to figure out whether Clancy knew right from wrong and concluded that she didn’t because “everything proved she loved her children.”
“Everything proved that she loved her children, so she had to have snapped,” Carlson said.
District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet said whether the state will retry Clancy. The next court hearing is scheduled for September 29 in Plymouth Superior Court.
