Zelenskyy urges parliament to oust prosecutor general over graft turmoil
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged parliament to quickly remove Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko over corruption investigations
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged parliament Monday to move quickly on ousting Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, as a series of graft investigations pushed tensions to a new high.
Kravchenko submitted his resignation last week, calling it a “conscious political decision,” after a corruption investigation reached his office. Investigators have accused one of his subordinates of running a fraud scheme, though Kravchenko himself has not been charged or named a suspect.
Various corruption scandals have hurt Zelenskyy’s approval ratings at a time when Ukraine is still fighting for survival against Russia's 4 1/2-year full-scale invasion.
On Monday, Kravchenko said he had issued a formal notice of investigation of Semen Kryvonos, who leads the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), one of the agencies that had examined his office’s conduct.
Kravchenko also posted a video on Telegram accusing Kryvonos of using fraudulent means to escape accountability for a corruption-related offense dating back to 2008.
Kravchenko's announcement that he was traveling abroad while his future was being decided drew public criticism. He responded on Telegram that the trip includes meetings with international partners, where he plans to raise concerns about “unchecked influence” within Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies.
NABU and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), which jointly pursued the case that prompted Kravchenko’s resignation, said in a joint statement Monday that they view Kravchenko’s claims as a continuation of a systematic attack on independent anti-corruption bodies, one they said began last summer when an active push emerged to subordinate NABU and SAPO to the the Prosecutor General’s Office.
They also said that Kryvonos was not served any notice that he was being investigated.
“The statements of the prosecutor general, who recently resigned, are currently public in nature and carry no legal weight,” their statement said.
Zelenskyy submitted a formal request to parliament Monday.
“This prosecutor general has only one path ahead: dismissal from office. That is exactly what I told him,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram. “Ukraine has seen all the reasons why. If he wants to call it political pressure, he’s free to call it that. I am asking members of parliament to support this dismissal without delay.”

Srinagar, Sep 14: Former minister and senior political leader Imran Reza Ansari has urged the Jammu and Kashmir Government to take strict action over alleged landfilling at Brari Nambal, saying partial demolition of the structures would not be enough to address the damage caused to the waterbody.
In a statement, Ansari said the action at Brari Nambal risked becoming an “eye wash” if it ended with partial demolition alone. Referring to a report by Greater Kashmir, he said landfilling had allegedly continued for nearly 15 days.
“The bigger question is: who brought the material, who carried out the filling, and how was it allowed to continue?” he asked.
Ansari called for identification of those responsible, removal of the entire filling and restoration of the waterbody at the encroacher’s cost.
He also demanded a proper investigation into the alleged violation and said that wherever offences were established, FIRs and prosecution should follow.
“Partially demolishing what was built after allowing the damage to happen is not enough. We need accountability for the original act as well as for any failure of monitoring,” he said.
Ansari stressed the need to protect Kashmir’s remaining lakes, wetlands and other waterbodies for future generations.
“We need to keep something for our generation. Our children deserve to inherit clean lakes, wetlands and water bodies, not filled-up land and concrete,” he said, adding that the remaining natural water systems must be protected from further destruction.
He further said that protecting waterbodies and enforcing existing laws did not require statehood, but required “political will, administrative seriousness and responsible citizenship.”
Quoting the Qur’an, Ansari said, “And We made from water every living thing.” (Qur’an 21:30)
“Water is a trust and a source of life. Protecting it is not merely an environmental responsibility; it is a moral responsibility,” he said.
Ansari urged Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to take cognisance of the matter.

Climate tech startup Mitti Labs has signed a four-year agreement with Google to supply 1 Mn Carbon credits till 2030, which it describes as one of the largest nature-based offtakes to date The financial terms of the agreement have not been disclosed. However, Mitti Labs said the deal is a fixed contractual offtake covering 1 Mn credits, delivered between 2027 and 2030. Mitti Labs said payments will be made upon delivery of the verified carbon credits, with no upfront financing involved in the agreement. The credits will primarily be generated from Mitti Labs’ rice farming projects in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka. The startup currently has programmes covering more than 1 Lakh hectares in India. “We are currently working on expanding both across India and Southeast Asia. This deal with Google doesn't just validate the quality of the projects, the use of our MRV and the scalability of our projects, but will also help us scale our India projects,” cofounder Xavier Laguarta Soler told Inc42. Kate Brandt, Google’s chief sustainability officer, said Mitti Labs’ approach could cut methane emissions while conserving water and helping smallholder farmers adopt more efficient irrigation practices. “Mitti Labs' approach delivers critical near-term atmospheric impact by cutting methane emissions, while conserving billions of gallons of water and empowering smallholder farmers to deploy advanced water-management practices. We’re excited to partner with them to help accelerate and scale their solution across India,” Brandt said. The agreement comes a month after Mitti Labs raised $9.5 Mn in a Series A round led by Aramco Ventures. The funding is being used to expand its operations across India and develop new greenfield projects in the Philippines and Indonesia. Cutting Methane By Changing How Rice Is Grown Rice farming is a major Methane producer, a potent greenhouse gas. Flooding fields creates oxygen-poor conditions in which methane-producing microbes thrive. Mitti Labs works with farmers to introduce a practice known as alternate wetting and drying (AWD). Developed by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), the technique involves allowing fields to dry periodically before they are irrigated again. The approach can reduce the conditions that produce methane while using less water, as per Mitti Labs, without affecting crop yields. Mitti Labs trains farmers and provides support as they adopt the practice. It also shares revenue from the resulting carbon credits with participating farming communities. Mitti Labs’ AI platform combines high-resolution synthetic aperture radar, remote sensing and biogeochemical models with on-the-ground measurements to estimate changes in greenhouse gas emissions and water use. Water savings are also measured using flow meters. The GeoAI platform has been developed with support from NASA through a grant. Mitti Labs has also begun expanding outside India, with the Philippines serving as its first south-east Asian pilot market. It is exploring other major rice-producing markets in the region.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.
“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.
The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.
That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.
“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.
In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.
“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.
The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.
Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.
Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.
The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.
Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.
Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”
Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.
But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.
“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.
“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”
After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.
He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.

A cancer survivor hoped to work — then she lost her Medicaid disability coverage
Taya Hailstone has been in remission from childhood Hodgkin lymphoma for five years. But the cancer's lasting damage to her organs and nerves can make basic tasks, like loading a dishwasher, hard.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Still, Montana's health department decided last year that Hailstone is no longer eligible for low-cost disability health coverage through Medicaid. The department switched her coverage to the state's Children's Health Insurance Program, another Medicaid program — three months before she aged out.
Before making the decision, the state didn't seek records from the medical team treating Hailstone, according to letters from those doctors reviewed by KFF Health News. Rather, the administrative ruling came after state officials learned the now-19-year-old had stopped receiving Social Security disability payments. She said she did that because she hoped to get healthy enough to work and save some money — beyond what's allowed under the strict income caps tethered to those payments. But her health changes day to day, and she said for now she's still too sick to consistently work.
Hailstone, who lives with her mom, has been able to keep Medicaid coverage while they appeal the case. She said that without Medicaid she can't afford the treatment to manage the aftermath of her cancer.
"It feels like this process was made to make you give up," Hailstone said.
Patients with disabilities have long struggled with administrative hoops, blunders and confusion when trying to qualify for federally subsidized health coverage because of their illness. Now, new federal Medicaid work requirements mean states face the additional task of deciding who qualifies for a medical exemption. That means reviewing medical cases for an even larger swath of Medicaid enrollees.
Attorneys, researchers and advocates who specialize in public aid said disability cases like Hailstone's — though separate from the incoming work requirements — are an indication that states aren't ready to decide who should be exempt from those requirements. As a result, they said, more people will be denied coverage in an opaque process.
"This will be the story of millions of people," said Anthony Wright, who heads Families USA, a national nonprofit that advocates for ways to make healthcare more accessible.
Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson with the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, said the state doesn't comment on individual Medicaid cases.
An estimated 18.5 million people will have to meet the new federal requirements, by proving they're working, going to school, or volunteering to keep their Medicaid coverage, according to the Congressional Budget Office. More than 40% of those enrollees live with a chronic health condition, according to KFF.
Some will be excused from those rules if they can prove they're too sick to work.
More than 5 million people are expected to lose Medicaid coverage by 2034 because of the work requirements, according to the CBO.
Work requirements become law
Many Republican policymakers and the Trump administration have touted Medicaid work requirements to preserve coverage for the neediest. Congress made that national policy through last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and gave states until January 2027 to implement work-for-coverage rules.
Some states are starting those checks early. Montana began in July. Nebraska initiated work requirements in May.
In the federal law creating the work requirements, Congress allowed states to exempt people who have an illness that qualifies them as "medically frail." Many states created plans for those judgment calls, only to be surprised when federal officials released rules for the requirements that went beyond what Congress outlined, by also requiring enrollees to prove their illness makes it too hard to work.
Families USA and other organizations have argued the new rules force states to set up a patchwork of systems that, together, would be larger and more complicated than the Social Security Administration's own disability review system. Last year, that federal program cost more than $5 billion to administer to roughly 7 million people nationally. For comparison, Wright said, the federal law provided $200 million for states to share as they implement the work requirements. States are paying contractors millions of dollars to prepare often already flawed public aid systems to meet the new standards.
In June, 25 states sued the Trump administration over the medical frailty rules, arguing they're too hard for patients to meet and for states to assess. That case is ongoing.
Hailstone was diagnosed with blood cancer at age 10. Her intestines tore, which led to their partial removal. As a result, her body struggles to process food and she can face severe dehydration. She said lingering side effects from her cancer treatment can leave her mind foggy and cause her hands and feet to swell enough that it's hard to grip a fork or walk across a room.
Cancer dominated nearly half her life. It left mental scars, too.
"Some days you feel fine and then you suddenly crash," Hailstone said.
Hailstone and her mom live in Roundup, a central Montana town of roughly 2,000 people. They regularly make the nearly two-hour round-trip drive to Billings for specialized care. She typically has three medical appointments a week to see her physical and occupational therapists and a mental health counselor.
Hailstone said she's lucky she has her mother's help navigating Medicaid. Her mom, Kyla Hailstone, said that the state hasn't clearly defined how it determined her daughter's disability status and that its appeal process has been slow and dysfunctional.
Taya Hailstone would qualify for Medicaid based on her income if she can't prove her eligibility for disability coverage. But that would mean proving she's too sick to meet the work requirement — putting her in the same position of having to rely on a state review of her illness.
"If I lose this, this is life-changing," Hailstone said.
"Things fall through the cracks"
Hailstone qualified as disabled through the federal government as recently as 2024, about a year before the state said it was dropping her coverage. State officials can do their own medical review to determine whether someone meets the federal definition of a disability to access Medicaid.
"Whether that happens is always a bit of a crapshoot just based on state capacity," said Megan Dishong, deputy director of the Montana Legal Services Association, which helps low-income people navigate public programs. "Things fall through the cracks."
Ebelt said the state health department accepts disability decisions from the Social Security Administration. The state agency can conduct an internal disability determination if a person doesn't have one from the SSA, but Ebelt said it doesn't have to if a person qualifies for coverage another way.
"We are committed to treating every client with respect and helping those who are eligible receive appropriate Medicaid coverage," Ebelt said.
Montana instituted a three-month grace period for the work requirements. State officials won't begin disenrolling people for noncompliance until October.
Pamela Herd, a University of Michigan social policy professor who has studied bureaucratic obstacles to public benefits, said convoluted disability cases are common enough for attorneys to specialize in accessing aid.
"When we've designed public programs in ways that people can't figure out whether they're eligible without consulting lawyers, we've done something wrong," Herd said. "That has huge, huge implications for what's to come."
Montana officials have said they'll automatically review medical records that could help patients qualify for an exemption. Even so, the federal guidelines released in June mean patients will probably still face additional steps to guarantee an exemption.
Meanwhile, already overstretched doctors worry they'll face the burden of judging whether someone's illness qualifies them for a work exemption.
Dishong said that between now and October, Montana officials could offer more clarity on how the process will work. She said she's worried the state will end up "with a slow-roll mess" instead.
"This is a problem that's just starting," Dishong said.
As for Hailstone, she's now reapplying for Social Security disability payments. That aid would limit how much she can work. But it would also guarantee access to Medicaid.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

- Sega is partnering with Netflix to bring three of its franchises to the screen: Crazy Taxi, Sonic the Hedgehog, and Stranger Than Heaven.
- Crazy Taxi will be the first to make the jump, followed by an animated Sonic series on Netflix that Sega describes as a “series built for kids.”
- Meanwhile, RGG Studio’s Stranger Than Heaven will get a live-action drama film, with the game itself set to release on January 14, 2027.
Sega is giving its video game library a Hollywood makeover with Netflix adaptations for Crazy Taxi, Sonic, and Stranger Than Heaven. According to Netflix’s press release on its multi-picture deal with Sega, Crazy Taxi is the first adaptation in line. Dan Gregor and Doug Mand, the writing duo behind The Naked Gun 2025 reboot, are writing the project.
An animated Sonic: The Hedgehog series is the next in Sega and Netflix’s lineup of video game adaptations. Toru Nakahara, head producer at Sega, has urged viewers to “Expect something cute yet cool for ‘Sonic.”
Meanwhile, according to the Netflix press release, the live-action Stranger Than Heaven adaptation will be an action drama adapting RGG Studio’s 2027 title.
“Great games already have what every adaptation is chasing — characters people love, worlds they know by heart, and fandoms that show up,” said Brandon Riegg, the VP of Nonfiction and Transmedia at Netflix, about the deal with Sega.
He added, “With Crazy Taxi, Sonic, and STRANGER THAN HEAVEN, we get to work across three completely different eras of SEGA’s catalog, celebrating everything fans love, while introducing them to new audiences.”
Original Film’s Neal H. Moritz and Toby Ascher and Sega’s Toru Nakahara, the producers behind the Crazy Taxi movie, have also commented on Netflix and Sega’s relationship, saying, “This film is for anyone who’s spent hours behind the wheel of a yellow cab on their Dreamcast, with the music cranked up, smashing through everything in sight just to make the next fare.”
On the other hand, the animated Sonic Netflix series will be a “high-voltage, comedic, yet emotionally grounded series built for kids who want to feel a little edge, a little attitude, and a lot of ‘that’s my crew’ wish fulfillment”, Sega revealed.
All three franchises have recently been in the spotlight. Sonic recently joined Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4, while the closed beta for Crazy Taxi World Tour just wrapped up. Meanwhile, Stranger Than Heaven remains on track to launch on January 14, 2027.

Elon Musk is seemingly done attacking Apple over its decision to integrate ChatGPT into iPhone features.
Back in 2024, when the partnership was first announced, Musk slammed the integration as an agreement from Apple to let OpenAI install “creepy spyware” on users’ devices. The next year, he sued, claiming the partnership gave the firms a “monopoly” on Apple users’ AI prompts, which allegedly harmed competition in both smartphone and chatbot markets.
For Musk, the fight with Apple seemingly escalated after he believed that his chatbot, Grok, was perhaps being illegally blocked from topping Apple’s App Store rankings. Last August, he claimed that “Apple is behaving in a manner that makes it impossible for any AI company besides OpenAI to reach #1 in the App Store, which is an unequivocal antitrust violation.”
However, on Monday, Musk confirmed in a court filing that he has resolved all claims against Apple. The filing does not indicate if there were any negotiated settlement terms or otherwise explain why X would suddenly seek a voluntary dismissal. What is clear is that Musk agreed to never raise the claims again against Apple, while notably refusing to drop the same claims against OpenAI.
Now, it seems that Musk plans to advance claims that OpenAI relied on the deal—which Apple emphasized was never exclusive—to monopolize the chatbot market.
OpenAI has already slammed Musk’s lawsuit as another attempt to harass the AI company as Musk’s rival AI firm, now called SpaceXAI, races to catch up. Last fall, OpenAI mocked Musk’s claims as baseless, emphasizing that Musk won’t even “hazard a guess” at what portion of the chatbot market is being foreclosed by the OpenAI/Apple deal. Instead, Musk claimed it could be anywhere from 0 to 55 percent, based on “back-of-the-envelope math” that OpenAI thinks the court should reject.

Everyone knows that when you’re at Olive Garden, you’re family.
But in the 44 years since the casual Italian-American restaurant chain was founded, few have embraced it with the ardor that Braden Sinclair has. In fact, way back in his Little League days, a coach named him “Breadsticks.”
“I had to go to Olive Garden for my birthday, ate too much, missed an entire game,” Sinclair tells WIRED. “One of my coaches decided that because of my initials being B.S., and my number being 11—which he said looked like breadsticks—and then that story, that I had to be called ‘Breadsticks’ for the rest of the season.”
He maintained that close relationship with the chain for many years, until, in 2019, he was rewarded with an almost unfathomable distinction: Sinclair is one of just 50 human beings on the planet to ever secure an Olive Garden Lifetime Pasta Pass.
Unlike the thousands of 13-week Never Ending Pasta Passes that the chain has offered at various intervals since 2014—this summer, a batch of 10,000, priced at $100 apiece, sold out within seconds—Sinclair’s heavy gold card bears no expiration date. It entitles him to as much pasta, toppings, breadsticks, and soup or salad as he cares to eat, for as long as the chain endures and he remains a loyal customer. (No delivery, though, to be clear. A pasta bowl so bottomless demands that one take a seat of honor for the dine-in experience.)
How exactly does Sinclair wield his kingly rights at Olive Garden? All is revealed on his new website, Lifetimepastapass.com, where he crunches the many numbers—both financial and dietary—on his many meals there. And, with a continually updated poll that decides what he should order the next time he drops in, it’s easily the closest you’ll ever get to having the lifetime pass yourself.
Sinclair nabbed his license to feast during a special promotion, when Olive Garden announced that the first 50 people to buy a temporary pasta pass would have the opportunity to upgrade it to the lifetime pass for an extra $400. To this day, Sinclair wonders if his timing was really that good or if the company deliberately selected him to receive the ultimate prize.
“I had sort of a joking relationship with their Instagram for years, just like chatting back and forth,” he explains, adding that it felt a little “weird” and something like “divine intervention” that he won given his coziness with the brand. An Olive Garden vice president of marketing FaceTimed him with the good news, he recalls.
Reactions to the card from Olive Garden employees range from awe to confusion. “They always take it back to the kitchen, show it to people,” Sinclair says. “Managers will come out and ask questions. The other end of the spectrum has been having to kind of prove it's real, which is rare, and I totally understand. Like, if I managed a restaurant and someone came in with a gold card that said I don't need to pay, I would also have questions.”
Now a 33-year-old father of two young kids, Sinclair doesn’t gorge on heaping plates of carbohydrates the way he used to (and, since frequenting Olive Garden makes him more conscientious about the rest of his diet, he’s avoided packing on the pounds). But he says the Lifetime Pasta Pass somewhat justifies his continued fixation on the restaurant, which was a familiar comfort when his family temporarily relocated from Maine to Wisconsin during his childhood. In 2016, he paid homage to the place with a tattoo of its famous rotary cheese grater; the caption reads “SAY WHEN.” He also began collecting vintage T-shirts that the chain had released in the 1980s and 1990s.
This year, Sinclair unveiled the project that brought all of his Olive Garden experiences together in one place. Lifetimepastapass.com documents his “infinite tour of Italy” by showcasing not only his backstory and extensive merch collection but all the data you could ever want about how he has used his rare privilege: number of restaurant visits since 2019 (112), bowls of pasta eaten (152), calories consumed (154,817), meal value ($1,878.87) and total tips ($607.00).
You can also keep tabs on a map of which locations Sinclair has tried—while the South Portland, Maine, restaurant is his home base, he has ventured up and down the Eastern Seaboard. Other charts show his most favored pasta type (rigatoni), sauce (alfredo), and topping (crispy chicken fritta), as well as the monthly frequency of his Olive Garden visits; he dined there nine times in August, the most since he set a personal record of 20 visits in October 2019, shortly after winning the pass.
With a decade of experience in data analytics and visualization, Sinclair saw all this as a fun application of his talents. But he also wanted people to have “skin in the game,” as he puts it—so he built a dashboard where anyone can vote on the combination of ingredients that make up his next pasta order.
“I thought it was just gonna be a joke among my friends,” Sinclair says. “You know, share it on Instagram, so maybe 10 of my friends would go in and vote, and then the next day five, and then the third day no one would care, and it would be over.” Instead, after he shared the project on a couple of subreddits, he was stunned to tally over 700 votes on his next meal. He wound up eating angel hair with spicy alfredo (a new sauce offering) and crispy shrimp fritta.
“A big reason why I wanted to do this is I just kept getting rigatoni with alfredo, five-cheese marinara, and crispy chicken, like on repeat,” Sinclair says. “I was like, ‘I need to branch out.’” His best discovery so far? “I realized that alfredo and meatballs is an insane combination,” he says. “It's so good.”
In some ways, Lifetimepastapass.com is a reflection of Sinclair’s belief that the card comes with great responsibility. Besides tipping diligently, he also skips the refills, aiming to be a “respectful” and “low-impact” diner who doesn’t flaunt his status or make a shift harder for staff. “I see some pictures of people with the [regular] pasta passes who go crazy,” he says. “Bowls full of grated Parmesan just because they can.” Meticulously tracking his own Olive Garden journey toward various virtual “trophies” earned by hitting benchmarks in categories such as “lifetime breadsticks eaten” (he’ll reach the bronze level at 100, gold at 1,000) and “longest streaks of consecutive weeks with at least one visit” seems, by comparison, a kind of reverence for the institution.
If there’s an unexpected downside to the Lifetime Pasta Pass, it may be a certain loneliness at the top. Because Covid-19 hit shortly after people claimed the cards, the promotion has been largely memory-holed, and whatever plans Olive Garden could have had to celebrate or connect the winners were never realized. Sinclair has stumbled upon only a couple of other passholders via social media and has no idea how often others may go to the restaurant these days.
Meanwhile, it’s not always easy to convince your pals to meet up at a restaurant just because you eat there for free. “There's only so many times I can go sit at the Olive Garden by myself,” Sinclair says. “I have some friends who are nice enough to go with me, but oftentimes they’ll just kind of sit there and eat some breadsticks.” And though Sinclair’s wife is an admitted fan of the chain—she’s eaten there with him since their high school days and promised in her wedding vows to go whenever he wants—he finds it “wisest” to seek alternatives whenever they manage a kids-free date night.
The good news is that Sinclair’s 4-year-old is a likely Olive Garden devotee in the making. “I'll probably start bringing my oldest son a little more just because he's obsessed with pasta,” he says. “I think he'll genuinely enjoy it.”
Just not before a Little League game, of course.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

The precise composition of ancient Egyptian paints, binders, adhesives, and similar materials used to make artifacts is largely unknown, in part because a full analysis would require taking samples that would damage those valuable artifacts. The development of cutting-edge, non-destructive techniques has been helping to unlock those secrets, aiding conservation efforts.
Most recently, researchers have used mass spectrometry-based proteomics to analyze the glues and adhesives in a broad set of Egyptian artifacts, according to a new paper published in the journal Science Advances. They found plenty of expected sources, such as animal collagens and egg proteins, but also plant proteins, specifically from sesame and drumstick tree (moringa) cereals.
As previously reported, the ancient Egyptians had a highly formalized (and easily recognizable) painting style, and there has been considerable interest in gaining insights into the specific pigments and painting techniques employed. Common pigments included hematite and realgar for red; goethite and orpiment for yellow; Egyptian blue; Egyptian green; carbon-based black; and calcite, gypsum, anhydrite, and huntite for white. (Just last year, Washington State University researchers were able to re-create Egyptian blue by mixing together silicon dioxide, copper, calcium, and sodium carbonate in varying proportions and heating them at very high temperatures akin to those of ancient kilns.)
Many pigments available to ancient Egyptian artists have elemental markers detectable by X-ray fluorescence imaging. Macro-XRF imaging in particular has previously been used (in combination with hyperspectral imaging) to study a Greco-Roman painted funerary portrait from the second century CE, as well as to determine the remnants of color on marble at Delphi in Greece. In 2023, scientists used a portable MA-XRF imaging device to study ancient Egyptian paintings, part of a broader project investigating tomb chapels in the Theban Necropolis.

"I am ready to join hands. I am ready to form an alliance. Today is the time to talk. Don't cry later after the elections are over. We don't want the BJP to come to power again.”
Asaduddin Owaisi, AIMIM
That was Asaduddin Owaisi's outreach-cum-warning to Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav in July at a rally in Moradabad while he launched AIMIM’s campaign for the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections due early next year.Seeking alliance with opposition parties is now a part of Owaisi’s playbook to counter allegations of being a vote-cutter and the B-team of the BJP. We have seen AIMIM adopt similar strategy in other states like Maharashtra and Bihar. In both these states, it went all out to seek space in larger opposition alliances before deciding to contest on its own when its offer was rejected. Then the "rejection: became a part of Owaisi's campaign: we asked you to come in, you kept us out, so don't blame us for what happens next."So, when Owaisi reached out to Samajwadi Party in July, it was on expected lines and did not come as a surprise. But there is now a twist in the tale.Owaisi’s Uttar Pradesh plans suffered a jolt this month when one of his most trusted aides and the party’s national spokesperson Syed Asim Waqar dumped the party to join the Congress.Waqar, who rose to prominence defending the AIMIM and its politics, was a prominent voice for AIMIM in Uttar Pradesh and hence his crossing over to the Congress potentially impacts Owaisi's bid to make electoral inroads in UP.
But more than his exit, it was his parting remarks that will bother Owaisi. “Being in the AIMIM for so many years, I felt that we pay lip service by stating that the BJP must be removed, but on the ground, we don't fight the BJP; we fight the Congress, the SP; we are fighting every other person who wants to remove the BJP,” Waqar said when asked about his decision to leave the AIMIM.Justifying his switch, Waqar said, “If we (AIMIM) keep fighting the opposition and do not allow it to blossom, then we are helping the BJP. I have decided that if we are true nationalists and want to remove the BJP honestly, then our objective should be to fight the BJP. If we are fighting the enemies of the BJP, then we are friends of the BJP. In reality, if someone is fighting the BJP across the country, it is Congress, Rahul Gandhi and his team."Now, this is precisely the point which the opposition parties make against Owaisi and his AIMIM.
AIMIM’s UP plans
Uttar Pradesh has been a difficult story for Owaisi. His AIMIM failed to win a single seat in the 2022 assembly elections in the state. And that makes the 2027 challenge a real test of whether the Bihar formula will work or whether Akhilesh is right to believe that AIMIM is a rival he can afford to ignore.Even while offering to join hands with Akhilesh, Owaisi chose to kick off AIMIM's 2027 campaign from Matera in Bahraich, a seat held by the Samajwadi Party. He also announced AIMIM’s candidate from the seat making his intent very clear.Owaisi questioned what SP leaders had done for the area despite getting Muslim votes, while saying AIMIM was ready for an alliance only if it was treated with 'respect' and given 'equal status'.The party has dropped enough signals to suggest that it is preparing for a much bigger push in UP in 2027. The party has also divided the state into zones and appointed regional in-charges as part of its attempt to strengthen the organisation before the election.AIMIM accepted that its performance was not up to the mark in 2022 but asserted that the party has spent the last few years trying to correct that.
Bihar is AIMIM’s strongest base outside Telangana.
AIMIM's Uttar Pradesh president Shaukat Ali has said the party could contest around 200 seats if it fights alone. He has also kept the door open for a possible understanding with the BSP."Our natural alliance, if we were to forge one, would be with the BSP. Muslims and Dalits together account for nearly 40% of the vote share, enough to defeat both the SP and BJP," Ali said.The Samajwadi Party and the Congress will keep a close watch on AIMIM’s BSP outreach as it can have the potential to disrupt a lot of political calculations in the state. However, for now Mayawati has made it clear that her BSP will not forge any alliances with any party for elections.
What makes UP challenge both interesting and difficult
The 2027 assembly elections in UP is likely to see a very keen contest for Muslim votes. The switching of sides by Asim Waqar exposes the keen contest among the non-BJP parties for support of Muslims in the upcoming elections.
Non-Yadav OBCs form the biggest bloc in UP’s caste arithmetic.
The Congress, which would consider this AIMIM import as a big boost to its prospects, had contested the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in alliance with the Samajwadi Party, and, as of now, they are both part of INDIA bloc ahead of next year’s assembly elections.But this alliance has not stopped the two parties from taking measures to consolidate their individual support bases. Last month, the Samajwadi Party got a boost when the son-in-law of Congress MP from UP’s Saharanpur Imran Masood joined the party in the presence of Akhilesh Yadav. Imran Masood has been very vocal against SP and its chief Akhilesh Yadav accusing them of imposing as the ‘big-brother’ in SP-Congress alliance for the 2027 UP polls.For the SP, the Alpsankhyaks (read Muslims) form an important component of Akhilesh Yadav’s PDA outreach. In fact, his success in Uttar Pradesh till now has been largely powered by the Yadavs and the Muslims. And while, Akhilesh desperately tries to broaden his support base by reaching out to the Dalits, women and even the Pandits, he cannot make big gains without the support of Muslims.However, that does not stop the Congress from making its own outreach to the community in a bid to try and win them back. After all, for several decades the Muslims had contributed to the electoral success of the Congress. It was only with the rise of regional parties that they drifted away from the grand-old-party. So, it will naturally be happy with Asim Waqar on its side.The AIMIM, which is the third pole of Muslim politics in the state, will try to take advantage of the posturing and war of words between the two alliance partners as it tries to find its space in the state.AIMIM has shown that it can become a serious player where its support is concentrated. What it has not yet shown is that it can do the same in Uttar Pradesh, where the Samajwadi Party remains the main beneficiary of Muslim votes against the BJP.
Where AIMIM matters and where it doesn't
In the 2023 Telangana assembly election, the party contested nine seats and won seven, underlining how strong its hold remains in parts of the state.Bihar has been its most successful experiment outside Telangana till now. The party managed to win five seats in 2020 and repeated the number in 2025, mainly in the Seemanchal region.In Maharashtra, AIMIM has pockets of support but won just one assembly seat in 2024. In Uttar Pradesh, the challenge has been tougher. In the 2022 assembly election, AIMIM contested 96 seats but failed to win any. Its statewide vote share remained below 1%.
AIMIM’s Rajasthan experiment
Owaisi’s move to contest the Panchayat and Municipal body elections in Rajasthan shows the party’s intent to expand its base in states where it was not a player till now. The AIMIM chief maintains that the state needs a strong third political alternative apart from the ruling BJP and the Congress which have been the dominant players in state’s politics till now.In a bid to disturb the duoploy, Owaisi has announced that if Rashtriya Loktantrik Party chief Hanuman Beniwal emerges as a third force, the AIMIM will support him and work together to challenge both major political parties.Owaisi said, “Hanuman Beniwal and AIMIM together will make the lives of BJP and Congress leaders difficult.” He also appealed to voters to support AIMIM candidates and RLP candidates contesting elections on the party’s bottle symbol.
The BJP would be smiling either way
While the Congress and the other opposition parties keep an eye on AIMIM’s political moves, the BJP perhaps would not be worried much.When Owaisi had reached out to Akhilesh, BJP wasted no time in mocking the proposal. Former BJP spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla had then called it a 'friend request' to Akhilesh and accused both parties of vote-bank politics.
Akhilesh Yadav and Owaisi have long competed in appeasement politics. Now they have set aside the contest over who will be the bigger 'bhaijaan' and are looking at a 'bhaijaan collaboration'. Owaisi is effectively sending Akhilesh ji a friend request. They are two sides of the same coin
Asaduddin Owaisi, AIMIM
For the BJP, Owaisi can be useful either way, more so in Uttar Pradesh.If AIMIM contests separately and takes away even a small number of votes from SP-Congress in close seats, the BJP may benefit. If AIMIM joins the alliance, the BJP can use Owaisi's presence to sharpen its attack on the opposition over minority appeasement.
Catch-22 for opposition parties
The opposition parties are reluctant to accept Owaisi’s offer to ensure that non-BJP votes, especially of the Muslims, do not split. They know that Owaisi’s offer is like a double-edged sword.Most of these opposition parties like the RJD in Bihar, Samajwadi Party in Uttar Pradesh have banked heavily on the support of Muslims for their politics. If they accept AIMIM as an ally, they fear that Muslims will back Owaisi and gradually this will weaken their own minorities’ politics.
Second, any opposition alliance with AIMIM will give the BJP a very strong weapon to engineer reverse polarisation. Since Owaisi is known for a very aggressive hardline brand of politics on issues concerning the minorities, the opposition will find it difficult to dissociate itself from the AIMIM. And this will give the BJP an opportunity to mobilise the Hindus against the opposition parties and eventually corner them.

AstraZeneca disclosed that a breast cancer pill failed in a pivotal trial testing it as a first-line therapy in advanced tumors, a result that could limit the use of the medicine, STAT notes. The drug, camizestrant, in combination with another medicine did not outperform standard treatment on a measure of how long patients went before their cancer progressed. The drug earlier this month won accelerated approval in the U.S. as a treatment for patients who develop a mutation in their tumors that’s a sign of emerging drug resistance. Had the trial been successful, it could have opened up a much larger market for the drug.
Scholar Rock received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the first-ever therapy that targets the loss of muscle in spinal muscle atrophy, raising hopes that patients with the rare neurological disorder might have a better chance of moving and walking independently, STAT writes. The FDA approved the drug, Isembyld, for use in adults and children 2 years and older who are currently receiving SMA therapies that target SMN2, a key gene for neurons that control movement. The approval marks another step forward for patients with spinal muscular atrophy, a rare and progressive disease that destroys nerve cells that control speaking, breathing, and walking. Babies who go untreated usually die by the age of 2.

New Delhi: Crude prices extended their rally on Monday after talks between Iran and other West Asian countries on operations in the Strait of Hormuz were postponed, while attacks by Houthi militia on a Saudi airbase added to concerns about further conflict in the Red Sea region.
The November contract of Brent crude on the Intercontinental Exchange was at $109 a barrel at around 6.40 pm, up 4.20% from its previous close. The October contract of West Texas Intermediate rose 4.42% to $104.47 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Al Jazeera reported that the Houthis had taken control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, consolidating their hold over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key chokepoint for maritime traffic in the region. The waterway handles about 12% of global trade, including 11% of maritime oil trade.
Yemen’s Houthis said they launched a large-scale ballistic missile and drone attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, according to Al Jazeera. Last week, the Houthi militia captured the Red Sea city of Mocha, widening its hold over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Separately, negotiations in Oman between Iran and Gulf Arab states were postponed at the request of some regional countries, according to Iranian media. The postponement followed an attack on an Iranian commercial cargo vessel that killed one person in the Strait of Hormuz.
The escalating hostilities in West Asia are raising the risk of supply disruptions, threatening to increase India’s crude import bill while adding to inflationary and fiscal pressures.
India, which imports about 90% of its crude oil, remains particularly exposed to sustained price increases. Estimates by Bank of Baroda show that a persistent $1 increase in crude prices can raise the country’s annual import bill by around ₹18,000 crore. At about $120 billion annually, India’s oil import bill accounts for about 17% to 25% of its total merchandise imports.
The pressure was building even before the latest surge. India’s crude oil import bill for the April-July period reached $63.37 billion, up 56% from a year earlier, and already represents more than half of the total oil import expenditure in the preceding financial year.
In August, India’s retail inflation rose to a 20-month high of 4.82%, driven by higher fuel and food prices, taking it above the Reserve Bank of India’s 4% target midpoint for the third consecutive month since January 2025. Wholesale inflation also edged up to 9.92% in August from 9.78% in July, according to government data released on Monday.
S&P Global Energy, in a recent analysis, said that prospects for a definitive resolution to the Iran conflict had dimmed and crude oil markets were settling into a prolonged new normal in which disruption risks are persistent rather than episodic.
It added that crude oil production in West Asia is unlikely to return to pre-war levels by the end of 2027.
As a result, West Asian crude oil and condensate exports are now expected to average about 10 million to 16 million barrels a day on a monthly basis through 2027, compared with about 20 million barrels a day before the war in January-February 2026. S&P Global Energy projected that crude oil prices would remain in the $80-$100-a-barrel range through 2027, with Dated Brent averaging around $90 or higher for the rest of 2026 and $86 next year.

KSEB seeks nod to buy additional power at higher price amid Keralam power crisis
Kozhikode , The KSEB has decided to approach the state government seeking permission to procure additional power at higher prices to meet the rising demand amid a power shortage in the state, Electricity Minister Sunny Joseph said on Sunday.
Keralam has been experiencing power outages, particularly at night, amid a sharp rise in consumption and difficulties for the Kerala State Electricity Board in procuring additional electricity from other states.
"We are currently exploring all options to procure as much power as possible from central government institutions and other states. Even if it means buying at a higher price, permission should be granted by the state," Joseph told reporters here.
He said he would write to the chief minister seeking permission to purchase additional electricity at higher prices and a similar request would be made to the Kerala State Electricity Regulatory Commission.
KSEB board members will also visit other states and hold discussions with electricity department officials there to explore the possibility of arranging additional power supply to Keralam, he said.
"The CM has granted permission for it. I have spoken with the KSEB Chairman regarding this, and the board members are also ready," Joseph said, adding that he would not elaborate on the proposed visits at this stage.
Asked whether solar power could be an option, he said it was worth considering.
"We have solar production, but the mechanism to store and process it for nighttime use-like Battery Energy Storage Systems-has not become effective yet. We will think about ways to encourage and bring everyone into it. They need to be given incentives," he said.
He also said the state is prepared to purchase electricity generated by consumers for nighttime supply at a higher price.
"This period has brought difficulties that compel everyone to think. A new policy is needed-a policy aimed at increasing production," he said.
The minister also appealed to the public to avoid unnecessary electricity consumption and said the current situation required responsible use of available power.
He said former minister V M Sudheeran had drawn his attention to street lights remaining switched on during the day.
Joseph said street lighting was mostly managed by local self-government bodies and not directly by the KSEB.
He also urged people to reduce unnecessary decorative lighting at night.
"When a resource is scarce, if we understand our limits and use it carefully, there will be some change," he said.
The minister said the KSEB and state government should not be blamed for the present power shortage.
He also said the current crisis could have been avoided if the long-term power purchase agreement signed during the Oommen Chandy government had continued.
According to Joseph, the Electricity Regulatory Commission had decided to scrap the agreement, while the previous LDF government decided to challenge the decision only after six months, by which time the supplier had withdrawn from the agreement.

As calls for artificial intelligence regulation intensify, US President Donald Trump’s team have made it clear that if lab leaders want to implement an industry-wide slowdown, they’re going to have to do it themselves.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called on the US government to regulate AI companies within a wider effort to slow the pace of the technology’s development in an essay published Saturday. The essay received rare endorsement from both OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns chatbot Grok, following a week of intense debate about the technology’s threats to human safety. Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella also called for pacing development.
Calls for AI slowdown and regulation have intensified after a number of researchers voiced major concerns in the last week about the speed of the technology’s advance. “AI progress is increasing,” former DeepMind researcher Rishub Jain told WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.”
But David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wrote on X, “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel … Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”
Amodei had requested the government enable competing AI companies to work together on standards without breaching antitrust law, either by participating in discussions or issuing a waiver for the companies involved. He also called for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party, though critics wondered how effective this would be. “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know,” Sacks wrote.
Concerns about the US ceding its lead in the technology to China have caused the US government to mostly push back against the notion of slowing the pace of its development. “You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We’re leading China on AI,” he added, “and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
The US largely views China’s AI ecosystem as an economic and national security threat, and has previously been caught short by the country’s advances in the technology. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday. “So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel.”
In the meantime, companies say they are going to start taking voluntary steps to reestablish public trust that they are acting responsibly. On Sunday night, OpenAI’s Altman committed to a proposal by Amodei to give embedded third party evaluators employee-level access to their firms to check practices and products were safe, and report incidents. While these measures will have “significant costs,” he wrote on X: “Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”

I cannot overstate the importance of having an air purifier that not only has enough power to actually purify a room's air but also caters to your home's particular needs. Pollutants like wildfire smoke, pollen, unventilated gas stoves, pet allergens, and even litter box odors can be potentially harmful additions to the air you breathe in your home.
Air purifiers from Coway have been a consistent top pick in our guide to the Best Air Purifiers for years, including the Coway Airmega Mighty2, which was released in March this year. Its predecessor, the Coway Airmega Mighty, had been our reigning “Best Affordable Air Purifier” for many years as well. I was excited to test the newest mid-size option built for medium to large rooms in Coway's Airmega line, where it sits between the compact Airmega 50 or 100 and the higher-capacity 350 or 450 models.
Released at the end of August, Coway’s Airmega Halo is an affordable, lightweight air purifier that aims to deliver whole-room air purification at an accessible price point. Plus, its focus is on promoting a healthier night's sleep with smart sleep features and quiet noise levels when in sleep mode.
Overall, it delivers on most of its promises, but I ran into some problems during field-testing that made me question its sensor, and I wish it had more transparency with pollutant levels.
Simple Design That’s Maybe Too Simple
The Halo is only 9.7 pounds, making it lightweight and portable as far as air purifiers go, but it doesn't have accessibility features like a top handle or wheels for easier moving. It has a small cutout in the back to grip, but because I have an upper-limb disability, moving it was awkward—I essentially had to hug the purifier to maneuver it, since I don't have large hands that can easily grip the inlet.
The purifier's cylindrical design with a 360-degree air-intake structure draws in polluted air from all sides, making for fewer spatial constraints and more options for placement around the home. The inside of the machine uses Coway's HyperVortex filtration system, which is an aerodynamic fan and duct design that Coway states is “inspired by eagle wings and golf ball dimples.” It uses wing blades to stabilize airflow, along with aerodynamic blades for powerful airflow for the generator fan and dimples to reduce air resistance for smoother air intake.
Setup was extremely easy—I just needed to unscrew the bottom, remove the filter from the plastic protective covering, screw the bottom back on, and plug it in. There's no need for a Wi-Fi connection, no app, and no remote. I started testing air purifiers earlier this year, and I've found I actually like having a connected remote, or better yet, an app that allows me to monitor air quality and adjust settings from afar. This model had neither. I also appreciate getting transparent numbers of pollutant levels directly from the machine rather than relying on colored lights, but this machine had the latter.

Pennsylvania says an unvaccinated woman has died from measles-related complications
An official in Pennsylvania has confirmed the measles-related death of a 40-year-old woman. Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong told NPR that the woman, who died on Saturday, was unvaccinated.
"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," a statement from the coroner's office said.
Officials have not released the woman's identity, but said she was a resident of Jefferson County. This is the third death that Pennsylvania state officials have linked to measles this year. No other states have announced measles deaths in 2026.
On Friday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 676 measles cases so far this year. It also reported 52 new positive cases from Wednesday to Friday.
Pennsylvania officials and the federal government have clashed over the number of measles-associated deaths in the state in recent weeks, as the U.S. faces a nationwide resurgence of the illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared that the highly contagious virus had been eradicated from the U.S. in 2000.
Last week, the CDC reported more than 3,200 confirmed measles cases in the country.
The agency said it was reviewing whether to count two measles-related deaths involving infants in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. After Gov. Josh Shapiro announced the state's first two deaths, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said on X the announcement appeared to have been "premature" and "may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers."
This clash is notable, as NPR's Rob Stein has reported. "The CDC usually defers to the state's determination" of cause of death in this kind of outbreak, "so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country."
The CDC lists the number of measles cases reported in each state for 2026, as well as the number of hospitalizations. The agency has not listed the number of deaths for this year. Instead of giving a figure, there is an asterisk that explains: "The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause."
Kennedy has said on X that NCHS "will update as it receives and reviews submitted records."
The Jefferson County Coroner's Office also emphasized measles can lead to severe complications at any age.
"While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly," said Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver in a statement. "Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community."
The county coroner's office is working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. Pennsylvania and South Carolina have the highest numbers of confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to federal data.

Defense agencies of Mexico and the US have announced they are implementing a new collaborative strategy to combat drones used by criminal organizations. The operation, dubbed High Eagle, or Águila Alta, builds on recent tests of anti-drone technologies carried out along the border between the two countries.
The first phase of the strategy took place between August 31 and September 2 along the border between San Diego and Tijuana, Mexico. Initially, both military forces—simultaneously on the ground from their respective territories—tracked commercial drones used by criminal entities. In the second phase, the agencies neutralized the unmanned aerial vehicles, with support from fixed and mobile anti-drone systems. These activities began on September 7 and will continue through September 21.
The information released by Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense, known as SEDENA, does not specify the kind of technology involved in the mission. However, US Northern Command has suggested that the operation might employ high-energy lasers. These extremely concentrated beams of light can—in various phases—detect, track, illuminate, damage, or destroy drones from a distance.
The US Army has invested in a particular laser system known as the Locust platform, which is designed for mounting on military vehicles. Authorities have had this technology at their disposal since September of last year, when the company that produces the system, AeroVironment, delivered the first two functional prototypes to the Armed Forces.
So far, it has not been confirmed that these systems are being used in Operation High Eagle, though the Mexican authorities have increased access to these state-of-the-art weapons. Last month, SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement allowing the Mexican military to access the US Army’s digital marketplace for acquiring anti-drone systems at competitive prices.
Representatives from both countries have stated that the aim of this new operation and recent agreements is to strengthen efforts against organized crime, especially human and drug trafficking. Earlier this month, the US Northern Command announced it had disabled or destroyed approximately 300 drones linked to criminal activity this year, a third of which were taken down in August. Within recent weeks, 11 of the targets were involved with cartels.
The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group. According to SEDENA, it aims to ensure security on both sides of the border, while respecting the national sovereignty of both nations and “prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times.”
The US ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, stated that the agreement would strengthen both countries’ ability to combat cartels and address bilateral security challenges.
