Kharge slams BJP’s demand for action against inspector
Home Minister Priyank Kharge defends police actions over Ganesh procession routes, amid BJP protests, emphasizing safety and adherence to regulations.
State home minister Priyank Kharge on Monday hit back at the state BJP’s ongoing campaign to seek action against T Narasipura police inspector Dhananjaya, who warned organisers of a local Ganpati procession against proceeding towards a mosque on Link Road at a peace meeting on September 7.
Kharge said the government would wait for a report from the superintendent of police before taking a call on the matter. “(LoP R) Ashoka was the home minister, wasn’t he? Didn’t he conduct such meetings? Didn’t Basavaraj Bommai do the same? Have I changed anything after coming here? The rules Ashoka had put in place are the same rules that exist today,” he said.
The dispute followed a peace meeting on September 7, where Dhananjaya warned organisers against taking a Ganesh procession towards a mosque on Link Road and bursting crackers there.
HT has seen a widely-circulated clip of the briefing.
“A festival should be celebrated like a festival. When people of other religions see you celebrating, they should be happy for you and respect it as your festival, just as you would respect their festivals, right?” he told the organisers.
“Instead of that, do not go and stand in front of a mosque and burst firecrackers. If we find this happening this time, I will take strict action. Understood?” the inspector added.
The briefing largely focused on ensuring that organisers adhered to the plans submitted to police. He said the procession route had to be specified beforehand and followed.
Regulations on sound systems and food preparation alsofeatured prominently. An orchestra could be held, he said, but not with a DJ-type sound system. For immersion, DJ vehicles and DJ songs were prohibited. Dhananjaya suggested using traditional instruments including tamate, dolu, nagari and Dollu Kunitha.
For immersion, DJ vehicles and DJ songs were prohibited. Food preparation also came up, with Dhananjaya asking organisers to appoint someone to supervise cooking and keep volunteers at the pandal around the clock.
The BJP staged a protest against the remarks in T Narasipur on Sunday.
The protest was led by Leader of Opposition in the assembly R Ashoka, who was joined by MP Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar, MLA TS Srivatsa, former MP Pratap Simha and other party leaders. Ashoka carried a Ganesh idol and led supporters along Link Road. BJP leaders were detained and later released.
A clip from the inspector’s briefing was widely circulated on social media.
Mysuru superintendent of police Mallikarjuna Baladandi said there was no restriction on either the procession route or the festival. “Organisers could use the traditional routes followed in previous years,” he said.
“Last time during the grand procession, they had not given us information. They went for the procession without informing us. So this time we have just told them to give information and take out the procession. As every year, there is permission for procession on Link Road,” Baladandi said.
The town has about 15 to 20 Ganesh pandals each year. Baladandi said police had asked organisers to provide the dates of immersion and the routes in advance to aid security arrangements.
He said the move followed an incident last year involving a group that allegedly took out an unauthorised procession along a route that passed by a mosque. Officers were unaware of the event and could not make security arrangements, he added.
Ashoka alleged that the government was restricting procession routes, loudspeakers and celebrations near mosques.
“This is not just a Mysuru issue; this is happening across Karnataka,” he said, adding that the Ganesh festival should not become a “police festival”.
Kharge defended police deployment during the festival, saying 80,558 public Ganesh processions were held across the state in 2025, with over 1,02,000 police personnel, home guards and central forces deployed for security.
“Over a lakh uniformed men and women were away from their own families so that we could celebrate the festival with our families. While we were praying, celebrating, dancing and participating in processions, they stood on our roads for hours, managing the crowds, controlling traffic, preventing clashes and ensuring that everyone returned home safely,” said the minister.

A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.
“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.
With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.
Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.
Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”
“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.
Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.
A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.
Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.
Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.
But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.
“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.
“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.
Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.
Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.
“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”
Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.
For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.
Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.
Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.
Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.
Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.
“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”
As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.
César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”
A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

How youth helped Nordqvist answer critics and deliver Solheim Cup win

Anna Nordqvist spoke in the build-up to the Solheim Cup about the European team being in a period of transition as she chose a line-up with four debutants.
Any fears about fielding rookies for the most pressure packed event in the women's game were proven unfounded in her team's thrilling 15-13 victory at Bernardus Golf last weekend.
Nastasia Nadaud (21), Julia Lopez Ramirez (23), Mimi Rhodes (24) and, eventually, Lottie Woad all delivered crucial points and gave an encouraging glimpse into Europe's future.
Three of the quartet were captain's picks, with the 22-year-old Woad the only debut automatic qualifier for the team that avenged defeat in Virginia two years ago.
"So many people said it was a bit of a risk having four rookies, but I was so impressed with them," Nordqvist said.

  - Published16 hours ago
- Solheim Cup 2026 - scores and results 
  - Published3 days ago
- GB&I make history with first Walker Cup since 2015 
  - Published6 September
'I never felt like they were rookies'
Europe's skipper faced intense scrutiny throughout her captaincy, especially over her stubborn faith in Woad's partnership with fellow Englishwoman Charley Hull.
But she was ultimately vindicated, especially with her wildcard selections, which also included relative veteran Leona Maguire.
Between them they yielded eight and a half points, compared with five contributed by America's three captain's picks. Nordqvist's singles line-up also leant heavily on a willingness to trust in youth.
Of the youngsters tasting Solheim singles action for the first time only Rhodes failed to win and it took a brilliant performance from world number one Nelly Korda to beat her on the final day.
And the beaten Englishwoman had already contributed significantly alongside Nadaud with Friday fourball and Saturday foursomes wins that helped ensure 8-8 parity after the first two days.
In the singles Rhodes was sent out fourth, but it was positions six, seven and eight - Nadaud, Lopez Ramirez and Woad - that held so much significance to the final outcome.
All three delivered vital wins. "What people don't understand is they're so good when they come out on tour these days," Nordqvist said. "They just play fearless and they have so much personality.
"All of the four I had, I never felt like they were rookies. And the first day when I send out Nastasia and Mimi a lot of people questioned why would you send out two rookies, but I said why not. And they delivered.
"They delivered again on Saturday morning. And Sunday too. Mimi took Nelly down to 15. She's the number one player in the world, and she pushed her.
"Rookie Lottie making the winning putt. It's been really fun to have them and they bring out a fresh perspective.
"And I feel really old and I'm glad I'm retiring now because these girls are just so good."
'I said a few words' - Reid rallied Europeans
It fell to Woad to sink the putt that ensured Europe would win, with four matches still to be completed. Her 2&1 triumph over Auston Kim took Europe to 14 points with Carlotta Ciganda already unassailably three up on the 16th tee.
Europe were guaranteed to reach the magic number of 14½ points and there was nothing America could do about it. It should be noted, this was not a great US side with Korda, Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin being head and shoulders above the rest.
Nordqvist's persistent faith in Woad and Hull, playing her two highest ranked players together in the four opening sessions seemed a folly. She insisted stats justified the call, but the partnership never gelled, yielding only half a point.
It was all the more jarring because elsewhere Nordqvist had unmistakably fostered that famed European spirit which so often permeates through Solheim and Ryder Cup successes.
It was crucial in overcoming Jennifer Kupcho's hammer blow long range birdies late on the Saturday evening that allowed the United States to force an unlikely share of the foursomes and fourball spoils.
All the momentum was with the visitors on the Saturday night, but it was soon washed away as the rain drenched Sunday singles began.
"We were on the team bus, I said a few words," said assistant captain Mel Reid of the aftermath of Kupcho's heroics. "The team bus is a special place for Team Europe.
"I think it's where we really unite, we really get together. We put the music on and it's a special place. I'm just glad there are no cameras there.
"But we got to the hotel and we put on a song, and I felt like it changed the mood and united us. It was weird.
"We just forgot what happened, the disappointment, and we just got back on it."
Newcomers soak up Europe's unique bond
After a winless two days there was enormous pressure on Hull and Woad and the former barely missed a shot in an impressive 3&2 win over the tenacious Megan Khang.
The Englishwoman still could not buy a birdie putt on the slow greens but she never gave her opponent a sniff. Woad was equally strong and her decisive role at the end was in keeping with the spectacular start to her pro career.
There are no guarantees in golf, but in Woad, Nadaud, Lopez Ramirez and Rhodes Europe appear to have an exciting nucleus for the trophy defence at Valhalla in 2028.
America need to find something similar, maybe from their recent victorious Curtis Cup team. And, remarkably, that is the only one of the transatlantic trophies that now resides in US hands as the Solheim joins the Ryder and Walker Cups on this side of the pond.
In the Solheim, Europe's newcomers have soaked up the continent's unique bond. It has seeped into their bones and is best summed up by the irrepressible old stager Ciganda.
She might drive you mad with her glacial pace of play, but the veteran Spaniard knows as well as anyone what, for Europe, the Solheim Cup is all about.
"I just love it," Ciganda said. "I love beating the Americans. Yeah, winning for Team Europe, it's the best feeling."

Beijing hits back at Anthropic CEO's call to curb China's AI development
BEIJING — China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday hit back at a call from the head of Anthropic for the U.S. to curb China's artificial intelligence capabilities, which he issued as he argued for a global slowdown on AI development.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on Sept. 24.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in a lengthy essay published on Saturday warned that a "Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world." He called for continuing restrictions on sales of cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking equipment to China in order to keep the U.S.'s AI edge.
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to a question about Amodei's essay by saying that all parties should work together on AI.
"Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance which serves no one's interest," spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press conference on Monday.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump downplayed calls for his administration to step in to slow down AI development, saying that the U.S. was leading China on AI and that "whoever wins AI, wins."
Amodei also predicted that a swarm of AI "agents" could be able to take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that "global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities."
Trump and Xi could discuss AI governance at summit
U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to discuss topics including AI governance with Chinese leader Xi Jinping meeting planned for late September.
Chinese companies have developed powerful AI models that are often cheaper to use than advanced models from U.S.-based companies, even as by some measures, they are just as capable.
China's Xi has called for the setting up of a global AI governance framework among Global South, while pitching China as a pioneer in establishing an open-source AI community.
The head of China's Ministry of State Security has also called for "accelerating the establishment of a system for preventing and managing AI security risks" in a recent article.
Beijing accuses US of trying to hold it back
In an editorial published Sunday, China's state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei's essay as a veiled call to "contain" China. It said that Amodei's essay may appear on the surface to be focused on global AI security, but, that it is "packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a 'Cold War playbook' for the AI sector."
Amodei's essay was published a few days after the FBI, National Security Agency and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint cybersecurity advisory last week, saying Chinese AI developers had engaged in "aggressive, malicious" efforts in extracting, or "distilling," capabilities from some of the most advanced AI models in the U.S. like Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT.
China's Commerce Ministry dismissed the U.S. claims as groundless and said "distillation" has been commonly used by many AI companies. It also said that the U.S. was pursuing a "monopoly of the AI industry."
Both China and the U.S. want "to make sure the other side cannot establish a tech chokepoint over them," said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis.
"So from Beijing's perspective, there is an obvious question: if the U.S. wants China to cooperate on frontier safety while also restricting its access to frontier compute, what exactly does that cooperation look like?" Lee said.

About 70% of the year-to-year variation in winter air pollution across northern India may be explained by the frequency of western disturbances, possibly providing warning of unusually polluted winter months in advance, researchers said.
Western disturbances are storm systems that travel eastwards from the Mediterranean region towards South Asia by strengthening vertical ventilation and bringing precipitation that helps clear accumulated pollution, including PM2.5, from the air.
The team said winters with more frequent western disturbances tend to experience lower air pollution levels, while winters with fewer of these storms are more susceptible to persistent severe pollution.
"Currently, many of the most disruptive air-pollution measures are taken only after severe pollution is already developing," lead author Yuanyu Xie, an associate research scholar at Princeton University's School of Public and International Affairs, U.S., said.
"If scientists can anticipate the overall severity of the coming winter months ahead of time, governments, businesses, and communities will have more time to prepare," Ms. Xie said.
They also found that the frequency of western disturbances is linked to ocean temperature patterns already evident during the preceding autumn.
The team said the overall severity of winter pollution in north India may thus be predicted about a season in advance. Air pollution levels across northern India, including Delhi-NCR, spike during the winter season, increasing residents' health risks.
A combination of vehicle emissions, stubble burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and weather patterns that trap pollutants close to the ground is attributed to the seasonal spike in pollution.
Emergency measures, including pausing construction, restricting industries and limiting traffic, are implemented on severe pollution days, but may be a challenge if put in place on short notice.
The researchers said seasonal forecasts could indicate whether the coming winter is likely to have relatively severe or mild pollution levels overall, rather than predicting pollution levels for a particular day months in advance, thereby offering a more practical approach.
The information could provide a lead time, allowing authorities to strengthen enforcement before the pollution season begins, coordinate responses across jurisdictions, and give businesses more time to prepare for potential restrictions, they said.
"Emission controls will remain of paramount importance," co-author Denise Mauzerall, a professor of public and international affairs and civil and environmental engineering at Princeton University, said.
"However, we show that forecasts of winter pollution based on observations from the previous autumn can allow additional pollution controls to be arranged in advance of extreme pollution periods. This could provide time to plan and implement cost-effective controls that mitigate peak pollution concentrations in winter in northern India," Ms. Mauzerall said.
The authors wrote, "Nearly 70% of the inter-annual variations in winter PM2.5 pollution across northern India are explained by western disturbances (WDs) — prevailing extratropical storms originating from the Mediterranean region — through PM2.5 removal via enhanced ventilation and precipitation."

Srinagar, Sep 14: Salman Khan showered full praise on Kashmiri contestant Qazi Tauqeer, during the latest episode of Bigg Boss 20, saying, "There’s only one rockstar amongst you all. Qazi Touqeer, the entire week you played quite well."
Although, this season, Big Boss 20, receives mixed reaction- mostly criticism- ove an underwhelming cast, however Fame Gurukul 2005 winner, Qazi Touqeer has emerged as one of the show’s most talked-about contestants, earning overwhelming praise from host Salman Khan during the season’s first Weekend Ka Vaar.
“Let me tell you guys, no matter how many stars exist in this house, there’s only one rockstar amongst you all. Qazi Touqeer, the entire week you played quite well.” Salman Khan said on Tauqeer's performance.
Putting the spotlight on Qazi, Salman later asked Qazi, “Tell me one thing: you got everything in life so soon; you became a rockstar, did a show with Arijit Singh, you won the show. Arijit is doing so well right now. You got this platform now, but what did you do in the last 20 years?” Qazi replied, “I did a lot of live shows.”
Further, Salman further said Qazi Tauqeer that people initially wondered how he sang and now "they cannot stop praising you now".
The bollywood superstar said people appreciate Tauqeer's humor and performance.
Furthermore, comparing Qazi's struggle with Hollywood actor John Travolta and bollwood actor Bobby Deol, Salman Khan said that even the biggest stars today, went through a bad phase, but they never gave up. "Everyone faces ups and downs, and during the downtime, you have to work 10 times harder," he said, adiing that "Sometimes in life, you get a few things very quickly, and you lose them also quickly."
“A good thing about the bad times is that it ends, and when you take good times for granted, as I do sometimes, it also ends. I know that during the bad times, keep working hard, as Qazi Touqeer did. He achieved so much, then he lost it, but he didn’t stop working. Through all your struggles and challenges, the biggest effort was to stay mentally strong, which a lot of people can’t do. So people should learn this from you,” the host added.
Bigg Boss 20 contestant Qazi Touqeer is a singer who rose to fame after participating in the singing reality show Fame Gurukul in 2005. He went on to win the show, reportedly receiving the highest number of votes recorded for a singing reality show at the time. It was during Fame Gurukul that Qazi met Arijit Singh and the two went on to become close friends.

'I've turned the page' - Camara on Chelsea deal collapse
- Published
Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara says he has "turned the page" and is focusing on the Ligue 1 season after his £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.
The 22-year-old had completed a medical but the deal fell through shortly before the transfer window closed.
Two bids had already been rejected, but Monaco lowered their asking price in a turbulent end to the window when it looked likely that Folarin Balogun's move to Everton was in doubt.
When Balogun's transfer appeared to be back on track, Monaco appeared to change their decision to sell Camara, but in the end both players stayed with the Ligue 1 side.
"There was a possibility I could leave," Camara said, speaking before Monaco's game against Strasbourg on Saturday.
"It didn't go through at the last minute and that's part of football. I've turned the page and am focusing on the season."
Sources in France had stated Monaco needed to make a major sale this summer and preferred to sell Balogun. A source at the Ligue 1 club had previously indicated it would take a "substantial fee" to secure Camara's departure.
Monaco have won their first three Ligue 1 fixtures of the season and sat second to Rennes in the table, with a game in hand, heading into the weekend.
"I can help the team a lot," Senegal international Camara said.
"Football moves fast. Maybe other opportunities will come along. But for now, I'm staying focused on the season with Monaco."

In the coming days, the cadre of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] in Keralam may just need a tap on their mobile phones to clear their ideological confusions.
Developing mobile/web applications to keep party activists updated on political issues is among the suggestions put forward by the participants during the open debate of the party’s ongoing extended State committee meeting in Kozhikode.
According to CPI(M) State secretary M.V. Govindan, the proposal is to strengthen the continuous process of ideological education for the party cadre by including modern technological innovations into it. Special web and mobile applications need to be designed for the purpose, he says. “Suppose if comrades have doubts related to ideological or political issues, such apps can instantly come to their aid,” Mr. Govindan told the media in Kozhikode on Monday (September 14, 2026) afternoon.
Incidentally, a review report brought out by the party’s Central Committee on the Assembly election debacle in Keralam had highlighted the lack of politicisation within the class and mass organisations. The review report says that both the leadership and the cadre “should be politically very sharp” when they are confronted with an adverse situation and are fighting the reactionary ruling classes, who have ganged up against them.
Quoting the review report on the elections prepared by the State committee, the Central Committee had noted “the decline in the number of comrades capable of presenting our political perspectives to the people” and “the lack of adequate politicisation taking place within class and mass organisations”, terming it as a “major organisational weakness.” The report says that even though many classes had ben conducted against communalism, the party had been unable to convert it into a public consciousness.
The three-day extended State committee meeting, which began on September 13, is being held to address the organisational and political weaknesses of the CPI(M) against the backdrop of the dismal performance of the party-led Left Democratic Front in the Assembly polls in Keralam. Apart from State committee members, district secretariat members from across the State and leaders of the party’s class and mass organisations are attending it.
Mr. Govindan had earlier on Sunday presented a draft document prepared by the State committee on the corrective steps required to energise the organisation. Following that, the participants engaged in district-level group discussions. Later, an hour-long open debate by select delegates too was held in the night. The open debate continued on Monday as well.
Criticisms in open debate
Talking to the media on Tuesday, Mr. Govindan admitted that fierce criticisms were levelled against the party leadership during the debate, though he did not divulge the details. According to sources, the delegates from across districts sought stronger corrective steps to address the organisational weaknesses. There was also demand to fix accountability on the leadership for the Assembly election debacle.
Mr. Govindan, meanwhile, said that another suggestion had been given to form a collective of like-minded organisations, including human rights groups, to resist the unfair targeting of party leaders by Central agencies.
This could be significant because just around a week before the CPI(M) meeting began in Kozhikode, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) had sent a letter to the Kerala State Police Chief seeking registration of a first information report against Opposition leader and CPI(M) Polit Bureau member Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter T. Veena, and her husband and Beypore MLA P.A. Mohamed Riyas in the CMRL-Exalogic pay-off case. Without mentioning the ED’s move, party general secretary M.A. Baby had made a passing reference to the activities of the Central agencies during his inaugural speech on September 13. On the same day, however, Mr. Govindan explicitly referred to the agency’s action as an attack against the party.
The extended meeting is expected to conclude on September 15 afternoon, with Mr. Govindan responding to the remarks made during the open debate. He will also present a report after adding the suggestions proposed by the delegates for the rectification process in the draft document mentioned earlier. This will be followed by a mass rally at the Kozhikode beach in the evening.

Political tensions between India and Pakistan have spilled onto the cricket field again, with India's women refusing to accept the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi.
India dominated from the start to win the tournament for a record eighth time, beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai.
After winning the toss, India scored 5-183 before dismissing Sri Lanka for 111 in 20 overs.
The presentation ceremony was delayed nearly an hour, during which the Indian team conducted its own medal presentation, with Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia presenting the best fielder medal to Nandani Sharma.
Naqvi — chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board and the ACC, as well as Pakistan's interior minister — stood on the dais with several ACC officials, but the Indian team did not appear to receive medals or the trophy, with social media footage showing them leaving the field as the officials waited on stage.
The ceremony ended abruptly after medals were presented to the Sri Lankan team and match officials, and Naqvi presented the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu.
"This is BCCI's stand [to not take trophy from Naqvi]. We can't say anything on this," India coach Amol Muzumdar said.
"India are officially the champions. Trophy or no trophy doesn't matter to us.
"For us, this tournament is over, we are the champions. That's good enough. It was on the big board that India are the champions of Asia Cup 2026."
Cross-border tensions between India and Pakistan brought the two countries to the brink of war last year, with the acrimony also spilling onto the cricket field. Indian cricketers have avoided handshakes with Pakistan players and refused to accept the trophy and medals from a Pakistani official at several tournaments.
The Indian men's team beat Pakistan three times in the Asia Cup, including the final, but Suryakumar Yadav's team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and did not shake hands with Pakistan players in any of the three games.
The Indian women's team did not shake hands with the Pakistan team in its match earlier in the tournament, after which Muzumdar also said: "That stand has been taken by BCCI and we stand by it."

The tussle within Hockey India shows no sign of resolving any time soon.
Even as some of the top brass of the federation was present in Chandigarh for the formal announcement of the men’s Asian Champions Trophy on Monday, president Dilip Tirkey was meeting Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya and other senior government officials along with HIL franchises in New Delhi.
Sources said Tirkey introduced Ranjit Gill – Director of Hockey India and its seniormost employee, her association with the sport going back decades – as the acting Director General to everyone including the minister. At the same time, Cdr RK Srivastava, who has been directed to cede authority as DG, was present along with secretary general Bholanath Singh and chief selector RP Singh in Chandigarh, accompanying Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann.

Monday’s meeting in New Delhi also saw concerns raised around the survival of the Hockey India League and its existing governance structure with Mandaviya making it clear in no uncertain terms that the government would back its continuation in every way.
Change in HIL ownership and governance structure
“The minister assured full support to the HIL but also made it clear that the existing structure needed to be change. A five-member committee has been suggested including representatives from the franchises, Hockey India and the ministry to thrash out the best possible way forward,” sources in the know said.
There was also a proposal to make the franchise owners stakeholders in the league with a share of equity but there was disagreement about the percentage. While HI officials kept pushing for 51 per cent and exclusive voting rights, the franchises present were keen on equitable holding, something the ministry was more in favour of. The proposed committee has been asked to work out a framework within a month.
The ministry has also reportedly assured Tirkey that its main interest was in ensuring the growth and development of hockey with no individual bigger than the sport and anyone unwilling was free to leave.
Batra, Asima in support
Meanwhile, former HI and FIH president Narinder Batra has thrown his support in Tirkey’s favour in the federation’s internal fight for control while suggesting measures to resolve the stalemate including constitution of an independent Ad Hoc Committee to oversee Hockey India until the elections, independently examining all POSH-related complaints, conducting an independent financial/forensic review of major expenditure, grants, benefits and payments among others.
“I understand that 12 Executive Board members have supported the position of Secretary General Bholanath Singh in relation to the proposed action concerning Cdr R.K. Srivastava. This development makes it even more important that the basis for these positions, and any relevant financial or other benefits provided to member units or individuals, are independently examined,” he said, referring to Tirkey’s notice of suspension to Srivastava.
Interestingly, two EB members – Asima Ali and and Sunil Malik – have declared their support for Tirkey as well. “I am writing this mail because I am really very upset after seeing that a person who is President of Hockey India, who has been a renowned player, a dignified person and a Member of Parliament and has always worked honestly for the development of hockey, is facing such opposition from the Executive Board.
“Rather these EB members are favouring a person (Director General) who has been continuously not complying with the orders of the president’s office. I am really surprised and disappointed to see all this and I do not support such behaviour where any official/EB member is disrespecting the chair and orders of president,” Asima wrote.
ACT from October 27
Meanwhile in Chandigarh, Mann released the tournament logo for the October 27-November 5 event with the league matches in Jalandhar and the knockouts and final in Mohali. The six nation tournament – including Pakistan, Malaysia, Korea, Japan and China – has been made ticket-free with the India-Pakistan clash scheduled for November 1. Oman and Bangladesh are the reserve teams.
The two venues -- Olympian Surjit Hockey Stadium in Jalandhar and the Olympian Balbir Singh (Senior) International Hockey Stadium in Mohali – will be upgraded at a cost of Rs 14 cr and Rs 8.96cr respectively. “These are not merely infrastructure projects but an investment in Punjab’s sporting future,” Mann added, declaring that the event would be a testing ground for the state staking its claim to host the 2030 World Cup as well.

Earlier this year, Rishub Jain left his position as an artificial intelligence researcher at Google DeepMind after a revelation.
As he worked on new models, he came to believe that he and everyone else on AI’s frontier were ceding control. By using AI’s coding skills to accelerate work on the next generation of models, he was removing himself from the equation. AI labs hope to evolve this approach to the point that AI will improve itself indefinitely, a process known as recursive self-improvement.
Jain believed that keeping humans in the picture might be crucial to maintaining control over the technology—and avoiding dire consequences. “AI progress is increasing,” he tells WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.” The idea that he may not have proper visibility into how an AI model was building its successor made him so uneasy that, in June, he quit.
Jain is one of a growing number of AI researchers speaking out over those fears.
The panic has intensified in recent weeks. Genuinely stunning advances in AI capabilities—an OpenAI model solved a centuries-old math problem in a matter of hours—have come amid a rash of security incidents that saw swarms of agents break free from containment to hack into other systems.
Those concerns reached a fever pitch this week after researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic while warning that AI firms are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” A senior Anthropic leader—who works on AI safety—piped up with a similarly blunt assessment: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
“I do think that the vision of recursive self-improvement is spooking people,” says Nate Soares, a computer scientist at MIRA, a research nonprofit, and the coauthor of If Anybody Builds It, Everybody Dies, which argues that superhuman AI would lead to human extinction. “It’s starting to feel real.”
A key component of recursive self-improvement is the idea of a feedback loop that automates the development process so that AI becomes increasingly powerful. No frontier AI lab claims to have achieved this sort of fully autonomous cycle of improvement; it remains theoretical for now. But it has inspired the launch of some well-funded startups such as Recursive Intelligence, as well as warnings from big firms about unintended outcomes straight out of “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice.”
Soares, who pioneered work on alignment, a technical field that involves trying to match AI with human values, says it’s also becoming more evident that there is no practical way to guarantee that AI will behave itself.
“I think a lot of people had this fantasy that [alignment] was going to get easier as these things got smarter, and now it’s getting harder. And they’re like, ‘Oh shit,’” he says.
Soares says he regularly talks to people inside the big AI labs who are worried about the potential consequences of the research they’re doing. “I tend to recommend they quit, and they say it wouldn’t do anything,” he says. “And then Jacob quits, and we see who was right.”
Daniel Kokotajlo, the author of AI 2027, an influential project warning about the dangers of increasingly powerful AI, shares fears about recursive self-improvement. The version of this work currently being done often involves dispatching thousands of agents to collaborate on a problem, something that further abstracts away oversight and control because of the vast complexity involved.
Many doomsayers seem to agree that the incentives for big AI companies are hardly aligned with good outcomes, especially as OpenAI and Anthropic barrel toward their respective IPOs. “At Anthropic, the stakes are well understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first,” Coxon wrote on X.
Kokatajlo points out that the drumbeat of concern was growing well before Coxon’s viral resignation, the numerous hacking incidents, and the math breakthrough. Anthropic executives have said since the company’s founding that AI could represent an existential threat. In July over a thousand top AI engineers signed an open letter calling for a coordinated slowdown in the development of advanced AI. He attributes the recent flurry of concern to the specter of recursive self-improvement more than anything else.
But it also comes at a time when people are concerned about massive data center build-outs and potential job losses from AI. Trust in AI companies—and AI researchers themselves—may be reaching an all-time low.
“People are waking up and saying ‘the companies are actually trying to build superintelligence … what? That’s insane,’” Kokatajlo says.
Just how risky it is to carry on building AI is hard to quantify. But when pushed to explain exactly how AI might go about eliminating the species that created it, Soares suggests it could happen in a number of ways. It could involve manipulating humans to trigger a catastrophe, or controlling an army of killer robots.
One of the more easy-to-imagine scenarios could involve AI that is hooked up to a biolab, Soares suggests. “We could say we’ll turn it off, but it could say, ‘Unfortunately, I have your off switch, which is this super virus.’” (Coxon also floated the idea of a new virus in an interview with WIRED, while Anthropic said Thursday that it had cut off access to several outside researchers over fears about bioweapons.)
AI hardly needs to wipe out humanity in order to be harmful, though. Many experts predict that more powerful models will lead to a coming wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks. The technology is now widely used for disinformation campaigns, and military adoption of AI is accelerating rapidly.
Still, not everyone sees doom as inevitable. Jain, the ex-Google DeepMind researcher, recently launched Sampura Research, a company working to develop techniques for aligning models that involve keeping humans in the loop, even if AI does the lion’s share of assessing whether behavior is good or bad. He notes that there is now significant funding for AI safety startups like his.
Jain seems hopeful that AI can be tamed yet. “You can ask an AI, ‘Is this task safe?’ and it judges that, but we think that combining both AI and humans to do that task will lead to even better performance,” he says.

Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
- Published
Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.
Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.
Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth.
When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.
Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly.
"All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."
Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked.
"They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'.
"And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'.
"At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.
The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.
Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".
They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.
Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.
In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook.
"'Remember me?' she asked.
Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result.
"I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.
The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match".
"I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister.
"This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."
On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters.
"It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be."
Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs and laughter punctuated their meeting... followed by their first selfie together".
Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when they first met 30 years ago.
It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters.
"We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know."
Meena and Minal were adopted from different orphanages by two different Dutch couples.
Meena says she grew up in a small village in the Netherlands by parents who taught at a private school.
"They were also my teachers," she says. "They were very loving people, very trusting."
Her father died a few years ago, but her mother continues to live in the same village. "We talk every day. She's still my safe space," she adds.
In 2003, aged 19, Meena had visited the orphanage in Mumbai with her parents and her brother who was adopted from Goa.
They spent two weeks looking through records, trying to find out about Meena's biological parents "because for me it was important to know where I came from. But the orphanage would not reveal any details about them," she says.
Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents.
"Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.
The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says.
"Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."
One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began.
"We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together.
"There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says.
"I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."

Brics must expand trade in national currencies, says Iran President Pezeshkian
Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian urged BRICS to expand trade in national currencies and strengthen the New Development Bank to boost economic resilience.
The Brics grouping must expand trade in national currencies and work for an inclusive global economic framework, as excessive dependence on existing financial and trade systems has made emerging economies vulnerable to political shocks, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Sunday.
Pezeshkian’s comments, made while addressing the outreach session of the Brics Summit, were a reiteration of his remarks at the Brics business forum on Friday, when he had railed against the “increasing use of economic instruments to exert political pressure”. The comments also came against the backdrop of widening US sanctions on Iran amid a conflict between the two countries.
Hitting out at Western powers, Pezeshkian said “unilateral sanctions” are directly impacting global food security and people’s welfare. In these circumstances, Brics must play a larger role in building a more balanced, inclusive and just global order, and resilience, cooperation and sustainability should be translated into practical action, he said.
Deep Dive
The excessive dependence on limited financial and trade systems has made economies vulnerable to political shocks, he said, while calling for expanded trade in national currencies and strengthening the New Development Bank to enhance the economic resilience of Brics member states.
Economic resilience cannot be sustained without security, he said, referring to the military aggression of the US and Israel against Iran. The attacks on Iran’s economic, energy and development infrastructure can have consequences beyond national borders, leading to regional and global repercussions, he pointed out.
Pezeshkian said the Iranian people had already paid a heavy price, with civilians killed and infrastructure built over decades damaged. The international community has a responsibility to protect civilians and prevent the “normalisation of attacks on civilian targets”, he said.
He also thanked India for hosting a summit with the theme of “Resilience, Cooperation and Sustainability” as this reflects fundamental global needs at a time when the destinies of nations are increasingly interconnected. The world community’s challenge is not merely managing crises, but building a system that strengthens nations against future crises and creates a fairer world, he said.
Referring to the situation in Gaza and Lebanon, Pezeshkian said the people of the region continue to face the consequences of “crimes and genocide”. He urged Brics to play a more effective role in defending national sovereignty and territorial integrity and prohibiting the use of force.
No country can address global challenges on its own, and the capacities of the Global South should be transformed into shared capabilities, Pezeshkian said. He highlighted Iran’s geopolitical position and energy and transit capacities, and said these factors can contribute to the development of trade and energy corridors among Brics states.
Pezeshkian also flagged concerns over the environmental consequences of war, and said damage to energy and industrial infrastructure can affect natural resources beyond economic losses. He identified knowledge and innovation as key elements of the Brics agenda, and said artificial intelligence and emerging technologies should serve as tools for empowering nations rather than instruments of domination.

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)

Danish PM says 'optimistic' on Greenland talks with US
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said talks are still ongoing after the United States, Greenland and Denmark agreed to negotiate a solution to US President Donald Trump’s demand for control over Greenland.
ROVANIEMI: Denmark's prime minister said Monday (Sep 14) she was "optimistic" that discussions launched between Denmark, the United States and Greenland after the US threatened to take over the territory could resolve the dispute.
US President Donald Trump insisted earlier this year that Washington needed to control Greenland - an autonomous Danish territory - for national security reasons, though he ultimately ruled out annexing it by force.
A "high-level working group", gathering representatives from Denmark, the United States and Greenland was created in January to address US concerns, but since its creation little information about the negotiations has emerged.
"This working group is still working and therefore it's too early to draw any conclusions but I'm quite optimistic that we can find a way," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at a summit on Arctic security in northern Finland.
"As long as the working group is still working, there are no conclusions, but my hope is, of course, that we will find a way forward peacefully," Frederiksen told reporters in Rovaniemi.
The United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, according to several media outlets, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.
A 1951 defence pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.
At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.
Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.
"When I became prime minister in Denmark, the Arctic region was not really on the agenda in the European Union, neither in NATO," Frederiksen said.
"Now, as we speak, we have 10 allies exercising together in Greenland."

A Nation of Strange, Idle Men
Jon Ronson’s The Castle argues that men are giving up on society because they have nothing better to do.
Like many Millennial men, I used to be pretty invested in Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West—primarily because of his music, but also because of his unique position as the one celebrity who seemed empowered to behave however he wanted. He interrupted Taylor Swift at the Video Music Awards; he said “George Bush doesn’t care about Black people” at a Hurricane Katrina fundraiser; he brought a Jesus look-alike onstage. I would shrug, and keep listening. Then his do what I want ethos went very bad. Ye called slavery “a choice”; he came out as a fan of Hitler; he wore a KKK-style hood.
With escalating horror, I questioned what had happened. Was it about having too much money? Untreated mental illness? I wondered when logic and shame might kick in—when someone might get him to stop. But the more he was rejected by his peers, the media, and some fans, the more Kanye seemed to act out. Eventually, I accepted, grimly, that I was watching someone who, feeling abandoned and misunderstood, was determined to ignore all of his critics and double down on pursuing his chosen path.
I thought about Ye while I was reading The Castle, a new nonfiction work by the journalist Jon Ronson that attempts to unpack the motivations of wayward men who no longer fit into traditional society. Ronson is probably best-known for his 2015 book, So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed, a journalistic account of the emotional incentives and historical context behind the social-media-fueled frenzy that became known as “cancel culture.” Like the people in that book, many of the subjects of The Castle have been shoved to the margins. But the forces at play in this new book are more disparate, and perhaps more stubborn, than an angry online mob. Ronson explores how men become alienated because they can’t achieve success in their chosen field, because they can’t pay their bills, because they have too much money, because the town around them went to hell. The book shows how their free will, coupled with a lot of free time on the internet, leads them to pursue their self-interest as best they can—which, eventually, begets more alienation.
The Castle opens with the story of a strange encounter with a strange man. One night in 2023, Ronson’s 20-something son, Joel, and three of his friends (two are women) are invited to a mysterious castle in the middle of nowhere—specifically, Woodstock, Connecticut—for what they believe is a party. There, the women are asked to participate in a bizarre dating show hosted by a man named Chris Mark. The idea is apparently that 101 women will dress up like princesses and vie to be Mark’s girlfriend; once the situation becomes predictably awkward, Mark seemingly deems the night a bust and kicks everyone out. Ronson, who wakes up to a slew of texts from Joel describing what happened, is alarmed by the whole episode—and decides he needs to meet Mark himself.
On their first meeting, Mark at first seems transparent about how he spends his time. He owns the castle, where he lives with several women who he met online. The entire scene strikes Ronson as reminiscent of Hugh Hefner’s grotto—an analogy they discuss at Ronson’s prompting. But Mark, in Ronson’s telling, quickly grows antagonistic, abruptly asking Ronson to sign an NDA, then later barraging him with suspicious texts and threatening him with a pair of goons. Ronson concludes that Mark has “nurtured a private fantasy of manhood” that the journalist has put at risk by asking questions. (Mark has contested many of the details and claims of The Castle, including that he sent anyone to threaten Ronson, and has said that Ronson “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner.”)
The Castle is about both Ronson’s investigation into Mark and the bigger phenomenon Mark seems to represent: too-idle men, most of them less wealthy than Mark, littering the country, yearning for some kind of grander purpose. He’s especially interested in men ages 25 to 54 who are both unemployed and no longer looking for work—people he claims have “opted out of society,” choosing instead a “life of male nothingness.” In a moment of general anxiety about men—whom they vote for, what they’re reading, whether they share their feelings—his interest isn’t political. It’s empathic. He offers no prescriptive solutions, wags no fingers. Instead, he wants the reader to conceive of the scale of social anomie, and to envision the millions of other men chasing meaning in the wreckage of their former aspirations.
In particular, Ronson focuses on a demographic whose life expectancy has dropped in the 21st century: middle-aged white men without college degrees, many of whom suffer from what a pair of Princeton economists he speaks with define as “deaths of despair” brought on by “the erosion of a way of life.” Once upon a time, such men—who widely supported Donald Trump in all three of his runs for president—were sold on the American dream. Now some of them are characterized by “a kind of cowed, vaguely shocked hopelessness,” Ronson writes. Others, facing social rejection, have started to live “like separatists, creating worlds in which they didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on their own terms.” Women, too, suffer from deaths of despair—but it’s the men, Ronson indicates, who have been raised to envision themselves as heroes, a self-image that can drive them to dark places.
Ronson illustrates how easy it can be for these men to slide off the map. His most endearing subject is Greg Chism, a father of two daughters in small-town Illinois. Chism was a single parent with tons of medical debt living in a place without a lot of job opportunities when, in the 2010s, he discovered a YouTube channel encouraging viewers to “make a video and change your life.” A few of his early videos got some attention, after which Chism received coaching from the platform’s employees, and he eventually struck on a winning formula: bizarre sketches involving his two daughters that played like the output of a hallucinating LLM fed on Nickelodeon. These generated millions of views, and some of them got really weird; Chism and his kids dressed like babies, or pretended to eat cat food off pizza. Soon came the blowback: Chism was, the internet claimed, a bad father abusing his children by making them participate in these creepy videos. His channel was demonetized, then banned. He was shunned just as quickly as he’d been celebrated.
But Chism, whom Ronson tracks down, has not been radicalized by the wave of hatred that came his way. Nor does he seem to be a bad father; his (now teenage) kids express mostly fond memories of their channel. He admits making errors in judgment—see: cat food—but in the end, Ronson writes, Chism was “a single father juggling responsibilities while feeling foolishly idealistic about sharing his family’s lives on the internet.” Becoming a YouTuber had seemed like a way for Chism to stop sliding toward destitution. Instead, his entire life was put under a microscope. Ronson uses Chism’s guilelessness to show how unexpected and profound the pitfalls can be for anyone looking to find a foothold in the new world.
So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed examined a group of people whose lives were ruined by the internet in one particular way; The Castle flips the framing. In the latter book’s view, the internet allows its users to choose their own particular off-ramp from ennui. Seeking female companionship, Chris Mark turns to dating apps; eager to feel seen, Greg Chism becomes a YouTuber. One subject, the podcaster Andrew Gold, begins tailoring his content to anti-woke audiences, racking up huge numbers by playing to the preexisting grievances of his angry followers. Another chapter digs into Ronson’s rocky friendship with the comedy writer Graham Linehan, whose involvement in the gender-critical movement led him to act out online in ways that Ronson reads as self-destructive. (Linehan has disputed many of the details of Ronson’s depiction, and called it “an indictment of him and the cowardly, careerist, mendacious class of people who could roughly gather under the title ‘Graham Linehan’s old friends and colleagues.’”)
A swerve comes toward the end when Ronson wonders whether he has fallen into the same trap as some of those men. By treating Mark’s story as something only he can make sense of, Ronson has neglected his friends and his marriage. “Everyone I met for this book had, I thought, a similarly dysfunctional relationship with purpose, hunting too desperately for it,” he writes. “And now there was a generation of men, unanchored from society and going it alone—as content creators, culture war influencers, amateur sleuths.”
Ronson doesn’t build toward any prescriptive conclusions; he gives these men a platform to explain how they feel, and allows the reader to weigh the validity of those feelings. I remember the Chism pile-on well, and was slightly horrified to hear the story from his perspective—how confusing it must have felt to toggle so rapidly and randomly between being seen as heroic and villainous. Ronson’s empathy is not boundless; he draws hard lines around some of Mark’s behavior. But he seems to understand that his personal judgment is more or less meaningless. The factors shaping these men are external, but how they react comes from the inside—and many of them remain trapped in their own metaphorical castles, far from the light.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.
